limitations: No limitations section. The authors concede in the discussion that positive margin, one of the two most influential predictors, is not a usable preoperative selection criterion, and that extrahepatic disease, the other, must be regarded as a relative contraindication - so the two strongest factors are left out of the score

They concede that more sophisticated markers (tumour ploidy, oncogene and tumour suppressor expression) may stratify outcome further, and were excluded only because they are not widely available outside academic centres
The one-point-per-factor weighting was chosen for simplicity even though the relative risk of death differed across the five criteria

The survival advantage of resections of less than a lobe over a lobe or more is conceded to be partly explained by the higher perioperative mortality of the larger operations (4.1% vs 0.5%); the apparent effect of blood loss disappeared entirely once perioperative deaths were excluded (p=0.3)
Part of the fall in hospital stay from 13 days in 1986 to 8 days in 1998 is attributed to the administrative change of no longer admitting patients the day before resection
Bilaterality was dropped from the score because it was not significant and, as Blumgart states in the discussion, cannot be separated from tumour number and size

Blumgart states in the printed discussion that a score of 5 would not cause them to refuse resection to any patient, and that he does not know what to do with high-score patients; the published abstract names six criteria where the paper uses five
critique: The score was derived and assessed in the same 1001 patients with no split sample, bootstrap, calibration check or independent cohort. The discussion calls this 'attempts to validate this system using the largest single-institution experience', which describes derivation, not validation.

The score is not monotonic in the stratum it is used to triage: 5-year survival is 20% at score 3 but 25% at score 4, and median survival 20 months against 22 months (Table 5). The paper reports the figures and does not mention that the ordering fails.

The strata that anchor both ends hold 52 patients (score 0) and 14 patients (score 5). No confidence interval is given for any survival estimate anywhere in the paper, and the headline claim that no patient with a score of 5 survived 5 years is a statement about 14 people.

The comparison that justifies the score over tumour number alone is an r-squared computed across six group means (0.92) against one computed across three (0.80), with no test of the difference, no confidence interval, and groups ranging from 14 to 350 patients.
123 of 1001 patients (12%) had no preoperative CEA, one of the five score components, and the paper never states how they were scored or whether they were dropped from Figure 3 and Table 5.

The statistical method is given as one sentence - proportional hazards regression in True Epistat - with no statement of whether the model was stepwise or full, no test of the proportional hazards assumption, no collinearity diagnostics and no account of missing data. Iwatsuki raised exactly this in the printed discussion and the reply ('thank you for telling me what we should have done') did not answer it.

CEA above 200 ng/mL tracks tumour burden and a node-positive primary tracks the disease-free interval, so awarding each a separate point counts the same risk twice; only bilaterality was tested for redundancy and discarded, and the remaining four were not.

The four thresholds (>1 tumour, >5 cm, >200 ng/mL, <12 months) are used as though derived, but no cut-point analysis is shown. The 200 ng/mL CEA cut differs by nearly an order of magnitude from the 30 ng/mL in Nordlinger's score, which the paper cites approvingly two paragraphs earlier, with no reason given for the difference.

The cohort is the resected subset. Blumgart states in the discussion that 79% of patients taken to the operating room were resected, rising above 90% once staging laparoscopy was added, and nobody turned down before exploration is counted at all, so the score describes prognosis conditional on having been selected and resected at this institution.

Practice changed substantially within the series - trisegmentectomies rose from 13% to 31% of annual cases, intraoperative ultrasound became standard only in the last 6 of the 13 years - but no analysis by era is presented and the model is fitted across the whole period as if homogeneous.

Median follow-up of survivors was 32 months, shorter than the endpoints claimed. The 5-year (37%) and 10-year (22%) figures are actuarial with no numbers at risk printed on any curve; the only actual count given is 136 five-year survivors among the 551 patients resected before 1994.

88 patients with extrahepatic disease were resected and left in the denominator while extrahepatic disease is simultaneously declared a contraindication to resection, and 97 patients had an arterial infusion pump placed during an era when an MSKCC adjuvant hepatic arterial infusion trial was running (cited in abstract form as reference 20). Adjuvant therapy is recorded nowhere and adjusted for nowhere.

The 3 cm subgroup result offered as the benchmark any ablation trial must beat (median 56 months, 5-year survival 47% at score 0-2, n=236) is a post hoc subgroup of a selected surgical cohort, matched for nothing, and is the only place in the paper where resection is compared with ablation.

No separate editorial or comment on this paper was found in PubMed; the only independent published critique is the discussion printed with the article (Pitt, Beazley, Terblanche, Iwatsuki, Wanebo, Bismuth).
10493478.n: 1001 consecutive patients undergoing hepatic resection for metastatic colorectal cancer at Memorial Sloan-Kettering over 13 years (237 extended hepatectomies, 394 lobectomies, 370 resections of less than a lobe); 581 men and 420 women, median age 61, median 2 tumours and median size 4.2 cm; 123 had no preoperative CEA and 88 had extrahepatic disease
10493478.bottom_line: Establishes that resection of colorectal liver metastases at a high-volume centre yields 37% 5-year and 22% 10-year survival at 2.8% operative mortality, and that five factors knowable before operation separate that outcome from 60% to 14% at five years. It does not validate the score: it was derived and assessed in the same 1001 patients, its extreme strata hold 52 and 14 people, and survival is higher at a score of 4 than at 3. The two most influential predictors of death, a positive margin and extrahepatic disease, are deliberately excluded because they cannot be known preoperatively, so the score ranks patients a surgeon has already chosen rather than choosing them.
10493478.funding: Supported in part by NIH grants RO1CA76416, RO1CA72632 and RO1CA61524 to the first author; no conflict-of-interest or industry disclosure statement appears

limitations: The authors report that the whole Kaplan-Meier survival curves did not differ significantly (p=0.21 by log-rank, p=0.11 by Wilcoxon) and that the curves appear to converge at 80 months, where only six patients remain at risk so a single death moves the curve sharply
Only 55% of patients had been followed for five years, and the two-year endpoints were chosen because at design only 25% of such patients were disease free at two years

Dose adjustments for hepatic toxicity meant the total floxuridine delivered was less than planned in most patients, and the authors state they cannot tell whether a lower dose would suffice or whether a high first dose carried the effect
Systemic fluorouracil dose in the combined group was about 15% lower than in the monotherapy group

Pump-related complications were more frequent than in the centre's own earlier hepatic arterial infusion series, which the authors attribute to combining pump implantation with hepatectomy and to a learning curve, concluding that both procedures should be undertaken only by highly trained surgical and medical oncologists
Overall progression-free survival improved much less than hepatic progression-free survival, which the authors read as showing that other agents are needed alongside regional therapy

Twenty-one patients were found on later pathology to have positive margins and one positive portal nodes, and three combined-therapy patients were retrospectively found to have had metastases at entry; all were kept in the analysis, and the authors switched from reporting recurrence to reporting progression because of it
critique: The headline result is a landmark reading of curves that do not differ. The statistical plan states that the log-rank and Wilcoxon p values are the comparisons of the entire Kaplan-Meier curves, and those are 0.21 and 0.11; the 86% against 72% two-year survival difference (p=0.03) is taken off the same curves by normal approximation at a single timepoint. Both appear in the paper and only the second appears in the conclusions.

The sample size was computed with a one-sided test at an alpha of 5%, which is a two-sided alpha of 10%, and the paper then states that two-sided tests were used in the final analysis. The trial is therefore underpowered for the analysis it reports.

Two primary endpoints were declared - two-year overall survival and two-year progression-free survival - with no adjustment for testing both. Progression-free survival at two years gave p=0.07, and the curve comparison gave p=0.01 by Wilcoxon and p=0.06 by log-rank, two tests disagreeing about the same data with no prespecified rule for which governs.

The adjusted risk ratio that carries the survival claim (2.34, 95% CI 1.10-4.98) comes from a model chosen by best-subset selection in 156 patients, retaining primary tumour site and largest lesion size. A data-dependent search producing a significant covariate-adjusted effect, where the unadjusted comparison of whole curves is null, is not independent evidence.

The hepatic progression model adjusts for surgical margin status - a pathology finding that became known only after randomisation and that was positive in 21 patients - alongside disease-free interval, again in a selected model, to produce the relative risk of 5.39 (95% CI 2.36-12.31).

Only 156 of 386 resected patients (40%), and 156 of 514 evaluated (30%), entered the trial. Patients were randomised in the operating theatre by the team performing the resection, and no allocation concealment mechanism is described; 35 were excluded by surgeon decision and 16 judged not appropriate for the protocol.

Two different randomised comparisons are pooled. Patients with prior fluorouracil and leucovorin were initially excluded, then admitted under expanded criteria to a different pair of regimens (hepatic arterial infusion plus fluorouracil versus fluorouracil alone), and the results are reported as one trial.

What was delivered is not what was randomised. Only 26% of combined-therapy patients received more than half the planned floxuridine, 6 of 74 never received any hepatic arterial infusion at all, five died before any chemotherapy, and the systemic component was dosed about 15% lower in that arm. The comparison as executed is reduced systemic therapy plus partial regional therapy against full systemic therapy.

Device morbidity is substantial and is reported without being weighed against the benefit: 16 pump or catheter complications including 6 pocket infections, 2 early hepatic artery thromboses, a pseudoaneurysm and 3 pumps perfusing extrahepatic territory, with AST tripling in 65%, bilirubin above 3.0 mg/dL in 18%, four biliary stents, and 29 against 18 hospitalisations for toxicity (p=0.02).
No quality-of-life or patient-reported outcome was measured, in a trial of a surgically implanted pump whose dominant toxicity is biliary and whose benefit is claimed at a two-year landmark.

Salvage treatment ran against the combined arm and is unaccounted for: 46 against 33 patients received further chemotherapy and 9 against 1 underwent repeat liver resection in the monotherapy group. The analysis makes no allowance for this, in either direction.

The comparator and the staging are both obsolete: bolus fluorouracil with leucovorin as the only systemic therapy, no oxaliplatin, irinotecan or biological agent, no RAS or BRAF selection, and surveillance by three-monthly CT with no MRI or PET, in a cohort where 27% had four or more metastases.

This is one centre, one surgical team, and the authors themselves conclude the procedures require highly trained surgeons and medical oncologists - so the trial supports adjuvant hepatic arterial infusion only where such a team exists, a condition that the subsequent literature citing this trial as the basis for the approach generally does not state.

A linked comment and letter (PMID 11127528, Urbach and Hansen, Langenbecks Arch Surg 2000;385:436-9) was identified in PubMed but neither its text nor its abstract was available here, so no argument from it is reflected in this record.
10615075.n: 156 patients randomised intraoperatively at Memorial Sloan-Kettering out of 386 resected for colorectal liver metastases and 514 evaluated for resection (74 to hepatic arterial floxuridine plus systemic fluorouracil, 82 to systemic fluorouracil alone); 105 of the non-participants declined and 35 were excluded by surgeon decision. Median follow-up 62.7 months, with 91% followed at least two years and only 55% for five years
10615075.bottom_line: This is the single randomised trial on which adjuvant hepatic arterial infusion after liver resection rests, and what it shows is a large reduction in hepatic recurrence - two-year hepatic progression-free survival 90% against 60%, with 7 of 74 against 30 of 82 liver recurrences. It does not show a survival benefit by its own whole-curve analysis: the Kaplan-Meier comparison gives p=0.21, the positive survival claim is a two-year landmark, the trial was powered one-sided and analysed two-sided, and the adjusted hazard comes from a best-subset model. Only 26% of patients received more than half the planned floxuridine, 6 of 74 received none, and the combined arm got about 15% less systemic drug, so the regimen that produced this result is not the regimen described.
10615075.funding: Supported in part by National Cancer Institute grant R01 CA61524 for the study of therapies for hepatic metastases from colorectal cancer. No conflict-of-interest or industry disclosure statement appears; the implantable pump used was a single named commercial device (Infusaid model 400)

limitations: The authors name as a criticism of the study that the systemic arm received bolus fluorouracil and leucovorin, which was standard when the trial opened in 1996 but has since been superseded by regimens containing irinotecan, oxaliplatin or bevacizumab
They note the once-daily-for-five-days fluorouracil schedule used has subsequently been shown to be more toxic than infusional fluorouracil
They argue the systemic arm's 20-month median survival is comparable to newer combinations because patients progressing on fluorouracil could receive the newer agents afterwards
They note that adding concurrent systemic therapy with newer agents to hepatic arterial infusion might have improved the regional results, and that this would be the subject of future work
They address, and reject, the suggestion that this was an unusually favourable cohort, citing 79% synchronous disease and 70% with more than 30% liver involvement
critique: No limitations section exists, and no sample size calculation, power statement, interim analysis plan or stopping rule for the primary endpoint appears anywhere in the methods, in a trial of 135 patients reporting a 4.4-month survival difference at p=0.0034.

Multiplicity was controlled for the quality-of-life endpoints and not for efficacy. Four quality-of-life outcomes were judged against a Bonferroni-adjusted threshold of 0.0125, while thirteen baseline variables were tested against three time-to-event endpoints - roughly forty comparisons - with no adjustment at all, and the sex-by-treatment interaction (p=0.016) comes from that set.

By the paper's own prespecified threshold the quality-of-life claim fails: physical functioning differed at 3 and 6 months with p=0.038 and p=0.024, both above the 0.0125 level the statistical plan set. The abstract and conclusion nonetheless report better physical functioning with hepatic arterial infusion.

The survival result sits oddly with the progression data and the paper does not reconcile them. Overall time to progression was identical (5.3 against 6.8 months, p=0.95) and extrahepatic progression was significantly faster with regional therapy (7.7 against 14.8 months, p=0.029). A survival advantage with no delay in progression and worse extrahepatic control has no mechanism offered beyond hepatic control.

Post-progression therapy is the strongest non-treatment predictor of survival in the paper's own table (p=0.0014) and is handled by entering it as a covariate; what each arm actually received after progression is never tabulated, in a trial whose defence of its obsolete comparator is precisely that control patients got modern drugs later.

Thirteen percent of randomised patients (18 of 135) never received protocol treatment, three of them regional-arm patients with catheter problems, and seven patients later found to have had extrahepatic disease at entry were kept in the analysis.

Treatment intensity differed between arms in a way that is reported and not analysed: a median of three cycles of regional therapy against four of systemic therapy, in a comparison framed as the same drug delivered two ways - which it is not, since the regional arm received floxuridine with dexamethasone and the systemic arm fluorouracil with leucovorin.

The molecular marker analyses cannot support the predictive reading they invite: thymidylate synthase in 40 and p53 in 42 biopsies, all from regional-arm patients, with no systemic-arm comparison, and the headline survival difference by thymidylate synthase level non-significant at p=0.17.

Biliary toxicity is the real price and is not weighed against the 4.4-month gain: bilirubin above 3 mg/dL in 18.6% against 0%, grade 3 or worse alkaline phosphatase in 33.8% and transaminase elevation in 27% of regional patients, four biliary stents, and a sex difference in biliary toxicity (men 38%, women 15%) that mirrors the sex difference in survival benefit without being linked to it.

Nine centres accrued 135 patients over five years, under three per site per year, and no centre-level or operator-level analysis is reported for an intervention requiring laparotomy, pump placement and continuing hepatobiliary management.
Cost was a stated secondary endpoint and no cost result is reported.
Internal inconsistencies: grade 3 or worse neutropenia is 2% in the published abstract and 0% in the Results, and biliary toxicity in men is 37% in the abstract and 38% in the Results.
No linked editorial or comment on this trial was found in PubMed, so no independent published critique informs this record.
16505413.n: 135 patients with unresectable liver-only colorectal metastases occupying less than 70% of the liver, randomised at nine sites between January 1996 and December 2000 (68 to hepatic arterial floxuridine with leucovorin and dexamethasone through an implanted pump, 67 to systemic bolus fluorouracil and leucovorin); 59% male, 79% synchronous, 70% with more than 30% of the liver involved. Eighteen patients (nine per arm) never received protocol treatment, and the median number of cycles delivered was three with hepatic arterial infusion and four with systemic therapy
16505413.bottom_line: Establishes that hepatic arterial floxuridine with dexamethasone beats bolus fluorouracil and leucovorin in unresectable liver-only colorectal metastases on survival (24.4 against 20.0 months, p=0.0034), hepatic response (47% against 24%) and systemic toxicity, at the cost of biliary injury in a third of patients and faster extrahepatic progression. It cannot establish regional therapy against modern systemic treatment: the comparator is a 1996 regimen the authors themselves call superseded, overall time to progression was identical, the trial reports no power calculation or interim plan, and the quality-of-life advantage fails the paper's own Bonferroni threshold. Its molecular marker work is single-arm and non-significant.
16505413.funding: Supported in part by National Cancer Institute grants to CALGB (CA31946), ECOG (CA23318), the CALGB Statistical Center (CA33601) and the participating centres. The disclosure table is garbled in this text extraction, but the article states that some authors or their immediate families indicated a financial interest; the pump used was a single commercial device

limitations: The sensitivity analyses in eligible and in resected patients, which are the analyses that reached significance, were not protocol-specified, although the authors state they were decided before data analysis

Counting unresected patients as events, as the protocol required, inevitably dilutes the observed treatment difference in any analysis that includes them; all such events were assigned to week 10 to avoid bias from the different timing of surgery between arms
The authors note a possible selection bias: fewer chemotherapy-arm patients failed resection because of extensive disease but more failed because of refusal or poor condition
The trial was not designed to separate preoperative from postoperative chemotherapy, and previous trials had shown a trend favouring postoperative treatment only

Whether oxaliplatin-induced vascular liver lesions compromise the safety of subsequent surgery is stated to be unknown; the authors note the risk rises with more than six preoperative cycles and that they gave only six
Inference about overall survival is explicitly deferred to longer follow-up

The primary endpoint analysis was released early: a stopping boundary for efficacy was added at 6.5 years because events had not accumulated as expected and, in the authors' words, the pressure from the medical community to have the results disclosed was very strong
critique: The trial missed its primary endpoint as randomised: progression-free survival HR 0.79 (95.66% CI 0.62-1.02), p=0.058. Significance is obtained only after excluding patients found ineligible (p=0.041) or restricting to those resected (p=0.025), and the Interpretation then states the regimen reduces the risk of progression-free survival events in eligible and resected patients - a conclusion phrased in terms of the two sensitivity populations.

The resected-patient analysis conditions on an event that occurred after randomisation and was influenced by the allocated treatment, which the authors acknowledge indirectly by noting the reasons for non-resection differed between arms. It is not a randomised comparison.

The headline analysis was triggered by a stopping rule invented mid-trial. The protocol required 278 events; at 6.5 years they had not accrued, a boundary was added using a gamma-family alpha spending function, an interim analysis at 235 events was shown only to the data monitoring committee, and the data were updated and released for an ASCO deadline at 254 events. All confidence intervals in the paper are therefore 95.66% rather than 95%.

What the trial tested is not what its title claims. Of 182 patients allocated perioperative chemotherapy, 143 of 171 completed six preoperative cycles but only 115 (63%) started postoperative chemotherapy and 80 (44%) completed it. The comparison delivered is six preoperative cycles plus whatever could be given afterwards.

Chemotherapy produced no increase in resection: 83% against 84%. In a trial of neoadjuvant treatment for resectable disease this is the most important negative result and it appears without comment on what the preoperative component was for, beyond progression-free survival.

More chemotherapy-arm patients were never operated on at all (22, 12%, against 8, 4%). Since non-resection was counted as an event at week 10, the arm that lost more patients to non-operation was penalised at a fixed early timepoint rather than at the time the decision was made - a convention that cuts both ways and is never examined in a sensitivity analysis.

The surgical cost is real and is argued away rather than weighed: reversible complications rose from 16% to 25% (p=0.04), driven by biliary fistula (8% vs 4%), intra-abdominal infection (7% vs 2%) and hepatic failure (7% vs 5%), one resection was abandoned for macroscopic chemotherapy liver injury, and the authors state they believe this moderate increase does not compromise the potential benefits.

Progression on preoperative chemotherapy in 12 patients (7%), four of whom became unresectable from new lesions, is reinterpreted as a biological marker of poor prognosis with the assertion that immediate surgery would not have benefited them - a counterfactual claim about four patients, made without data.

The population is the most favourable end of the disease: one to four metastases, no extrahepatic disease, half with a single lesion. The Discussion suggests the findings would probably hold in higher-risk patients, which the trial cannot support.

Progression-free survival was assessed on imaging in an unblinded trial, with no independent central radiology review described, and the authors note that the gap between imaging and surgical findings is the principal reason patients turned out unresectable.
No quality-of-life result is reported, in a trial adding twelve cycles of oxaliplatin-based chemotherapy around a major hepatectomy in patients who are candidates for cure.

Overall survival data existed - 139 deaths, 64 against 75 - and inference was deferred; the 2013 long-term report of this trial (also in this depot) found no survival difference, so the endpoint released early under community pressure was the only one that ever favoured the regimen.

The manufacturer of the trial drug supplied it free, funded an educational grant, had two named staff responsible for the trial at the company, and eight authors declare relationships with it, in a trial whose positive result exists only in non-prespecified populations.

Two linked items were identified in PubMed - Kopetz and Vauthey's Comment (PMID 18358910, Lancet 2008;371:963-5) and correspondence from Snoeren, Voest and van Hillegersberg with the authors' reply (PMID 18640447, Lancet 2008;372:202-3) - but their texts were not read for this record.
18358928.n: 364 patients aged 18 to 80 with one to four potentially resectable colorectal liver metastases and no detectable extrahepatic disease, recruited at 78 hospitals in 11 countries between October 2000 and July 2004 and assigned 1:1 to perioperative FOLFOX4 (182) or surgery alone (182); 52% had a single metastasis and 65% metachronous disease, 303 were resected (151 and 152), and 139 patients had died at this report
18358928.bottom_line: Establishes that six cycles of FOLFOX4 before and six after hepatectomy for one to four resectable colorectal liver metastases is deliverable, with a 7.3-point gain in three-year progression-free survival that did not reach significance as randomised (HR 0.79, p=0.058) and reached it only among eligible (p=0.041) and resected (p=0.025) patients. It does not show the regimen converts anyone - resection rates were 83% against 84% - and it does not show survival benefit, which the same trial later reported as absent at 8.5 years. The analysis was released early on a stopping boundary added mid-trial under acknowledged external pressure, only 44% of patients completed the postoperative half, and complications rose from 16% to 25%.
18358928.funding: Sponsored by the EORTC, with grants from the Swedish Cancer Society, Cancer Research UK, the Ligue Nationale Contre le Cancer and the US National Cancer Institute, and support from Sanofi-Aventis, which supplied oxaliplatin free of charge and gave an educational grant; two named Sanofi-Aventis staff are acknowledged as responsible for the trial at the company. Design, management, analysis and interpretation were done at EORTC headquarters independently of commercial interest. Eight authors declare consultancy, advisory, lecture or research relationships with Sanofi-Aventis

limitations: The authors state that median survival of 20.5 months reflects the unfavourable prognostic features of the cohort, that the risk of death as a first event was therefore high, and that the local control estimate may be artificially exaggerated because death and local failure are competing events

They argue against this using the favourable-primary subgroup (median survival 32 months, 2-year local control 97%), which they take to show local control was not substantially influenced by the competing risk
They state that differences in baseline prognostic features between this cohort and most surgical series limit any comparison between stereotactic radiotherapy and resection

They note that one grade 3 soft-tissue event six months after treatment prompted revised skin and soft-tissue dose constraints mid-study, and that a recommended soft-tissue dose-volume limit remains under investigation
They report that 13 of 49 patients were treated below the phase 2 dose of 60 Gy during escalation
critique: Local control was scored only in the 49 of 63 lesions (78%) with at least six months of imaging. Eleven patients were unassessable, five because they died before six months and two because records were lost after Hurricane Katrina. Excluding lesions in patients who died early from a local control estimate removes precisely the lesions most likely to have failed, and the 95% figure is quoted without that denominator.

The competing-risk argument the authors use to defend their estimate is circular: they appeal to the favourable-primary subgroup, which by definition has fewer early deaths and is also the subgroup with the best control, so the comparison cannot separate longer survival from better local control.

The pooled local control figure mixes dose levels across a phase 1 escalation and a phase 2 expansion, 36 Gy to 60 Gy in three fractions, and the dose-response claim rests on a within-cohort comparison (94% at 60 Gy) with no formal dose-response analysis. The linked JCO letter asks exactly this - whether a definitive regimen has been established.

Only 15 of 47 patients (32%) had colorectal metastases, and no colorectal-specific local control or survival figure is reported. The paper is routinely cited as evidence for stereotactic radiotherapy in colorectal liver metastases and does not contain that number.
Analysis is per lesion (49 lesions in 36 patients) with no clustering by patient, so patients contributing two or three lesions count repeatedly in the control estimate.

Every patient's first progression included a distant component, 83% progressed distantly at a median of six months, and median progression-free survival was 6.1 months. A local control rate of 92% at two years in a disease that progresses elsewhere within half a year describes the technique's reach, not a clinical benefit, and the paper does not report what that control bought.

Low-burden extrahepatic disease was permitted and present in 45% at entry, so the cohort is not the liver-confined population in which local therapy is being considered, and the survival figure (20.5 months overall, 12 months for unfavourable primaries) is not transferable to it.

Late toxicity is almost certainly underestimated: with median survival of 20.5 months and a median follow-up of 16 months for assessable lesions, hypofractionated doses to 60 Gy in three fractions have not been observed long enough for biliary stricture, chest wall or soft-tissue sequelae to declare themselves, and the one grade 3 event already forced a constraint change.

No radiation-induced liver disease occurred in a trial whose entry required at least 700 mL of normal liver below 15 Gy and lesions under 6 cm, so the safety result is conditional on a geometry that excludes the large or central tumours where the question is hardest.

The comparison the authors acknowledge they cannot make is the comparison that matters: these lesions were small (median 2.7 cm) and many would have been resectable or ablatable, and no surgical or ablative comparator exists in the trial or in the literature it cites.
Internal inconsistency: Table 1 gives the maximum lesion diameter range as 0.4 to 6.8 cm while the abstract gives 0.4 to 5.8 cm, against a protocol limit of under 6 cm.

A linked letter (PMID 19581532, Mirabel, 'Have we established a stereotactic body radiotherapy regimen for liver metastases?', J Clin Oncol 2009;27:e40, with the authors' reply at e41) was identified in PubMed but its text was not read for this record.
19255321.n: 47 patients with 63 liver metastases of mixed primary origin treated at seven US institutions between 2003 and 2007 (colorectal 15, lung 10, breast 4, ovarian 3, oesophageal 3, hepatocellular 2, other 10); one to three lesions under 6 cm, median maximal diameter 2.7 cm, 69% with at least one prior systemic regimen for metastatic disease and 45% with active extrahepatic disease. Thirteen patients were treated to less than 60 Gy during dose escalation and 36 to 60 Gy; 49 lesions in 36 patients were assessable for local control at a median follow-up of 16 months
19255321.bottom_line: Establishes that 60 Gy in three fractions to one to three liver metastases under 6 cm is deliverable with almost no high-grade toxicity and gives in-field control of 95% at one year and 92% at two, with 100% control for lesions of 3 cm or less. It establishes nothing about benefit: there is no comparator, every patient's first progression included a distant site, median progression-free survival was 6.1 months and median survival 20.5 months, local control was scored only in the 78% of lesions whose patients lived six months, and the authors concede that competing risk may inflate it. Only 15 of 47 patients had colorectal primaries and no colorectal-specific result is given, so the paper supports the technique's local efficacy in small lesions and not its place against resection or ablation.
19255321.funding: Supported in part by an American Cancer Society IRC / University of Colorado Cancer Center Seed Grant Award. The only declared interest is research funding to the senior author from the American Cancer Society; no employment, consulting, stock, honoraria or industry relationships are declared

limitations: The authors state that resection rates cannot be compared across trials because criteria for defining unresectable disease, the actual reasons for unresectability and the proportion of previously treated patients all vary

They conclude that a multi-institutional randomised trial comparing the best systemic chemotherapy with or without hepatic arterial infusion is needed to establish whether the pump increases resectability
They note that the high response rate may be due to the use of three active agents rather than to regional delivery
They report that previously treated patients did significantly worse than chemotherapy-naive patients (median survival 35 against 50.8 months, p=0.02)

They note that male patients had significantly more biliary toxicity in their earlier randomised trial, and that in this study no difference in dose or toxicity explains the sex difference in resection rate
critique: This is a single-arm phase I experience with no comparator, so the 47% conversion rate cannot be apportioned between the pump, full-dose triplet systemic therapy, portal vein embolisation, intraoperative ablation and the surgical aggressiveness of one high-volume unit. The authors say as much in calling for a randomised trial, and the result is nonetheless the foundation of the conversion claim for hepatic arterial infusion.

Resectability was adjudicated at a multidisciplinary conference by the surgeons who then performed the resections, in a study whose only endpoint is a change in that adjudication. No blinded or external re-review of the baseline imaging is described.

Conversion is a surrogate that this study shows does not deliver: median disease-free survival after R0 resection was 7.6 months (95% CI 5.2-12.9). Half the resected patients needed portal vein embolisation (12 of 23), ten needed intraoperative ablation and four were planned two-stage procedures, so the operations counted as conversions were mostly incomplete-by-resection-alone clearances followed by early recurrence.

Only 19 of 49 patients (39%) achieved an R0 resection, and three of those were pathological complete responses - that is, patients in whom no tumour remained to resect. The headline 47% includes R1 and R2 resections.

Response was scored by WHO-type criteria (50% reduction in the sum of products of diameters) rather than RECIST, which inflates the 92% response rate relative to any modern trial and makes the comparison with systemic-therapy series the paper draws inadmissible.

The female-sex finding (81% against 30% resected, p=0.002) emerged from a univariate scan of baseline variables in 49 patients with no multiplicity correction, is unexplained by dose or toxicity in this study, and is supported only by a consistent subgroup in the same group's earlier randomised trial - which was itself one of roughly forty unadjusted comparisons.

Two phase I schedules with different cycle lengths are pooled, and 22 of the 49 patients had already been published, so this is a partially overlapping update rather than an independent cohort - a point the paper does not make in its abstract.

The denominator excludes failures of the technique: seven of 55 candidates never reached protocol therapy because of hepatic artery stenosis, extrahepatic perfusion on the macroaggregated albumin scan or complications of the primary resection, so the pump's own failure rate is outside the reported conversion rate.

Hepatobiliary toxicity is reported only for the first two cycles of one schedule (alkaline phosphatase grade 3-4 in 15% and 11%, AST 19%, bilirubin 4%, diarrhoea 33%), with three later biliary stents attributed to progression rather than to therapy, so the cumulative biliary cost of the regimen is not quantified.
Resected livers showed mild to moderate steatosis in 67%, reported without any analysis of its relation to the two postoperative complications or to remnant function after embolisation.

Survival is measured from pump placement, which conditions on having had a pump successfully implanted and perfusing, and all survival figures are reported with a median follow-up of 26 months against medians of 35 to 51 months.

The regimen is not transferable as described: floxuridine and the implantable pump are unavailable in much of Europe, and the protocol requires a dedicated interventional and hepatobiliary service, with no centre-level or learning-curve data offered.
No linked editorial or comment on this paper was found in PubMed, so no independent published critique informs this record.
19470932.n: 49 patients with technically unresectable colorectal liver metastases treated at Memorial Sloan-Kettering on two pooled phase I schedules of hepatic arterial floxuridine and dexamethasone plus systemic oxaliplatin and irinotecan; 53% had received prior systemic chemotherapy, 73% had more than five lesions, 98% bilobar disease, 86% involvement of six or more segments and 90% a Fong score of 3 or more. Twenty-two of the 49 were previously reported in the 4-week-schedule phase I paper. Median follow-up 26 months
19470932.bottom_line: Shows that in genuinely extensive, mostly bilobar and half-pretreated unresectable colorectal liver metastases, hepatic arterial floxuridine with full-dose systemic oxaliplatin and irinotecan produces a 92% response rate and takes 47% of patients to an operation, with median survival of 39.8 months from pump placement. It does not show the pump is responsible, and it shows the conversions are fragile: there is no control arm, response was scored by pre-RECIST criteria, only 39% reached R0, half the resected patients needed portal vein embolisation and ten needed intraoperative ablation, and median disease-free survival after R0 resection was 7.6 months. Its own authors conclude that a randomised trial of systemic therapy with or without hepatic arterial infusion is what is needed.
19470932.funding: No funding statement appears; financial support is attributed to the senior author. Four authors declare honoraria from sanofi-aventis, one of them also from Pfizer, and the same author declares research funding from Pfizer and sanofi-aventis

limitations: Accrual was lower and follow-up longer than planned, so the trial closed with 46 of the intended 58 patients; the design assumed 90% power for a time to liver progression of 6 weeks in the control arm
The authors attribute the absence of a survival difference to rapid crossover: 70% of control patients received further therapy, including 10 who received radioembolization at similar activity
They state that the RECIST response rate of 9.5% was disappointingly low and that CT-based RECIST is known to be difficult for assessing response after radioembolization

They note that more grade 3 toxicity in the fluorouracil arm was probably due to lower efficacy and more rapidly progressive disease, since the events were indistinguishable from progression, and that fluorouracil dose intensity was non-significantly higher in that arm
They state that a proper assessment of the effect on survival would require randomised comparison against best supportive care, which they consider unrealistic to complete
They note the whole-cohort median survival of 8.7 months exceeds what is usually reported for refractory disease, which may reflect patient selection
critique: The primary endpoint is the one a liver-directed treatment cannot fail to move, and the control arm's own data show why: every control patient progressed first in the liver, so time to liver progression and time to any progression are the same curve in that arm. The trial measures where progression was detected, not whether the disease was controlled.

The only hard outcome is uninterpretable by the trial's own account. Survival was 10.0 against 7.3 months (HR 0.92, 95% CI 0.47-1.78), and the explanation offered is that 70% of controls received further therapy including 10 who crossed over to the same treatment. That is a design decision, not a confounder discovered afterwards.
Forty-four analysed patients cannot support any survival conclusion in either direction; the confidence interval spans a 53% reduction to a 78% increase in the hazard of death.

The comparator is protracted intravenous fluorouracil monotherapy in patients already refractory to fluorouracil, which is close to no active treatment, and the authors use the resulting toxicity difference (6 against 1 grade 3-4 events) as a safety argument for radioembolization while simultaneously attributing those events to disease progression.

Response was assessed by local radiology in an unblinded trial, and the paper's response to its own low RECIST response rate is to argue that RECIST is the wrong measure and that FDG-PET should be preferred - while conceding PET was not cross-calibrated between the three centres.

The disease-control figure that carries the clinical message (86% against 35%, p=0.001) is the sum of partial response and stable disease, and in a refractory population stable disease on a single unblinded CT is a weak endpoint.

Two randomised patients were excluded from efficacy - one for bone metastases, one for technical failure of microsphere administration - and the technical failure is precisely the kind of event an intention-to-treat analysis should retain in a trial of a procedure.
Baseline tumour burden differed substantially (median summed diameter 216 against 176.5 mm) in a 44-patient trial with no adjustment reported for it.

The single downsizing to resection is reported as a conversion and the same patient progressed extrahepatically 1.5 months after the operation; it is offered in support of future conversion studies without that outcome being weighed.

The trial predates and excludes most modern therapy: anti-EGFR and anti-VEGF agents were largely unavailable in Belgium during recruitment and only 12 of 44 patients had received an anti-EGFR antibody, so this refractory population is less pretreated than a refractory population today.

The conclusion that radioembolization should be considered a valid therapeutic option rests on a surrogate endpoint in 44 patients with no survival signal, and the device manufacturer funded the trial and supplied the microspheres.
No quality-of-life or patient-reported outcome is reported, in a trial whose claimed benefit is tumour growth control without a survival difference.
No linked editorial or comment on this trial was found in PubMed, so no independent published critique informs this record.
20567019.n: 46 patients with unresectable liver-only colorectal metastases refractory to or intolerant of fluorouracil, oxaliplatin and irinotecan, randomised at three Belgian centres between December 2004 and November 2007 against a planned 58; 44 were analysed (23 fluorouracil alone, 21 radioembolization plus fluorouracil) and 43 assessed for toxicity. Median sum of target diameters 216 mm in the control arm and 176.5 mm in the experimental arm; only 12 patients had received prior anti-EGFR therapy. Median follow-up 24.8 months
20567019.bottom_line: The first randomised evidence for yttrium-90 radioembolization in chemotherapy-refractory liver-only colorectal metastases: a single hepatic arterial injection added to fluorouracil lengthened time to liver progression from 2.1 to 5.5 months (HR 0.38) and raised disease control from 35% to 86%, with no added toxicity. It shows no survival benefit (10.0 against 7.3 months, HR 0.92) and cannot: accrual stopped at 46 of 58 planned patients and 70% of controls received further therapy, 10 of them crossing over to radioembolization. The primary endpoint was progression in the organ being treated, in an arm where every patient progressed there first, and the comparator was fluorouracil monotherapy in fluorouracil-refractory disease.
20567019.funding: Supported by Sirtex Medical Limited, which supplied the yttrium-90 resin microspheres; one author declares honoraria from Sirtex Medical. No other interests are declared

limitations: The authors name as a criticism of the study that the systemic comparator was FOLFIRI, because the trial was planned in 2005 when FOLFIRI was standard second- or third-line therapy and biological agents were not widespread; they acknowledge that adding oxaliplatin, bevacizumab, cetuximab or panitumumab increases survival over FOLFIRI alone
They state that concurrent systemic therapy with newer agents in the chemoembolization arm might have improved its results further
They state the study serves to establish the expected difference between the two options in order to plan future large randomised studies
They report that time to extrahepatic progression was similar in both groups
critique: The paper is internally inconsistent in places that bear on its conclusions: the extrahepatic progression p value is 0.064 in the abstract and 0.64 in the Results, the quality-of-life p value is 0.00002 in the abstract and 0.0002 in the Results, and enrolment closes in December 2008 in the Methods but October 2008 in the Results.

The design was powered to detect a 40% increase in median survival at two years in a two-centre trial, and 74 randomised patients produced a reported 7-month median survival gain with p=0.031. An effect of that size from a sample of this size, in a journal of this profile, with no independent verification, is the definition of a result requiring replication - and the authors say as much.

The two arms differ in intensity and duration as well as route: 70 procedures (two per patient, a month apart) against 277 FOLFIRI cycles capped at eight over four months, after which systemic patients had no protocol therapy while chemoembolization patients could be retreated. The comparison is of two treatment programmes, not of two delivery routes for irinotecan.

Six stratification factors are listed for a 74-patient trial - liver involvement, prior irinotecan, weight loss, CEA, KRAS status and p53 immunohistochemistry - which in a sample this small cannot balance and is not accompanied by any adjusted analysis.

The trial was open label, and response was scored by either RECIST or EASL criteria at investigator discretion - two different response definitions applied within one trial, in the arm where an embolic effect changes enhancement.

Quality of life was measured by a symptom scale while chemoembolization patients received prophylactic morphine, steroids, antiemetics and antibiotics around each procedure, so the reported eight months against three months of preserved quality of life compares a premedicated arm with an unmedicated one.

Grade 2 to 3 pain occurred in 30% of chemoembolization cycles and liver enzyme elevation above three times normal in 58%, with bilirubin rises in 18%; this hepatic cost is reported and then set aside in favour of the systemic toxicity comparison, which naturally favours a locoregional treatment.

The KRAS finding - 26 against 14 months and a major response in 14 of 14 wild-type patients - comes from a subgroup of a 35-patient arm with no multiplicity control, and would be remarkable if true for a treatment whose mechanism is local drug delivery and embolisation.

The suggestion that chemoembolization also delays extrahepatic progression, offered as evidence of systemic activity, rests on a non-significant difference (13 against 9 months) whose p value is printed two different ways, and contradicts the biology of an intrahepatic embolic therapy.

Post-progression therapy is invoked to defend the survival result - both arms are said to have had access to new drugs at progression and the difference to remain attributable to treatment - with no table of subsequent therapy by arm and no analysis supporting that attribution.
No funding or conflict-of-interest statement appears anywhere, in a trial of a commercially manufactured device, which makes the sponsorship of this result unverifiable.
The cost comparison (8,000 against 20,000 euro) is presented without any formal cost-effectiveness analysis, discounting, or accounting for the salvage therapy each arm went on to receive.
No linked editorial or comment on this trial was found in PubMed, and no subsequent randomised work has reproduced a survival advantage of this magnitude for chemoembolization in this setting.
22493375.n: 74 patients randomised of 144 evaluated at two Italian centres from December 2006, all with metachronous unresectable liver-only colorectal metastases occupying less than 50% of the liver after two or three previous lines of chemotherapy (36 to irinotecan-loaded drug-eluting bead chemoembolization, 38 to FOLFIRI); 35 per arm were treated, and liver involvement was 25% or less in 52 of 74. Seventy chemoembolization procedures were delivered against 277 FOLFIRI cycles. Median follow-up 50 months
22493375.bottom_line: Reports the largest survival advantage for any liver-directed therapy in this depot - median overall survival 22 against 15 months, hepatic response 68.6% against 20%, and quality of life preserved for 8 against 3 months - from irinotecan-loaded bead chemoembolization against FOLFIRI in heavily pretreated liver-only disease. The result should not be relied on: 74 patients at two centres, powered for a 40% survival difference, open label with investigators free to score response by RECIST or EASL, a comparator the authors concede was obsolete and capped at four months while the experimental arm could be retreated, p values that differ between abstract and results, and no funding or conflict statement anywhere. The authors' own framing is that the trial exists to size a larger one, and no larger trial has reproduced it.
22493375.funding: No funding, sponsorship or conflict-of-interest statement appears anywhere in the paper, in a trial of a commercial drug-eluting bead device

limitations: The trial was designed to detect a progression-free survival benefit and was not powered upfront for overall survival, which was a secondary endpoint

The surgery-only group did much better than assumed - 3-year progression-free survival 28.1% against the 21% predicted at design, and median overall survival 73.3 months among resected patients - which the authors say made a treatment benefit harder to show

Chemotherapy at first progression was given more often in the surgery-only group (77% versus 59%, p=0.0029); the authors state the reason is unclear and that data on treatments for second and later progressions were not obtained systematically

More patients in the chemotherapy group died of causes other than progression, protocol treatment or surgery (15 versus 10), which the authors suggest could have contributed to the absence of a survival difference
The 8.5-year analysis timepoint was not prespecified in the protocol but was a compromise based on the number of deaths reachable with the accrued sample size

The authors note that trials of this size cannot answer the survival question in this disease and that future progress will probably have to rely on surrogate endpoints such as progression-free survival or pathological response
critique: The not-powered-for-survival defence does not fit the authors' own arithmetic. Their post hoc calculation states that at least 194 deaths were needed for 80% power to detect a 10-point gain in 3-year survival; 221 deaths were observed. The trial therefore had the power it says it lacked for a difference of that size, and found an absolute 5-year difference of 3.4% with a 95% CI of -7.1 to 13.8.

The progression-free survival result that the whole recommendation rests on was released early under non-statistical pressure. The protocol required 278 events; at 6.5 years the events had not accumulated, so a stopping boundary for efficacy was implemented after the fact, an interim analysis at 235 events was shown only to the data monitoring committee, and the results were released for ASCO 2007 because - in the paper's own words - the pressure from the medical community to disclose was very strong.

Statistical significance for progression-free survival exists only in a sensitivity population. In all randomised patients the updated hazard ratio is 0.81 (95% CI 0.64-1.02, p=0.068); it reaches 0.78 (0.61-0.99, p=0.035) only after excluding the 22 patients found ineligible after randomisation. The Interpretation nonetheless states that FOLFOX4 should remain the reference treatment.

The case for the regimen is made by analogy rather than from the data: the 3.4% to 4.1% absolute survival difference is set beside MOSAIC's 4.2% at six years, a result that was statistically significant in 1347 patients. The paper argues that because a similar-sized difference was decisive in a trial five times larger, a non-significant difference here should be treated as real.

The conclusions are explicitly stated as belief rather than inference - the Research in Context panel says that although the results were not statistically significant, the authors believe perioperative FOLFOX4 should be the reference treatment, and the Discussion says they believe patients are likelier to receive chemotherapy if it is given before surgery. Neither claim is tested anywhere in the paper.

The excess non-cancer deaths with chemotherapy are used to explain the null result rather than examined as possible harm. The cause-of-death table shows 4 cerebrovascular accidents against 0 and 4 cardiac deaths against 2 in the chemotherapy arm, with 15 versus 10 other deaths in total, in a trial of a vascular-toxic drug.

The competing-risk and cancer-specific survival analyses said to show a trend favouring chemotherapy are reported in one sentence as not statistically significant, with the figures confined to the appendix, so the strongest version of the authors' case cannot be checked by a reader of the paper.

Post-progression management - the determinant of overall survival in this disease - was recorded only for first-line therapy at progression. Repeat surgery (40% versus 46%), radiotherapy (2% versus 9%) and symptomatic treatment (6% versus 11%) all differ between arms, and everything after the first progression is unrecorded.

The systematic review supporting the Research in Context panel searched PubMed only to December 1999 and Embase only to December 1999, in a paper published in 2013, so the evidence context offered alongside the long-term result is 14 years out of date and identified three trials.

Eligibility was narrow and favourable in ways that bound the result: one to four metastases, no extrahepatic disease, age 80 or under, and 52% with a solitary lesion. There is no central radiology review described, resectability was judged by local multidisciplinary teams, and the trial predates RAS and BRAF selection entirely, so neither the population nor the regimen choice maps onto current practice.

Twenty-two randomised patients (11 per arm) were found ineligible and 60 (30 per arm) were never resected, yet the paper's favoured analyses move between randomised, eligible and resected populations - with median survival of 61.3, unreported and 77.5 months respectively in the chemotherapy arm - without a single prespecified hierarchy saying which answers the question.

The maker of the trial drug supplied it free and gave an educational grant, and six authors declare relationships with that company, in a trial whose null primary-population result is nonetheless presented as supporting continued use of that drug.

A linked Lancet Oncology comment by Fong (PMID 24120479, 'Chemotherapy and resection for colorectal metastases', 2013) was identified in PubMed but its text was not available here, so its objections are not reflected in this record.
24120480.n: 364 patients aged 18 to 80 with one to four resectable colorectal liver metastases and no detectable extrahepatic disease, randomised at 78 hospitals in Europe, Australia and Hong Kong between October 2000 and July 2004 (182 per group); 171 per group were eligible and 152 per group were resected; 188 of 364 (52%) had a single metastasis. At a median follow-up of 8.5 years there were 221 deaths and 29 patients lost to follow-up
24120480.bottom_line: Establishes that adding six cycles of FOLFOX4 before and six after hepatectomy for one to four resectable colorectal liver metastases does not prolong life: at 8.5 years median survival was 61.3 versus 54.3 months, HR 0.88 (95% CI 0.68-1.14, p=0.34), with a 3.4% absolute difference at five years whose interval spans 7 points of harm to 14 of benefit. It does not establish the progression-free survival benefit that the authors use to keep recommending the regimen - that reaches significance only after excluding patients found ineligible after randomisation, and its original report was released early on a stopping boundary added mid-trial under acknowledged external pressure. The surgery-only arm lived a median 73.3 months after resection, which is the most useful number in the paper.
24120480.funding: Sponsored by the EORTC, with an educational grant from Sanofi-Aventis and grants from the Norwegian and Swedish Cancer Societies, Cancer Research UK, the Ligue Nationale Contre le Cancer and the US National Cancer Institute; Sanofi-Aventis also supplied oxaliplatin free of charge. EORTC headquarters states that design, management, analysis and interpretation were done independently of any commercial interest. Six co-authors declare consulting, advisory or research relationships with Sanofi-Aventis, the maker of oxaliplatin

limitations: This is an interim analysis closed for protocol-defined futility with only 123 of 212 required events (58%); the authors argue that further follow-up is unlikely to change the direction and that this analysis is the most accurate reflection of the intervention because all cetuximab was stopped on 1 November 2012

Some patients are excluded from the primary analysis for not having reached the assessment timepoint by that date, and others because retrospective testing showed KRAS mutation; the authors state these exclusions were balanced between groups
The regimen two and three chemotherapy backbones contained too few patients to detect or refute interactions, and too few patients received irinotecan to draw any conclusion about that combination

No biological mechanism for the detriment is identified; the authors state that a clear understanding is needed before any further neoadjuvant cetuximab study and that translational studies are in progress

They state that outcomes from a neoadjuvant strategy are difficult to extend to adjuvant treatment or advanced disease because of confounding inherent in the strategy, mainly surgery and the associated treatment interval

They note that KRAS exon 2 selection was insufficient to identify a benefiting cohort, and that BRAF and NRAS mutations are unlikely to explain inferior progression-free survival in patients who responded
No formal systematic review was undertaken, because the authors state only one adequately powered trial in this setting exists
critique: The primary result is an interim estimate at 58% of planned events, and the paper's defence - that further events are unlikely to change the outcome - was only partly borne out: the 2020 long-term report of this trial found the progression-free survival difference no longer significant (HR 1.17, 95% CI 0.87-1.56), while survival was worse with cetuximab.

The futility rule that closed the trial required the lower bound of the 95% CI for the progression-free survival hazard ratio to exceed 1, and the observed interval was 1.04-2.12. The trial stopped at the moment the interval cleared 1 by 0.04, which is the point of maximum play in a small number of events.

The accrual target was revised downward during the trial, from 340 to 268 patients, on the trial steering committee's suggestion after the CRYSTAL presentation; 257 were randomised and the efficacy analysis rests on 236 of them.

The analysis population is defined by a post-randomisation condition: patients had to have reached the timepoint for perioperative response assessment by the data cut, which in a trial where one arm progressed faster is not a neutral filter, and no sensitivity analysis including all randomised patients is reported.

Three chemotherapy backbones were permitted by physician choice, and the protocol changed twice during the trial - capecitabine dose reduced in 2007, then capecitabine with cetuximab withdrawn in 2010 after COIN toxicity data - so the comparator and the experimental regimen both changed while the trial ran.
Progression was determined by the local multidisciplinary team with no external or blinded radiological review, in an open-label trial whose only endpoint is radiological progression.

The subgroup analysis that carries the paper's interpretation - harm concentrated in good-prognosis patients - rests on nine minimisation factors and predefined subgroups in 236 patients, with intervals such as node-negative primary HR 2.09 (1.07-4.10) and non-synchronous presentation HR 2.33 (1.40-3.90). No interaction test or multiplicity adjustment is reported, and the authors themselves describe the surrounding subgroups as underpowered.

Response and progression-free survival move in opposite directions and this is reported as a methodological aside rather than examined: responders on cetuximab had median progression-free survival of 14.1 against 20.5 months (HR 1.52, 0.95-2.44), which the paper summarises as a poor association between progression-free survival and response - in a trial whose endpoint is progression-free survival.

Overall survival was immature and non-significant (HR 1.49, 95% CI 0.86-2.60), with the control-arm median not reached, so at this analysis the trial could not say whether the regimen shortened life; it took the 2020 report to show that it did.

Harm cannot be attributed to toxicity or to surgery, as the authors state, and no alternative is tested: three possibly treatment-related respiratory deaths with cetuximab against one cardiac death without, grade 3-4 overall toxicity 47% against 40%, and major postoperative complications 16% against 23% - fewer in the cetuximab arm.

Selection was by KRAS exon 2 only, with no NRAS, BRAF, mismatch repair or primary tumour sidedness data, so the population is not the one in which anti-EGFR therapy would be used today and the trial cannot say whether the harm would recur under modern selection.

Fourteen randomised patients turned out to be KRAS mutant or indeterminate on retrospective testing and were removed from the efficacy analysis, in a trial whose eligibility criterion was that mutation status.
No quality-of-life result is reported, and no patient-reported outcome, in a trial that found a treatment to be actively harmful.

The maker of the trial drug supplied it under a medical grant and reviewed the report, and eight authors declare relationships with it - which here works against the usual direction of concern, since the finding is unfavourable to that drug.

Two linked items were identified in PubMed - Fong's Comment (PMID 24807857, Lancet Oncol 2014;15:544-5) and correspondence from Hasegawa, Oba and Kokudo with the authors' reply (PMID 24988931, 24988933) - but their texts were not read for this record.
24717919.n: 257 patients with KRAS exon 2 wild-type, resectable or suboptimally resectable liver-only colorectal metastases randomised at UK centres between 2007 and 2012 (chemotherapy with or without cetuximab); the modified intention-to-treat efficacy populations were 117 and 119 patients who had reached the perioperative assessment timepoint, 198 were operated and 178 resected. Analysis to 1 November 2012 at an overall median follow-up of 20.7 months, with 123 of the required 212 progression events (58%)
24717919.bottom_line: The first trial to show that adding cetuximab to perioperative chemotherapy harms patients with operable KRAS exon 2 wild-type colorectal liver metastases: median progression-free survival 14.1 against 20.5 months, HR 1.48 (95% CI 1.04-2.12), with no gain in response, resection or margin and with the detriment falling on good-prognosis patients and on responders. It does not establish the size of the harm or its mechanism: the trial stopped for futility at 58% of planned events with the confidence interval having just cleared 1, overall survival was immature and non-significant, progression was judged locally in an open-label trial, and the authors could exclude toxicity and surgical quality as explanations without offering a replacement. The practical conclusion - do not use cetuximab here - was confirmed by the 2020 survival report, which also found this progression-free survival difference no longer significant.
24717919.funding: Funded and supported by Cancer Research UK with National Cancer Research Network support; cetuximab was provided under a medical grant from Merck KGaA, which reviewed the report. Data were held and analysed by the University of Southampton Clinical Trials Unit. Eight authors declare advisory board membership, honoraria or research funding from Merck or Merck Serono

limitations: The authors state that the retrospective, single-institution design makes universal application of the modified clinical risk score and of the findings questionable, and that randomised studies are desirable but unlikely

They state that actual margins cannot be assessed after ablation because no tissue is available, so radiological margin measurement is a less precise alternative, and that histopathological evaluation of the target tumour before ablation and of the ablation zone afterwards was absent

They state that the modified clinical risk score lowered the Fong size cut-off to 3 cm and the CEA cut-off to 30 ng/mL to describe this population, because only four patients had a CEA above 200, and that points were grouped into three risk levels because of the smaller sample
They state that validation of the score in larger studies is necessary
They note that patients treated for liver recurrence received mostly percutaneous radiofrequency ablation but a few had other treatments
critique: The margin finding that the paper is cited for is measured by subtracting pre- from post-ablation landmark distances on CT, and was impossible in a quarter of tumours (59 of 233), including fused defects. The margin-stratified recurrence figures (90% at 0 mm down to 5% beyond 10 mm) therefore come from 174 tumours selected by whether the measurement could be made, and fused defects - the hardest cases - are systematically absent.

The hazard ratio of 9.9 (95% CI 4.9-20) for a margin of 5 mm or less is a within-cohort association between a radiological measurement and radiological recurrence, both read on the same scans by the same service, with no pathological confirmation of either the ablation zone or residual tumour.

The before-and-after comparison around November 2009 - margins above 5 mm rising from 24% to 61% and local recurrence falling from 62% to 28% - attributes to immediate triple-phase CT a change that is inseparable from nine years of operator learning, improving CT and evolving systemic therapy. No concurrent control exists for the period effect.

The modified clinical risk score was rederived in the same cohort it is tested in, with two of its five cut-points moved to fit this population, and the resulting high-risk group holds 11 patients for survival and 20 tumours for local progression. It is apparent performance in the derivation sample with thresholds chosen after seeing the data.

Fifty-seven percent of patients (93 of 162) had already been reported in earlier publications from the same institutional database, so this series is not independent evidence of the earlier findings it extends.

Local tumour progression occurred in 113 of 233 tumours (48%) at a median follow-up of 55 months, which sits awkwardly with a technique effectiveness of 94% at the 4 to 8-week scan. The two numbers measure different things and the abstract leads with the first.

Survival is uninterpretable without a comparator in a cohort this heterogeneous: 72% were post-hepatectomy recurrences, the remainder unresectable, medically unfit or declining surgery, 31% had extrahepatic disease, and patients also received systemic therapy, hepatic arterial infusion and occasionally yttrium-90, none of it accounted for in the survival models.

The repeat-ablation survival comparison (65, 51 and 22 months for no progression, re-ablated progression and no longer an ablation candidate) is confounded by immortal time and by the reasons patients stop being candidates; the paper presents it as evidence that repeat ablation preserves survival.

Analysis moves between patients and tumours without clustering: local progression is analysed per tumour (233 tumours in 162 patients) with patients contributing up to several lesions, and no random effect or robust variance is described.

Nine operators performed the ablations with 70% of them by three, so the results describe a small number of high-volume interventional radiologists, and no operator-level analysis is offered in a paper whose central claim is that technique - margin creation - determines outcome.
Complications are counted per session (minor 16%, major 7% of 188 sessions) rather than per patient, which understates the cumulative burden in a cohort treated repeatedly.
One author declares grants and a consultancy with device and imaging companies as related to this article, in a paper recommending a technical change in how ablations are monitored.
A Results line prints 'margin 5 mm or greater' as a predictor of shorter local progression-free survival, which is a typographical error contradicting the abstract and the multivariate table.
No linked editorial or comment on this paper was found in PubMed, so no independent published critique informs this record.
26267832.n: 162 consecutive patients with 233 colorectal liver metastases (median diameter 1.8 cm) treated by CT-guided percutaneous radiofrequency ablation at Memorial Sloan-Kettering between December 2002 and December 2012, from 184 screened; 72% had already undergone hepatectomy, 51 (31%) had extrahepatic disease at ablation (lung only in 29), and nine operators performed the procedures with 70% done by three. Margins were measurable in 174 of 233 tumours (75%) and the modified risk score analyses used the 153 of 162 patients (94%) with a recorded CEA. Median follow-up 55 months
26267832.bottom_line: The clearest demonstration available that percutaneous radiofrequency ablation of colorectal liver metastases succeeds or fails on margin: local recurrence falls from 90% with no margin to 5% beyond 10 mm, and tumours over 3 cm do badly (median local progression-free survival 6 against 30 months). It also shows the technique's limit - 48% of 233 tumours progressed locally over 55 months despite 94% technique effectiveness at the first scan - and that survival of 36 months reflects a mixed cohort of post-hepatectomy recurrences, unresectable disease and refused surgery, with no comparator. The margin data come from the 75% of tumours in which margin could be measured, with no pathology, and the risk score was rebuilt and tested in the same 162 patients.
26267832.funding: Supported by National Institutes of Health grant R21 CA131763-01A1. One author declares institutional grants from GE Healthcare and AngioDynamics and a consultancy with GE Healthcare as activities related to the article; another declares an Amgen grant unrelated to it; all other authors declare no relevant relationships

limitations: The panel states outright that no strong evidence exists to support its central recommendation of chemotherapy first rather than colon resection first, and that three randomised trials addressing it were ongoing

The supporting LiverMetSurvey comparisons are conceded to be confounded: 5-year survival was no better with chemotherapy first than with primary surgery first (42% vs 47% in resectable disease, 31% vs 33% in unresectable), which the panel attributes to surgery-first having been reserved for patients with less widespread disease and the best prognosis

The meta-analysis cited as showing a survival benefit from resecting the asymptomatic primary when metastases are unresectable is described as questionable because of potential publication bias in non-randomised trials, and the randomised trials started to answer the question mostly closed early for poor accrual
ALPPS is reported only as increasing complications and mortality, with overall and long-term survival data still needed
The optimal resection margin width remains to be determined, and no biological marker has been identified that distinguishes synchronous from metachronous metastases
Burgundy registry survival figures are flagged as needing cautious interpretation because they cover 1976 to 2000
Some panel members were not present for the whole meeting and some abstained from voting on questions outside their area of expertise
critique: No systematic search is described. Meta-analyses, trials and practice studies were identified and circulated by the coordinator, with no databases, dates, search terms or selection criteria given, so the evidence base behind every graded recommendation is unreproducible.

Grade A in the Strength of Recommendation Taxonomy means consistent, good-quality, patient-oriented evidence, yet grade A is attached to recommendations that rest on nothing more than the panel's own vote - the nomenclature of synchronicity (question 1), the sequencing in a symptomatic primary (question 5), and that one-stage resection is riskier than staged (question 8), for which no comparative trial is cited anywhere in the text.

The 12-month cut-off adopted for early versus late metachronous disease is contradicted by the panel's own supporting figure: LiverMetSurvey showed no significant survival difference between metastases detected at diagnosis and those detected up to 6 months or 6 to 12 months afterwards, and a significant difference only beyond 12 months. The paper reports both and adopts the threshold regardless.

Voting denominators shift from question to question without explanation - 14 of 15, 10 of 11, 9 of 12, 8 of 12, 9 of 11, 2 of 11 - because members left or abstained, so 'complete agreement' in some scenarios means agreement among as few as 11 of the 15 named panellists.

The Delphi method, voting rules and the threshold that counts as consensus are relegated to Appendix 1; the main text gives only 'approved by all or a large majority', with no prespecified agreement percentage, no round structure and no record of how disagreement was resolved.

Two substantive claims are sourced to 'personal communication, Aimery de Gramont' from the GERCOR database - that response rates are higher in liver-limited disease, and that second-line response is independent of first-line response - unpublished data from a panel member that no reader can check.

LiverMetSurvey, the registry that supplies every supporting figure, is coordinated by the first author. Figures 2 to 5 carry no patient numbers, no confidence intervals and no p values, and the registry contains only patients who reached liver resection, so every strategy comparison is conditioned on having survived to surgery.

Where the registry numbers point the other way they are explained away rather than allowed to weigh: one-stage resection gave 5-year survival of 40% against 47% for liver-first and 44% for primary-first, and the reverse-approach advantage (42% vs 33% vs 28%) is described as supporting the recommendation despite not being statistically significant.

The meeting was funded by EXCEMED and the manuscript written with sponsor-funded medical writers, while the operative recommendations - six months of perioperative chemotherapy for everyone, at least four cycles of first-line doublet or triplet plus a biologic, response assessment every two months - all increase drug exposure. Merck Serono appears in ten of the fifteen disclosure statements.

The recommendation against targeted therapy after R0 resection of both sites carries grade A, but no randomised evidence is cited in that section; New EPOC, the trial that had shown cetuximab to shorten survival in exactly this population, is not discussed where the recommendation is made.

The six-month total duration of perioperative chemotherapy is stated three times as a recommendation with no supporting randomised comparison of durations in this population; the figure is carried over from adjuvant colon cancer practice without saying so.

A 1 mm margin is 'suggested as sufficient' on a single reference, two sentences after the same paragraph states that the optimal margin width remains to be determined; the qualifier is dropped when the sentence reappears as a consensus recommendation.

There is no limitations section and no statement of the limits of consensus methodology, no plan for updating, no external review, and no patient, methodologist, statistician or health economist on a panel of fifteen clinicians.
No linked editorial or comment on this consensus was found in PubMed, so no independent published critique informs this record.
