26417845.bottom_line: Fixes a usable vocabulary for synchronously detected colorectal liver metastases and sets out a defensible default sequence for four clinical scenarios, including that resection should not be withheld from patients merely stable after optimal chemotherapy. It does not establish that any of its sequencing recommendations improves survival: the panel concedes no strong evidence supports chemotherapy before colon resection, and the registry data it cites show survival no better, or slightly worse, with the strategies it recommends. Read it as a statement of what fifteen sponsor-convened experts would do in 2015, not as evidence about what works.

limitations: Only 84% of patients allocated to SIRT received it per protocol: 21 of 267 (7.9%) never received SIRT and 19 of the 246 treated had bilobar disease treated in one lobe only. The authors attribute this partly to randomising patients before assessing their suitability for SIRT and call the proportion unexpectedly high
Around 45% of patients had an intact primary tumour, which the authors did not anticipate, associate with inferior survival, and say had an uncertain impact on the primary endpoint
Ten control patients (3.8%) withdrew consent after randomisation and may have received SIRT off protocol while remaining in the intention-to-treat control analysis
Progression-free survival in the liver has not been evaluated in any other study, so the authors state there is no comparator to put their result in context

Overall survival was a secondary outcome, and during the seven-year recruitment period the authors decided to defer it to a preplanned pooled analysis of SIRFLOX, FOXFIRE and FOXFIRE Global because improving systemic therapy had made this trial's survival analysis inadequately powered

critique: The trial missed its primary endpoint - progression-free survival at any site, 10.2 against 10.7 months, HR 0.93 (95% CI 0.77-1.12), p=0.43 - and the abstract, conclusion and subsequent citation of this trial all rest on a secondary analysis of hepatic progression that the authors acknowledge has no precedent and no validation as a surrogate for anything.

The competing-risk framing of liver progression-free survival removes exactly the events that went against the intervention. Progression outside the liver is treated as a competing risk, and progression outside the liver is what increased: lung-only first progression rose from 7.3% to 23.5% and non-liver-only first progression from 7.9% to 27.7%, both p<0.001. The analysis that produces the 7.9-month gain is the analysis that discounts the harm.

The explanation offered for that shift - that lung progression was destined to occur in patients receiving a liver-directed intervention - is an assertion with no supporting analysis, and it is incompatible with the trial's own null result for progression at any site.

The endpoint a liver surgeon cares about did not move: resection rates were 36 of 263 (13.7%) against 38 of 267 (14.2%), p=0.857, despite liver response rising from 68.8% to 78.7% and complete response from 1.9% to 6.0%. The paper's own explanation, that most patients were unresectable because of lesion number and could never become resectable, means the population was chosen such that the response gain could not translate.

The trial was designed for an effect roughly three times what it found: the sample size assumed median progression-free survival rising from 9.4 to 12.5 months, and the observed difference was 0.5 months.

The significance threshold shifts between analyses without a rule. The methods state that unplanned exploratory analyses use p<0.01, yet liver response (p=0.042) and complete response in the liver (p=0.020) are reported as significant findings, and the site-of-progression analysis - which is where the paper's interpretation comes from - is not identified as prespecified or exploratory.

Microspheres were implanted a median of 20 days after randomisation, with a range out to 76 days, so part of the experimental arm's early follow-up is chemotherapy alone; this is not accounted for in any time-to-event analysis.

Roughly 40% of patients had extrahepatic disease, permitted by protocol as up to four small lung nodules or nodes in one area under 2 cm, in a trial of a liver-directed treatment whose primary endpoint is progression anywhere.

Table 3 prints total grade 3 or worse adverse events of 198 of 270 (73.3%) against 210 of 246 (85.4%) with p=0.516, a p value that cannot correspond to that difference in those denominators, and the near-doubling of grade 5 events (1.9% against 3.7%) is dismissed on p=0.279. Toxicity unique to the intervention - 9 gastric or duodenal ulcers, 7 ascites, 3 hepatic failure, 2 radiation hepatitis, all zero in the control arm - is described as anticipated and manageable.

Bevacizumab was optional in both arms and was not randomised, so a drug that materially affects progression-free survival varied by physician choice within each arm and is handled only as a subgroup in an appendix forest plot.

The trial was open label and the primary endpoint was imaging-based; the main text describes an assessment process to determine final outcome but does not establish independent blinded central review of progression, in a trial where one arm's patients have radiologically altered livers.

The sponsor is the device manufacturer, two of its employees are authors, it funded the medical writing, and most senior authors declare payments from it, in a trial whose negative primary endpoint was reported alongside a positive secondary endpoint that the same group invented for this trial.

The survival question the authors defer to the pooled analysis was answered negatively: the combined FOXFIRE, SIRFLOX and FOXFIRE Global report (Wasan 2017, also in this depot) found no survival benefit, so the one endpoint that could have justified the hepatic progression finding did not confirm it.

A linked letter (PMID 27621405, Ayoola and Ibraheem, J Clin Oncol 2016;34:4193) questioning whether liver progression-free survival is a valid surrogate was identified in PubMed but its text was not read for this record.
26903575.n: 530 chemotherapy-naive patients with non-resectable liver-only or liver-dominant metastatic colorectal cancer randomised at 87 centres in Australia, Europe, Israel, New Zealand and the United States between October 2006 and April 2013 (263 control, 267 SIRT); 246 received SIRT but only 84% received it per protocol, roughly 45% had the primary tumour in situ and about 40% had extrahepatic disease
26903575.bottom_line: Establishes that adding a single yttrium-90 resin microsphere treatment to first-line FOLFOX in unresectable liver-dominant colorectal cancer does not delay progression overall (10.2 against 10.7 months, HR 0.93) and does not convert any additional patient to resection (13.7% against 14.2%), while adding ulceration, ascites, hepatic failure and a doubling of grade 5 events. Its one positive finding, hepatic progression-free survival of 20.5 against 12.6 months, comes from a competing-risk analysis that treats as a competing risk the extrahepatic progression which the intervention made more common, and the pooled survival analysis the authors deferred to was subsequently negative. Read as a liver-metastasis paper, it is the clearest demonstration in this depot that better liver control without survival or resectability gain is not a benefit.

limitations: The authors state that all subgroup analyses are inherently limited, and that prospective data from well controlled studies are needed to confirm the observations

They note that early tumour shrinkage is a less clear marker than depth of response because early treatment discontinuation for toxicity can prevent a patient from reaching maximum shrinkage, and that minor or slow responders fall into the no-shrinkage group and may still benefit from continuing therapy
They note that early tumour shrinkage was measured at 6 weeks here against 8 weeks in CRYSTAL and OPUS, complicating cross-trial comparison of the magnitude of effect
They note that depth of response is retrospective in nature because its definition includes progression on first-line therapy, and occurs about 3.5 months after starting treatment
Patients whose imaging modality changed from CT to MRI, or whose baseline imaging predated randomisation by more than 28 days, and those without assessable scans, were excluded - leaving 330 of 400
Early tumour shrinkage and depth of response are reported as correlating almost perfectly (correlation index 0.96)
critique: Every load-bearing measurement is post hoc. The trial's prespecified primary endpoint was investigator-assessed response, which was negative (65.3% against 58.7%, p=0.18), as was progression-free survival (10.3 against 10.2 months, p=0.77). Early tumour shrinkage, depth of response, duration of response and time to response were all added afterwards, and the central radiological review was commissioned after the survival difference was already known.

The central review changed the result in one arm and not the other. Investigator-assessed response was 65.3% with cetuximab and central review made it 72.0%, while progression-free survival on central review moved numerically in favour of bevacizumab (8.4 against 9.7 months, HR 1.08). An ascertainment pattern that raises response only in the arm with better survival cannot be distinguished here from a real difference.

The analysis defeats its own surrogacy argument: among patients who achieved early tumour shrinkage, survival did not differ between the arms (HR 0.87, p=0.48). If shrinkage were the mechanism of the survival difference, equalising it should not equalise survival between regimens unless shrinkage is simply a marker of tumour biology - which the authors themselves then propose when they call it a general hallmark of treatment sensitivity.

Early tumour shrinkage and depth of response correlate at 0.96, so they are not two confirmatory findings but one measurement reported twice, and both are reported alongside multiple time-to-event and burden analyses with no multiplicity control in a post-hoc framework.

The two surrogates predicted survival in both arms with almost identical hazard ratios (0.52 on cetuximab, 0.49 on bevacizumab), which is what a prognostic marker does. Nothing in the paper establishes that acting on shrinkage - switching or intensifying treatment in a non-shrinker - improves anything, and the authors concede slow responders sit in that group.

Duration of response (4.7 against 4.6 months) and time to response (5.2 against 5.4 months) were identical, so the proposed mechanism reduces to depth of shrinkage alone; the paper's tumour-burden observation at last progression-free assessment (35.0 against 54.0 mm) is measured at a timepoint that differs between patients and is not adjusted for the time to that assessment.

The cross-trial picture is inconsistent and the paper does not engage with it: CALGB/SWOG 80405 compared the same two antibodies in 1137 KRAS wild-type patients and found no survival difference. This analysis's framework would predict one.
Primary tumour sidedness - which has since become the main determinant of first-line anti-EGFR selection and which would reorganise this entire comparison - is not reported anywhere.

Secondary resection of liver metastases was a FIRE-3 secondary endpoint and the reason a hepatobiliary reader opens this paper, and it is not reported in this analysis at all. A paper arguing that deeper shrinkage is what matters never says how many patients became operable.

The RAS wild-type population is itself a retrospectively defined subgroup: eligibility was by KRAS exon 2 from October 2008, and 75 of 475 retested samples proved RAS-mutant and were moved out, so the population in which the survival difference is reported was constituted after the trial ended.
The reported response confidence interval differs between text (64.3-74.8) and table 2 (64.3-78.8) for the same estimate.

A linked Lancet Oncology Comment (PMID 27733257, Davidson and Chau, 'Colorectal cancer trial endpoints: time for dynamic thinking?', 2016;17:1345-7) was identified in PubMed but its text was not read for this record.
27575024.n: 400 patients in the final extended RAS wild-type subgroup of FIRE-3 (of 592 randomised between 2007 and 2012, with 75 of 475 retested samples found RAS-mutant), of whom 330 had assessable serial CT scans for blinded central review (157 FOLFIRI plus cetuximab, 173 FOLFIRI plus bevacizumab); 188 RAS-mutant patients were analysed separately
27575024.bottom_line: Explains the FIRE-3 paradox in its own terms: with blinded central review, FOLFIRI plus cetuximab produced more early tumour shrinkage (68.2% against 49.1%), deeper response (-48.9% against -32.3%) and a lower residual tumour burden than FOLFIRI plus bevacizumab, while investigator-assessed response and progression-free survival were identical and survival was 8.1 months longer. It does not establish that shrinkage is the mechanism or a usable surrogate: everything measured here was added post hoc after the survival result was known, the central review raised response in one arm only, survival was identical between arms among patients who did shrink, the two surrogates correlate at 0.96, and CALGB/SWOG 80405 found no survival difference at all. For a liver surgeon the paper withholds the number that matters - secondary resection, a FIRE-3 endpoint, is not reported.

limitations: This is a phase 2 trial with a sample size below the phase 3 design originally planned, which the authors say would have offered better protection against imbalance between arms and better reassurance on external validity
Overall survival was a secondary endpoint of the phase 2 trial, whose primary endpoint was a 30-month survival rate above 38% in the combined arm
The trial was closed prematurely for poor accrual, driven by physician treatment preferences
The authors state that with this sample size small baseline imbalances - in the number of lesions and in synchronicity - could not be excluded, and they report sensitivity analyses adjusting for both

Complete tumour clearance required ablation combined with resection in 45.6% of the combined arm, and two patients were not completely treated (one positive margin, one lesion adjacent to the stomach)
The authors emphasise that the result depends on assessment by specialised multidisciplinary teams and experienced liver surgeons, with over 90% of patients enrolled in tertiary referral centres
critique: The survival comparison this paper is cited for was never the trial's question. The prespecified primary endpoint was a single-arm threshold - 30-month survival above 38% in the combined arm - so the between-arm hazard ratio of 0.58 (95% CI 0.38-0.88, p=0.01) is an unprotected secondary comparison at an analysis time chosen after the fact, with no multiplicity control.

The curves are superimposed for three years and diverge only where the numbers at risk collapse: median survival 45.6 against 40.5 months, 3-year survival 56.9% against 55.2%, and the headline separation appears at 5 and 8 years (43.1% vs 30.3%, 35.9% vs 8.9%) with roughly a dozen patients at risk per arm. A single hazard ratio is reported for curves that plainly do not satisfy proportional hazards, and no test of that assumption appears.

Accrual was 119 patients across 22 centres in five years, about one patient per centre per year, and recruitment failed because surgeons preferred one treatment. The enrolled population is therefore the narrow slice over which individual surgeons held genuine equipoise, and the paper offers no screening log to show what that slice looks like.

The intervention is complete liver clearance, not ablation. Only 30 of 57 treated patients had ablation alone; 26 also had a resection and one had resection alone, almost all through a laparotomy (89.5%). Any attribution of the survival gain to ablation, or any transfer to today's percutaneous practice, goes beyond what was randomised.

The quality of the ablations is reported and then left unexamined: 58.9% of ablated lesions had a margin under 1 cm and 8.9% no margin at all, with local failure as first progression in 9 of 56 patients and 11 of 170 lesions. No analysis relates margin to local failure, in a trial whose entire claim is that local control changes survival.

The experimental arm received less systemic therapy and more harm from the procedure: 6 of 60 patients never received systemic treatment at all, three because of postoperative complications, and one patient died of sepsis and multiorgan failure after ablation and surgery. Both facts are single sentences, and no morbidity table appears for an operation performed in 57 patients.

Baseline imbalance ran in the experimental arm's favour - median 4 versus 5 lesions and solitary metastases in 25.0% versus 11.9% - and the correction offered is univariate sensitivity analysis adjusting for lesion number dichotomised at four and for synchronicity, in 119 patients. That is not adjustment, it is reassurance.

Clearing the liver changed where patients failed: extrahepatic disease as the only first progression occurred in 25.0% of the combined arm against 13.6% of the systemic arm, while cumulative extrahepatic progression was identical at five years (60.4% vs 60.2%). The possibility that local treatment delays or displaces systemic control is not discussed.

The control arm is six months of FOLFOX4, with bevacizumab permitted only from October 2005 and no anti-EGFR antibody, no RAS or BRAF selection, and no maintenance. The authors defend it by noting the control arm's survival resembles modern series, which if anything argues that the trial's advantage would shrink against contemporary systemic therapy.

Unresectability was decided by each local multidisciplinary team with no central review, and included isolated lesions at the origin of the hepatic veins - lesions that many units would now resect or ablate percutaneously. The claim that these criteria still apply in the current era is asserted, not tested, about a trial that opened in 2002.

Salvage treatment differed systematically between arms - more systemic therapy in the control arm, more surgery and ablation in the combined arm - and the defence that survival after progression did not differ (19.5 vs 21.0 months, HR 0.86, 95% CI 0.56-1.31) comes from a supplementary analysis with an interval wide enough to hide a substantial effect either way.

The 36% eight-year survival in the combined arm is set beside the 40% of EPOC, a trial of one to four resectable metastases with a median of one lesion, with no matching and no acknowledgement that the populations are not comparable.

Three ablation device manufacturers supplied the needles used in the experimental arm free of charge. The EORTC's independence of analysis is stated, and the device contribution is not mentioned again.
No quality-of-life or patient-reported outcome is reported, in a trial comparing a laparotomy plus chemotherapy against chemotherapy alone.
No linked editorial or comment on this report was found in PubMed, so no independent published critique informs this record.
28376151.n: 119 patients aged 18 to 80 with liver-only, locally unresectable colorectal metastases and fewer than 10 lesions, randomised at 22 European centres from 2002 until premature closure in 2007 (60 to combined local plus systemic treatment, 59 to systemic treatment alone); 57 received local treatment - radiofrequency ablation alone in 30, ablation plus resection in 26, resection alone in 1 - with 170 lesions ablated, 89.5% at laparotomy. 92 of 119 patients (77.3%) had died at a median follow-up of 9.7 years
28376151.bottom_line: Provides the only randomised evidence that clearing all liver disease in unresectable, liver-only colorectal metastases adds survival to systemic therapy: 8-year survival 35.9% against 8.9%, HR 0.58 (95% CI 0.38-0.88), with hepatic progression at five years cut from 88.2% to 62.1% and no change in extrahepatic progression. It does not establish this as a trial of ablation or as a trial powered for survival: the design was randomised phase 2 with a single-arm 30-month primary endpoint, accrual failed at 119 patients because surgeons would not randomise, almost half the experimental arm needed resection as well, 89.5% of ablations were done at laparotomy, and the survival curves are indistinguishable for the first three years. Its control arm is six months of FOLFOX4 without modern biologics or molecular selection.

limitations: The comparison was non-randomised and spanned 21 years; the authors state that unmeasured prognostic factors could be unbalanced between groups and partly explain the survival difference, while arguing that the measured factors were worse in the hepatic arterial infusion group
The study period covers the introduction of irinotecan, oxaliplatin and targeted treatments, which the authors address by repeating the analysis in patients given modern systemic chemotherapy
No PET-CT staging data were available, which the authors answer by citing a study showing PET-CT rarely changed surgical management

They state that a randomised trial is needed to confirm that adjuvant hepatic arterial infusion improves survival in the current era, and that confirmation is most likely in node-negative and low-risk patients

They note the technique's complexity: pump placement requires an estimated learning curve of 25 procedures, and intensive medical oncology management plus nuclear medicine, interventional radiology and gastroenterology support is needed to prevent and manage biliary toxicity, bleeding and ulcer disease
They call for genomic data such as KRAS status to improve patient selection
critique: The propensity analysis is reported without the information needed to judge it: no model specification, no matching or weighting method, no covariate balance before and after adjustment, and no sensitivity analysis for unmeasured confounding. This is exactly the objection raised in the published letter from Zhang and colleagues, and the consistency of the effect across propensity quartiles does not substitute for showing balance.

Seven covariates are adjusted for - sex, age, year of resection, extrahepatic disease, number of tumours, size of the largest tumour and margin status - and the variables most likely to drive both pump placement and survival are not among them: performance status, comorbidity, response to prior chemotherapy, remnant volume, and whether the patient was a candidate for an institutional trial.

The treatment groups differ by six years of age (56.1 against 62.2) and by era, and fitness for an additional laparotomy and pump implantation is itself a prognostic selection that no measured covariate captures. A 23-month median difference in a non-randomised 21-year series is well within the range such selection can produce.

Hepatic arterial infusion is inseparable from more intensive treatment overall. Every pump patient received perioperative systemic chemotherapy by definition, pump patients had far more two-stage hepatectomy (5.6% against 0.5%) and ablation (17.3% against 6.1%), and the comparison is therefore between two treatment programmes, not between the presence and absence of one drug route.

Patients in whom the pump never worked or who did not complete the planned six cycles remained in the pump group for every analysis, which is the correct intention-to-treat handling but is never quantified: the paper does not state how many of the 785 actually received floxuridine or how much.

No procedure-specific complication rate, biliary toxicity rate or pump failure rate is reported anywhere in a paper recommending the technique, although the Discussion acknowledges severe ulcer disease, catheter dysfunction and the need for intensive management to preclude biliary toxicity.

The subgroup results that the paper leans on are post hoc splits with no adjustment for multiplicity, and they point the wrong way for the proposed mechanism: the largest differences are in node-negative primaries (129 against 51 months) and a clinical risk score of 0 to 2 (89 against 53 months), while no association is seen with extrahepatic disease, a positive margin or a score of 4 to 5. A liver-directed treatment that helps most where hepatic recurrence risk is lowest is more consistent with selection than with effect.

The clinical risk score used for those subgroups had 11% missing values, mainly preoperative CEA, with no imputation method described, and the subgroup totals in the text do not match those in the Discussion.

Preoperative and adjuvant pump use are pooled in the headline figure despite very different survival (median 71 against 46 months), and the preoperative group had by definition failed to be resectable upfront, so the single hazard ratio averages two different clinical situations.

The comparison is with the same institution's own non-pump patients over the same decades, which means both arms are subject to the referral patterns of a centre where hepatic arterial infusion is a signature programme; no external or multicentre cohort is examined.

The authors' defence of their earlier randomised trial - that the survival benefit would not disappear in the modern chemotherapy era - is made with this observational dataset, which cannot adjudicate it, and the randomised trial they call for had not reported at publication.

A published letter (PMID 28796585, Zhang and colleagues, 'Propensity Score Analysis: More Details, More Credibility', J Clin Oncol 2017) with an authors' reply (PMID 28796584) was identified in PubMed; its objection is reflected above, but its full text was not read for this record.
28426374.n: 2368 consecutive patients who had a complete curative-intent resection of colorectal liver metastases at Memorial Sloan Kettering between 1992 and 2012, of whom 785 (33%) received perioperative hepatic arterial infusion of floxuridine (653 adjuvant, 132 preoperative) and 1583 did not; 1442 received modern systemic chemotherapy containing oxaliplatin or irinotecan, and the propensity model used the 2332 patients (98.5%) with complete covariate data. Median follow-up of survivors 55 months; the series contains 215 actual 10-year survivors
28426374.bottom_line: The largest dataset on perioperative hepatic arterial infusion after resection of colorectal liver metastases: 2368 consecutive complete resections, with median overall survival of 67 against 44 months and a propensity-adjusted hazard ratio of 0.67 (95% CI 0.59-0.76), holding in the modern chemotherapy era and in the most recent decade. It cannot establish that the pump caused the difference: the comparison is non-randomised over 21 years, pump patients were six years younger and more recently treated, every pump patient also had systemic chemotherapy and far more two-stage surgery and ablation, the propensity model's specification and balance are not shown, and the benefit is largest in node-negative and low-risk patients - where a liver-directed treatment should matter least. The authors' own conclusion is that a randomised trial is needed.
