limitations: The imbalance in the patient-and-physician choice of mFOLFOX6 versus FOLFIRI limits any statistical comparison of the chemotherapy regimens and of their possible interaction with the antibodies

Only first-line treatment was mandated, patients going more than 28 days without treatment were removed from study, treatment holidays became more common during the trial, and the drugs, schedules and doses of subsequent therapy were not reliably collected, so the effect of later management cannot be inferred

Primary tumour site (right versus left colon) was not captured on study and had to be obtained post hoc by chart review; the authors note it has since been suggested to influence outcome as a biological surrogate

No adjustment was made for multiple comparisons in the secondary endpoints, which the authors state should be considered exploratory, and the subgroup analyses by expanded RAS, sex, race and chemotherapy are labelled unplanned and post hoc

Observed survival greatly exceeded the 22 months assumed at design, which the authors attribute to better regimens, exclusion of KRAS-mutant patients, lower tumour burden from better imaging, commercial availability of both antibodies after progression, and the 12% rendered disease free by surgery

The authors state their explanation for the discrepancy with FIRE-3 (routine use of bevacizumab beyond progression in the United States) is speculative, and that the FIRE-3 sequencing hypothesis is not addressed by this trial
critique: The conclusion of 'no significant difference' is a failure to reject, not equivalence. The trial was powered only for a hazard ratio of 0.80 and a 5.5-month survival gain, and the observed overall survival HR of 0.88 has a 95% CI of 0.77 to 1.01 - compatible with up to a 23% reduction in the hazard of death with cetuximab. The paper nowhere states what differences the data exclude.

The trial was released after the 11th interim analysis on the ground that neither arm could still meet the 5.5-month superiority goal, which is a futility stop against a large prespecified effect; the adjusted two-sided significance level at the final analysis was 0.06 and the observed p was 0.08, so the primary comparison stopped just short of a boundary that was itself relaxed by the interim schedule.

Local and central KRAS results agreed poorly: the kappa statistic was 0.52 with a 90% lower confidence bound of 0.32, against the 0.75 benchmark the statistical plan set. Yet from July 2010 eligibility could be established in any CLIA-certified laboratory. The paper reports the failed benchmark and does not revisit what it means for a trial whose eligibility is a mutation test.

The reported response-rate difference is internally inconsistent as printed: 4.4% with a 95% CI of 1.0% to 9.0%, an interval excluding zero, alongside p=0.13. Two incompatible methods are reported side by side and neither is reconciled.

Only 1137 of 2334 randomised patients (49%) appear in the analysis. The dual-antibody arm was closed and its patients removed from study, KRAS-mutant patients were excluded, and 333 of the analysed patients were registered before KRAS eligibility existed and had their status established retrospectively. The reported population is a retrospectively defined biomarker subset of a three-arm trial.

The stated treatment goal was imbalanced in the direction of the subgroup the paper leans on: cure was the intent in 17.1% (99 of 578) of cetuximab patients against 13.2% (74 of 559) of bevacizumab patients. Intent was recorded at randomisation but was not a stratification factor and is not adjusted for in the surgery analysis.

The surgical conversion result most relevant to liver metastases - 140 patients rendered disease free with median overall survival of 64.7 and 62.2 months - is reported without the number converted in each arm, without a denominator for who was ever a candidate, and without any adjustment. A median survival of over five years in patients selected by having responded enough to be operated on is a statement about selection, not about either antibody.

Response and progression were assessed by the treating investigator in an open-label trial with no blinding and no central radiology review, and progression-free survival was a secondary endpoint evaluated on that basis.

Expanded RAS testing was done only in 'a subset of specimens' after the trial closed; the main text gives no number, no proportion and no account of why some specimens were testable, yet the expanded RAS analysis is used to argue the primary result holds in the population now treated.

Centre was explicitly excluded from the analysis because there were too many sites (396), so a trial run largely in community practice carries no accounting for centre effect in a disease where multidisciplinary management and hepatobiliary surgical availability vary enormously between sites.

The only positive signal in the paper - cetuximab better with mFOLFOX6 (HR 0.83, 95% CI 0.71-0.98) but not FOLFIRI (HR 1.04, 0.79-1.35) - arises from a comparison across groups that patients and physicians self-selected into before randomisation, and the interaction test itself is not significant (HR 1.27, 95% CI 0.94-1.73, p=0.11). It is reported in the abstract-level narrative nonetheless.

Race was collapsed to white versus non-white for analysis because 82% of the sample was white, and ethnicity was reported only descriptively, so the trial can say nothing about either; this is a methods decision with no accompanying caveat.

Both drug manufacturers were inside the trial: Genentech makes bevacizumab, Eli Lilly supplied the cetuximab, and both are recorded as participating in protocol development and in the review and approval of the final manuscript of a trial comparing their products.

The 12% rendered disease free and the 41% still disease free at a median of 5.5 years are offered in the Discussion as an explanation for the high survival, but no CONSORT-style accounting of who was resected, when, or with what margin appears anywhere, so this depot's interest in the paper - conversion to surgery - rests on two sentences without a table.

Lieu and Messersmith's linked JAMA editorial (PMID 28632850, 'No difference, but not the same') argues that absence of a detected difference does not make the antibodies interchangeable; its text was identified in PubMed but not read for this record, so its reasoning is not reflected here beyond its title claim.
28632865.n: 1137 patients with centrally confirmed KRAS wild-type tumours (578 cetuximab, 559 bevacizumab) out of 2334 randomised and 3058 registered at 396 sites; median age 59, 440 women (39%), 874 deaths and 938 progressions by the December 2015 cut-off, median follow-up 47.4 months in the 263 survivors
28632865.bottom_line: Establishes that in KRAS wild-type metastatic colorectal cancer, first-line cetuximab and bevacizumab added to FOLFOX or FOLFIRI give median survival around 29 to 30 months with no detectable difference, and that median survival exceeds five years in the 12% whose disease can be surgically cleared. It does not establish the two antibodies are equivalent: the trial was powered only for a 5.5-month gap, stopped for futility against that gap, and leaves a confidence interval reaching to a 23% survival advantage for cetuximab. The chemotherapy backbone was self-selected rather than randomised, primary tumour sidedness was never collected, and the surgical conversion figures that matter most to a liver surgeon are reported without denominators or arm-level counts.
28632865.funding: National Cancer Institute grants to the Alliance for Clinical Trials in Oncology and participating centres (U10CA180821, U10CA180882 and others), supported in part by Eli Lilly, Genentech, Pfizer and Sanofi. The NCI, Eli Lilly, Genentech and Pfizer participated in protocol development and in review and approval of the final manuscript, and Eli Lilly provided the cetuximab. Most senior authors declare grants, personal fees or advisory roles with Genentech/Roche, Merck KGaA, Bristol-Myers Squibb, Lilly, Amgen, Bayer and others

limitations: Management of metastatic colorectal cancer changed substantially over the 8-year recruitment period, with bevacizumab and EGFR inhibitors becoming first-line standards and liver interventions including surgery and ablation becoming more common; the authors argue there is no reason to think this differed between groups
Some patients were found not to have met the entry criteria after randomisation, with sensitivity analyses excluding them reported as robust
The three trials were not identically designed, which the authors say is accounted for by the statistical methods used

Crossover was anticipated: 12% of patients randomised to FOLFOX alone later received SIRT and 8% assigned SIRT never received it, and the authors state the difference in exposure to post-trial treatments might have affected the primary endpoint

They speculate that better liver control may have biased physicians towards less intensive subsequent treatment, and that reduced later use of irinotecan may reflect prolonged myelosuppression after SIRT
Molecular subtypes were not available, and the right-sided primary finding is called exploratory with further analyses underway

The authors state that early use of SIRT with first-line oxaliplatin-based chemotherapy cannot be recommended in unselected patients, and call for study of SIRT in selected populations and as consolidation after chemotherapy
critique: The control arm was better treated in two ways that both bias against SIRT, and only one is acknowledged. Full-dose oxaliplatin was given in 59% of SIRT-arm cycles against 68% of control cycles, by protocol design; and bevacizumab was given to 197 of 554 SIRT patients (36%) against 256 of 549 controls (47%), an 11-point imbalance in a drug of proven benefit, despite planned biologic use having been made a stratification factor in May 2011. The bevacizumab imbalance is printed in the results and never discussed.

The paper states plainly that dose reduction data were not readily available, so the degree of chemotherapy attenuation in each arm cannot be quantified beyond the first 12 cycles, in an analysis whose central claim is that an added treatment confers no benefit.

The device manufacturer was inside the data. Sirtex employees were involved in all stages of two of the three trials and in the process of combining the three datasets, and the sponsor reviewed the manuscript. A pooled analysis conducted partly by the manufacturer of the device being tested needs independent replication of the merge, and none is described.

The only subgroup favouring SIRT is post hoc and built on partial data: primary tumour site was a post-hoc subgroup, side was known for just 718 of 1103 patients (65%), and the right-sided group numbers 179. No interaction test is reported in the text, no molecular data exist, and the authors nonetheless call for further studies in that subgroup - which is the reading the linked Comment then amplifies.

Liver control and extrahepatic failure move in opposite directions by almost identical magnitudes: subdistribution hazard ratio 0.51 (95% CI 0.43-0.62) for first progression in the liver and 1.76 (1.47-2.11) for non-liver progression or death. A treatment that relocates the first progression event without changing survival or progression-free survival has not controlled the disease, and the first figure is nonetheless reported as improved liver-specific control.

Response rose substantially (72% versus 63%, OR 1.52; liver response OR 1.78) and resection did not move at all (94 of 554, 17%, versus 88 of 549, 16%; OR 1.07). Across 1103 patients this is the most powerful demonstration available that radiological response in the liver is not resectability, and the paper offers it as a single sentence.

The toxicity comparison uses as-treated groups of 507 and 571 while efficacy uses randomised groups of 554 and 549, so the 47 patients assigned SIRT who never received it are counted as chemotherapy-alone for harms. The control arm's safety denominator therefore exceeds its randomised size, and the resulting excess toxicity with SIRT (OR 1.42, 95% CI 1.09-1.85) is if anything understated.

Post-trial therapy differed systematically and no analysis adjusts for it. Fewer SIRT patients went on to irinotecan, fluoropyrimidine, anti-VEGF or anti-EGFR therapy, and 66 of 549 controls (12%) crossed over to SIRT. The authors list both and offer no sensitivity analysis of the primary endpoint accounting for either.

Eight treatment-related deaths occurred with SIRT against three with chemotherapy alone - three from radiation-induced liver disease, one from off-target microsphere delivery, two surgical, one liver failure, one pneumonitis - and the Discussion summarises this as increased toxicity that did not translate into inferior overall survival.

Quality of life is reported only for the first 24 months as unadjusted EQ-5D-3L utility scores with no completion rates in the main text, and the one timepoint that differed (2-3 months, when SIRT toxicity peaks) is set aside as not clinically meaningful against a threshold borrowed from a cross-cancer suggestion.

Eligibility differed between the pooled trials in ways that matter for a liver-directed therapy - FOXFIRE allowed up to five lung metastases amenable to future local therapy, the other two allowed nodules by size - and biological agents entered FOXFIRE only from December 2014, so the trials contributing to the pooled estimate delivered different background therapy in different years.

The analysis cannot address the question a liver surgeon asks. Roughly half the patients had an intact primary tumour, 87% had synchronous disease, all were deemed unresectable at entry, and recruitment ran through the years in which ablation became routine, so the pooled result bears on first-line consolidation strategy and not on conversion or on resectable disease.
A linked Lancet Oncology Comment (PMID 28781172, Schmoll, 2017;18:1138-9) asking whether SIRT is only for right-sided tumours was identified in PubMed but its text was not read for this record.
28781171.n: 1103 chemotherapy-naive patients with liver-only or liver-dominant unresectable colorectal metastases randomised 1:1 across 14 countries from 2006 to 2014 in three trials (364 FOXFIRE, 530 SIRFLOX, 209 FOXFIRE-Global; 554 FOLFOX plus SIRT, 549 FOLFOX alone); 844 deaths at a median follow-up of 43.3 months, 122 patients (11%) retrospectively found ineligible, and safety assessed in an as-treated population of 507 and 571
28781171.bottom_line: Settles the first-line question: across 1103 randomised patients, adding yttrium-90 resin microspheres to FOLFOX does not prolong survival (22.6 against 23.3 months, HR 1.04, 95% CI 0.90-1.19), does not prolong progression-free survival, and does not convert a single extra patient to resection (17% against 16%), while raising grade 3 or worse toxicity and treatment-related deaths. It also shows why the SIRFLOX hepatic-progression result was not a benefit: first progression moved out of the liver as fast as it left it (subdistribution HR 0.51 in the liver, 1.76 outside). It cannot rule out benefit in selected patients: the control arm received more full-dose oxaliplatin and more bevacizumab, 12% of controls crossed over, and the one favourable subgroup - right-sided primaries - is post hoc, unmolecular and based on 179 patients.
28781171.funding: Bobby Moore Fund of Cancer Research UK and Sirtex Medical, the manufacturer of the yttrium-90 resin microspheres. The sponsor had no role in FOXFIRE's design, data collection or analysis, but Sirtex employees were involved in all stages of SIRFLOX and FOXFIRE-Global and in the process of combining the three trial datasets, and the sponsor reviewed the manuscript and provided comments. Most senior authors declare grants, personal fees or non-financial support from Sirtex Medical

limitations: Resectability was assessed at each centre by local multidisciplinary boards and the results may differ between centres
Volumetric methods were those routinely used at each centre and were not standardised; the authors argue serial measurements within each patient make the comparison reliable
The method of portal embolisation differed between centres, although the authors report that success and growth rates did not
The trial was not blinded and patients were informed of the operation they had been randomised to

The two-stage resection rate of 57% was lower than the 60-75% previously reported, which the authors attribute to including patients with very small remnants, the requirement of a kinetic growth rate above 2% per week, and the 30% remnant threshold; a 25% cut-off would have added one more two-stage success

Perioperative mortality remained high in both arms, which the authors say indicates that less invasive alternatives - laparoscopic ALPPS, microwave ablation along the division line, or partial ALPPS - may be considered
Long-term outcomes remain to be elucidated, so the authors state the oncological role of ALPPS remains uncertain
critique: The primary endpoint is defined so that the headline gap cannot survive real practice. By protocol, two-stage patients who crossed over to rescue ALPPS were counted as treatment-arm failures, so 92% against 57% describes a strategy in which a patient whose liver fails to grow after embolisation is simply abandoned. The paper's own figure for the strategy a surgeon would actually use - embolisation first, ALPPS as salvage - is 82% against 92% and is not significant, and it appears only in the Crossover paragraph.

Complications, mortality and margin status are all analysed per protocol among resected patients only (44 versus 28), so the arm that resected fewer patients is credited with the complications of its successes alone. The 21 two-stage patients who never reached resection contribute no morbidity to the comparison, and the 12 who then underwent rescue ALPPS contribute to neither arm. 'Severe complications identical at 43%' is a comparison of unlike denominators.

Every secondary endpoint is badly underpowered and reported as if negative. The sample was sized only to detect a 25-point difference in resection rate; the 90-day mortality odds ratio of 1.39 has a 95% CI of 0.3 to 6.6 and the margin odds ratio of 2.55 a CI of 0.9 to 7.1. The conclusion that ALPPS carries no higher mortality and no worse margins rests on intervals that exclude almost nothing.

Allocation was by sealed opaque envelopes distributed to the centres in numbered order and drawn locally, in an unblinded trial of two operations. Concealment therefore depended on envelope integrity at the site, and the surgeon who decided whether a patient had reached the 30% threshold, whether growth was adequate, and whether treatment had failed, knew the allocation throughout. No central adjudication of resectability, growth or treatment failure is described.

The control intervention was not one intervention. Portal ligation was used in 14 patients and embolisation in 35, the embolic agent differing by centre (histoacryl-lipiodol with particles in 28, embospheres in 7), with segment 4 branches embolised on demand. The claim that technique did not matter rests on a 14-versus-35 subgroup comparison with p values of 0.42 and 0.36 - an equivalence claim from an underpowered test.

The threshold explanation for the two-stage arm's underperformance does not add up: lowering the cut-off from 30% to 25% would have converted one patient of 49, roughly 2 percentage points of a 35-point gap. The rest comes from the kinetic growth requirement and from baseline remnants of 21-22%, which is to say from how the entry criteria were set.

The experimental operation was new to the participating units: the paper states that no patient with colorectal liver metastases and a remnant below 30% had ALPPS outside the trial at any participating centre during the study period. No learning-curve analysis, no centre-level outcome breakdown and no operator volume data are reported, in a trial of a technically demanding procedure with 8.3% mortality.

Blood samples were collected before both interventions for basic values and no liver function endpoint is reported anywhere, although whether rapid volume gain after ALPPS is matched by function is the central safety question. The only functional data in the paper are MELD scores in the table of deaths, and all seven deaths in the trial involved postoperative liver failure.

Patients could enter with extrahepatic metastases or an unresected primary tumour provided these could be addressed later, and 16 had extrahepatic disease, but neither was a stratification factor and the paper never reports how many patients completed the whole oncological plan. Resection rate in the liver is treated as the outcome without asking what proportion of patients ended up disease-free.

Ten patients with an initial remnant above 30% had ALPPS or two-stage hepatectomy off trial during the study period, with the decision made intraoperatively for chemotherapy damage or unexpected metastases, and one eligible patient chose embolisation. Their outcomes are not reported, so the denominator of patients actually facing this decision at these centres is larger than the trial's.
Three randomised patients were excluded after randomisation and the primary analysis is on 97 of 100; no intention-to-treat analysis of the primary endpoint including them is given.

The trial reports a surgical capability, not a benefit. Converting a patient from unresectable to resected is only valuable if it changes survival, and the companion survival report (Hasselgren, Ann Surg 2021) is a separate paper - so as published, this trial establishes that ALPPS gets more livers out and nothing about whether patients are better for it.

A linked comment (PMID 30724806, Giglio and Troisi, Ann Surg 2019) and a linked correspondence from the MD Anderson group (PMID 30169392, Vega and colleagues) were identified in PubMed but their texts were not read for this record, so their objections are not reflected here.
28902669.n: 97 patients analysed of 100 randomised (48 ALPPS, 49 two-stage hepatectomy) from 117 assessed at six Scandinavian university hospitals between June 2014 and August 2016; 68 men and 29 women, mean age 65 (SD 10), baseline standardised future liver remnant 21-22%, median 8 liver metastases at surgery, 16 with extrahepatic disease, and a primary tumour still in situ permitted
28902669.bottom_line: Establishes that when the standardised future liver remnant is under 30% after chemotherapy, ALPPS completes the resection in 92% of patients against 57% with portal occlusion and two-stage hepatectomy, with faster and larger hypertrophy and a two-week rather than six-week interval, at a cost of 43% severe complications and 8.3% 90-day mortality. It does not establish that ALPPS is the better strategy: the trial's own rescue data put embolisation-first-with-ALPPS-salvage at 82% against 92%, a non-significant difference, and the morbidity and margin comparisons are made only among patients who reached resection, so the arm that resected fewer patients is judged on its successes alone. No survival endpoint is reported in this paper, and all seven deaths involved postoperative liver failure.
28902669.funding: Medical Research Council of Southeast Sweden (FORSS). The authors report no conflicts of interest

limitations: The protocol's discussion states that patients will receive pump floxuridine without concurrent systemic chemotherapy, whereas the Memorial Sloan Kettering practice from which the expected effect size is taken always combines the two - the justification being that Dutch guidelines do not recommend adjuvant systemic chemotherapy after complete resection

It states that eligibility is confined to low-risk patients without extrahepatic disease because those were the subgroups in which the retrospective Memorial Sloan Kettering analysis found the largest association, and that this determined both the design and the sample size

It records that an earlier randomised trial of intra-arterial chemotherapy across 26 German centres was terminated early because of high complication rates, which is why the five participating teams were comprehensively trained and proctored and a pilot study was run first
It states that no interim analysis is planned for survival outcomes, with interim analyses only for postoperative complications and adverse events after 20 and 50 patients in the experimental arm
It notes that pump chemotherapy requires a well-trained large multidisciplinary team and that the technique has not been widely adopted despite the earlier randomised result
critique: This is a protocol with no patient data, so it cannot support any statement about efficacy or safety; anything built on it describes an intention. A results publication for the PUMP trial was not found on this search, so its outcome is unknown here.

The sample size is anchored to a retrospective propensity-score hazard ratio of 0.60 derived from 779 low-risk Memorial Sloan Kettering patients, with the control median taken from 228 patients at a single Dutch centre. A trial powered on an observational effect size will be underpowered if the true effect is smaller, which is the usual fate of propensity-derived estimates.

The experimental regimen is not the regimen the effect size came from. Omitting concurrent systemic chemotherapy makes the trial a test of floxuridine alone against surgery alone, so neither a positive nor a negative result transfers to the combined approach used at the centre that generated the evidence.

The design inherits a selection that points against the mechanism. Low-risk patients were chosen because the retrospective analysis found the largest association there, but a liver-directed treatment should help most where the risk of hepatic recurrence is highest; adopting a subgroup finding as the trial's eligibility criterion builds the observational data's most suspicious feature into the design.

The primary endpoint is progression-free survival from surgery rather than overall survival, in a question - adjuvant therapy after complete resection - where the two have repeatedly diverged in this disease, as EORTC 40983 and JCOG0603 both show.

No interim analysis for efficacy or futility is planned at all, so a trial powered on an observational estimate will run to completion whatever the emerging data show, with only safety monitored at 20 and 50 patients.

Randomisation is preoperative, before resectability and the absence of extrahepatic or nodal disease are confirmed at operation, which guarantees post-randomisation exclusions and makes the intention-to-treat population different from the treated one; the protocol does not describe how those patients will be analysed.

The trial cannot be blinded - the experimental arm carries a palpable subcutaneous pump and a cholecystectomy - while the primary endpoint is radiological progression, and the protocol describes no independent central imaging review.

Floxuridine is not registered in the European Union and the pumps are supplied in kind by their manufacturer, so the trial depends on a device company's contribution and on special access to the drug, which bears on whether a positive result could be implemented.

Hepatotoxicity management is detailed but its consequence for dose intensity is not: the protocol holds or halves floxuridine on modest rises in AST, alkaline phosphatase or bilirubin, and the earlier randomised trial of this regimen delivered more than half the planned dose to only 26% of patients. The protocol sets no minimum delivered dose for a patient to count as treated.

The exclusions remove the patients in whom adjuvant intensification is usually argued for - two-stage resections, liver-first strategies, any extrahepatic disease, prior ablation or intra-arterial therapy - so even a positive result would apply to a narrow slice of the resected population.

Cost-effectiveness and quality of life are secondary endpoints with no instrument or analysis plan given in the published protocol, in a trial whose intervention adds an implanted device and six cycles of hepatotoxic therapy to an otherwise completed curative operation.
No linked editorial or comment was found in PubMed, so no independent published critique informs this record.
30953467.n: No patients: this is the published protocol. It plans to randomise 230 adults (115 per arm, allowing 5% dropout, with 126 progression events required) with resectable colorectal liver metastases, no extrahepatic disease and a Fong clinical risk score of 0 to 2, across five Dutch centres from August 2018
30953467.bottom_line: Sets out the design of the only randomised trial to test adjuvant hepatic arterial floxuridine against resection alone in low-risk, completely resected colorectal liver metastases - 230 patients in five proctored Dutch centres, progression-free survival as the primary endpoint, no concurrent systemic chemotherapy. It reports no patients and no outcomes, so it establishes nothing clinically. Its design decisions are worth reading critically: the effect size and the low-risk eligibility both come from a retrospective propensity analysis, the regimen omits the systemic component used where that evidence was generated, randomisation is preoperative, and no efficacy or futility interim analysis is planned.
30953467.funding: Dutch Cancer Society (EMCR 2016-10516), with Tricumed GmbH supplying the IP2000V pumps in kind; both are stated to have had no influence on design, data collection, analysis, interpretation or writing

limitations: Multiple cancer types were included and the authors state they cannot exclude histology-specific differences in tumour biology affecting the benefit
The radiotherapy arm contained a large number of prostate cancer patients, which the authors say could have led to bias
Only a small number of patients had four to five metastases, which limits the value of the stratification factor, and the authors state no robust conclusion can be drawn beyond three metastases
The optimal dose and fractionation, and the maximum number of lesions treatable at acceptable risk, remain unknown
Three treatment-related deaths (4.5%) occurred despite strict dose constraints and peer review of all plans, and the authors advise treating more than five lesions only within trials
The prespecified endpoint of further systemic therapy cycles could not be ascertained and was converted to a yes-or-no variable
Quality of life was measured with a general rather than organ-specific instrument, and survival in both arms greatly exceeded the assumptions used for the sample size
The authors state that phase 3 trials are needed to show an overall survival benefit conclusively
critique: The survival result is not statistically significant by conventional standards and is presented as positive because the trial set its own threshold at a two-sided alpha of 0.20. The hazard ratio is 0.57 with a 95% CI of 0.30 to 1.10 and p=0.090, so the data are compatible with no survival effect, and 40 deaths in 99 patients cannot settle the question either way.

Control-arm survival was 28 months against the 9 months assumed at design - more than three times the planning estimate - so the trial was not powered for the population it enrolled, and the authors' explanation of this is confined to a limitation sentence.

The claim that a progression-free survival p value below 0.005 in a phase 2 screening trial can be considered definitive is asserted with one citation, in a trial of 99 patients with four histologies. Progression-free survival in a mixed-histology trial of local therapy is also the endpoint most favoured by treating the sites that are being measured.

Allocation produced striking imbalances for a 99-patient trial: 14 of the 16 prostate cancers and all three patients with five metastases fell in the radiotherapy arm. Prostate cancer has far better survival than the other histologies, and the paper offers no adjusted analysis excluding it.

Control patients received substantially more palliative radiotherapy (21 of 33, 64%, against 13 of 66, 20%), so the comparison is not radiotherapy against none but ablative radiotherapy against palliative radiotherapy plus systemic therapy - which bears directly on the lesional control endpoint.

Lesional control is computed per lesion (75 of 100 assessable against 28 of 57) with no clustering by patient, and the denominators are the assessable rather than the randomised lesions, with 191 lesions at baseline unaccounted for in that analysis.

Treatment-related mortality was 4.5% with none in controls, including a subdural haemorrhage after surgery for a radiotherapy-related perforated gastric ulcer. The abstract reports it, the Interpretation reports it, and no analysis weighs three deaths against a non-significant survival gain in 66 patients.

Quality of life was unchanged at six months (FACT-G 82.6 against 82.5, p=0.99) with no subscale difference, which undercuts the usual symptom-control justification for local therapy and is reported without comment on completion rates in the main text.
The trial is open label with no blinding of patients, clinicians or outcome assessors, and progression was assessed on imaging, in a trial whose firmest result is progression-free survival.

For colorectal liver metastases the trial contributes almost nothing directly: 18 patients had a colorectal primary (9 per arm) and 19 of 191 lesions were hepatic, and the comparator for liver-confined colorectal disease is resection or thermal ablation, neither of which was tested. ASCO's 2023 guideline excluded this trial from its evidence base for exactly this reason while recommending stereotactic radiotherapy on uncontrolled series.
Dose and fractionation varied (35 Gy in 5, 60 Gy in 8, 54 Gy in 3 fractions and others) with no dose-response analysis, so the intervention tested is a policy rather than a treatment.
The protocol contained no data-sharing plan and the data will not be shared, so the analyses cannot be independently checked.

A linked Lancet Comment (PMID 30982688, Loo and Diehn, 'SABR-COMET: harbinger of a new cancer treatment paradigm', 2019;393:2013-14) was identified in PubMed but its text was not read for this record.
30982687.n: 99 patients with a controlled primary tumour and one to five metastatic lesions, randomised 2:1 at ten centres in Canada, the Netherlands, the UK and Australia between February 2012 and August 2016 (66 stereotactic ablative radiotherapy plus standard of care, 33 standard of care alone); primary histology was colorectal in 18, breast 18, lung 18 and prostate 16, and only 19 of 191 lesions were hepatic. Just 7 of 99 patients had four or five metastases. Median follow-up 26 and 25 months
30982687.bottom_line: The first randomised evidence that ablating all sites of oligometastatic disease may prolong life: median overall survival 41 against 28 months and progression-free survival 12 against 6 months, with lesional control raised from 49% to 75% and no loss of quality of life. It does not prove a survival benefit - the design set alpha at 0.20, the hazard ratio's interval crosses 1 (0.30-1.10, p=0.090), control survival was three times the planning assumption, and 14 of 16 prostate cancers landed in the treated arm - and it cost three treatment-related deaths in 66 patients. For colorectal liver metastases it is background for the oligometastatic idea only: nine treated patients had a colorectal primary, 19 of 191 lesions were hepatic, and the relevant comparator, resection or thermal ablation, was never tested.
30982687.funding: Ontario Institute for Cancer Research and a London Regional Cancer Program Catalyst Grant; the funders had no role in design, collection, analysis, interpretation or writing. Four authors declare grant funding or honoraria from Varian Medical Systems, ViewRay, AstraZeneca, Bayer, Merck, Celgene or MSD, all stated to be unrelated to this project

limitations: No limitations section. The authors concede that adjuvant chemotherapy was deliberately omitted because adding it would have turned the study into an evaluation of two treatments, and say this should be the subject of future multicentre trials
They state that only one of the fifteen patients had metachronous disease, and that metachronous patients have a better prognosis after liver resection

They state that the comparison supporting benefit is an estimate: on the basis of published second-line figures and the lines of chemotherapy their patients had received, they assume these patients would have had a median survival of about 17 months without transplantation
They report that SECA-II patients were significantly better selected than SECA-I patients on Fong score, Oslo score, lesion number, lesion size, CEA and PET tumour-to-background ratio

They state that graft scarcity is the major obstacle to establishing the indication internationally, that adding it to waiting lists would worsen an already difficult situation, and that several transplant centres are already offering it outside registered prospective studies
They report Clavien-Dindo grade IIIa-IVa complications in 7 of 15 patients (47%)
critique: The headline figure is a five-year Kaplan-Meier estimate from a median follow-up of 36 months with a range starting at 5 months, resting on two deaths in fifteen patients. No confidence interval is given anywhere, and the number of patients still at risk at 60 months is not stated in the text.

The counterfactual that makes the result look transformative is constructed rather than observed. The assumed 17-month median survival without transplantation comes from published second-line figures in unselected patients and is applied to a cohort that had to survive a median 24 months from diagnosis, show at least 10% RECIST response, remain extrahepatically PET-negative, keep ECOG 0-1, hold a BMI under 30 and lose under 10% of body weight. Selection of that kind predicts long survival by itself.

The historical comparison carried over from SECA-I is built on an outcome-selected control group: 21 SECA-I patients were compared with the 21 of 47 NORDIC-VII patients with the longest overall survival. Choosing a comparator by its outcome is improper even when, as here, the choice runs against the authors' hypothesis.

The paper itself shows the improvement over SECA-I is selection, not technique: Fong score 3 against 2, Oslo score 2 against 1, 8 lesions against 5, 45 mm against 24 mm, CEA 15 against 2 ug/L, tumour-to-background ratio 5.3 against 2.6. An 83% five-year estimate obtained by restricting entry says what the criteria pick out, not what the operation does.

The Discussion describes the cohort as having extensive non-resectable disease with a median of 12 metastases of 45 mm, which are the figures at diagnosis; at transplantation the medians were 5 lesions of 24 mm. The burden used to argue the patients were desperate is not the burden they had when transplanted.

Survival depends on post-transplant surgery that is not counted as part of the treatment: 6 pulmonary resections in 5 patients, one liver resection, two lymph node resections with 50 Gy of radiotherapy, and palliative chemotherapy in two. What the 83% describes is transplantation plus an aggressive and individualised salvage programme.

Pulmonary metastases were resected a median 21.4 months after detection, at a median CT size of 7.5 mm (range 5-10 mm). Known metastatic disease was therefore watched for nearly two years by design, which shapes both the disease-free survival figures and the 76.4% no-evidence-of-disease rate at three years - a composite that counts patients re-rendered disease free by later operations.

Median disease-free survival was 13.7 months with 35% disease-free at three years, so the operation does not control the disease; the paper's framing moves the burden of the efficacy claim onto overall survival without reporting what proportion of survival time was spent with known disease.

Subgroup analyses are reported from fifteen patients with no adjustment: Fong 1-2 against 3-4 (p=0.044), fewer than 8 lesions (p=0.083) and N0 primary (p=0.065). With this sample size these are descriptions of individual patients.

No screening or referral denominator is given. The paper reports 15 transplants over about five years with no waiting-list dropout, but not how many patients were assessed, declined or excluded, so the eligible population cannot be estimated from this study - although the paper then extrapolates to US transplant volumes.

Immunosuppression was basiliximab induction with tacrolimus for four to six weeks and conversion to sirolimus, a regimen chosen in part for a presumed antitumour effect, with no comparison, no exposure data, no rejection rate and no graft outcome reported. It is an untested co-intervention inside the treatment being evaluated.

The harms are substantial and unweighed: grade IIIa-IVa complications in 47%, including biliary leakage and acute hepatic vein thrombosis, in patients whose own livers functioned normally, plus lifelong immunosuppression. No quality-of-life measure is reported.

The allocation question is answered by assertion. The claim that restricting selection to patients with 75-80% five-year survival will probably not lengthen waiting lists much is an arithmetic extrapolation from one centre in a country with unusual graft availability, offered alongside the authors' own observation that centres are already transplanting these patients outside trials.

Three linked comments were identified in PubMed - Azoulay and Lim, 'Shaking the Coconut Tree' (PMID 32310616); Gorgen and Sapisochin, 'What if Those Lesions are Gone?' (PMID 31567348); and Jegatheeswaran and Siriwardena (PMID 32398488) - but only their titles were available, so no argument from them is attributed here beyond the question of what to do when liver lesions have disappeared on imaging.
31188200.n: 15 patients transplanted for non-resectable liver-only colorectal metastases at Oslo University Hospital between April 2012 and November 2016 (SECA-II, NCT01479608); median 12 lesions (up to 100) with largest 45 mm at diagnosis, falling to a median 5 lesions and 24 mm at transplantation; 14 of 15 synchronous, 12 of 15 sigmoid or rectal, 8 of 15 on second or later line chemotherapy, median 24.0 months from diagnosis to transplant and 29 days (range 7-148) on the waiting list with no dropout. Median follow-up 36 months (range 5-60)
31188200.bottom_line: Reports the best survival ever published for unresectable liver-only colorectal metastases - Kaplan-Meier 83% at five years in fifteen patients - and shows that tightening selection beyond SECA-I (response to chemotherapy, more than a year from diagnosis, lower tumour burden and CEA) is what produced it. It does not show that transplantation caused that survival: there is no control arm, the 17-month comparator is an assumption applied to a cohort selected for the features that predict long survival, the five-year figure rests on two deaths at a median 36 months of follow-up, and median disease-free survival was 13.7 months with survival maintained by repeated lung metastasectomy. It is a proof of principle about selection criteria, with 47% grade IIIa-IVa complications and a graft each.
31188200.funding: Supported by Oslo University Hospital and the Norwegian Cancer Society. The authors declare no conflicts of interest

limitations: No limitations section. The authors concede only that the metachronous-disease findings are based on small numbers, that caution is probably warranted before offering transplantation to patients with right-sided primaries, and that the trade-off of stringent criteria is that few patients qualify - a Fong score of 0 to 2 would restrict transplantation to 30% of this cohort
They state the work is a retrospective analysis of data collected in the prospective SECA studies
They argue that because recurrence alone does not predict short survival, disease-free survival is not an appropriate outcome for assessing the efficacy of transplantation in this disease
They state that which selection criterion to adopt depends on local waiting times, waitlist mortality and access to living donation
They state that total world experience remains limited and that highly selected patients should be considered for transplantation only within prospective studies
critique: The three scoring systems are not independent and the paper does not report a multivariable analysis. All six patients with a Fong score of 0 to 2 also had a metabolic tumour volume below 70 cm3 and an Oslo score of 0 to 2 (three scoring 0, two scoring 1, one scoring 2). Comparing the scores' survival figures compares nested subsets of the same 19 patients, so nothing here can establish which score carries the information.

Both of the thresholds being evaluated were derived in the patients being used to evaluate them: the Oslo score came from the first SECA-I patients and the 70 cm3 metabolic tumour volume cut from the SECA-I cohort, and those patients make up most of this cohort. This is apparent performance, not validation, and the paper does not say so.

No survival estimate anywhere in the paper carries a confidence interval. The headline 100% five-year survival rests on six patients, five of whom were observed beyond five years; the Oslo 0 to 2 figure on 13 patients, eight observed beyond five years; and the right-sided result on four patients.

The cohort is defined by an administrative criterion - having had a PET scan within 90 days of transplantation - which excludes roughly half the patients transplanted in SECA-I and SECA-II. The excluded patients are neither counted nor described, so whether the scored cohort represents the transplanted cohort cannot be checked.

Two studies with materially different entry criteria are pooled. SECA-II required at least 10% RECIST response to chemotherapy and more than one year from diagnosis; SECA-I required neither. A prognostic score evaluated across a cohort whose selection rules changed partway is measuring the rules as much as the patients.

Table 3 compares right- and left-sided patients across twelve baseline variables in 4 against 15 patients, and every comparison is non-significant - including Fong score (3.5 vs 3), Oslo score (2.5 vs 1), lesion size (75 vs 34 mm), CEA (140 vs 4 ug/L) and metabolic tumour volume (123 vs 23 cm3), all numerically worse on the right. The sidedness survival difference is then attributed to tumour biology without any attempt to separate it from that burden.

There is no comparator of any kind. The claimed superiority of transplantation is argued against published figures for palliative chemotherapy, regorafenib and TAS-102 in unselected patients, applied to a cohort selected for good performance status, chemotherapy response, a long interval from primary surgery and a negative PET - the very features that predict long survival without transplantation.

Only 2 of 19 patients were relapse-free, and median disease-free survival was 19 to 23 months even in the favourable groups. The claim that disease-free survival is therefore not an appropriate efficacy measure converts the study's central failure into a methodological argument; the survival that remains is produced by repeatedly resecting slow-growing pulmonary metastases, which is a different intervention from transplantation.

Multiplicity is unaddressed. Three dichotomised scores are each tested against overall survival, disease-free survival and post-relapse survival, alongside sidedness, CEA, KRAS status and synchronicity, producing roughly twenty p values from 19 patients with no adjustment and no prespecified primary comparison.

Every threshold used was chosen by this group - Oslo score components at 5.5 cm, 80 ug/L, two years and progression on chemotherapy; Fong dichotomised at 2; metabolic tumour volume at 70 cm3 - and no alternative cut-point, spline or continuous analysis is shown, so the apparent sharpness of each threshold cannot be distinguished from a choice fitted to these data.

The CEA finding is reported selectively: all nine patients with an elevated CEA at transplantation relapsed within two years, which is stated as informative, while the corresponding survival comparison was null (40% vs 60%, p=0.150) and the post-relapse survival comparison more so (50% vs 13%, p=0.424).

The feasibility figure the paper ends on - 0.24 to 0.51 eligible patients per million per year, equal to 1-2% of annual US transplants - is extrapolated from 19 patients at one Norwegian centre by arithmetic that is not shown, in a country with an unusual graft supply.

One patient died at 7.7 years of an unrelated cardiovascular event and is handled in the survival analyses without any competing-risk treatment, in a cohort on long-term immunosuppression where no graft outcome, rejection or immunosuppression-related morbidity is reported at all.
No linked editorial or comment on this paper was found in PubMed, so no independent published critique informs this record.
31674105.n: 19 patients transplanted for non-resectable liver-only colorectal metastases at Oslo University Hospital in the SECA-I and SECA-II studies who had 18F-FDG PET/CT within 90 days of transplantation; 15 left-sided and 4 right-sided primaries, all previously treated with fluorouracil and 12 on second or third line at transplant. Median follow-up 85 months
31674105.bottom_line: Shows that among 19 patients transplanted for unresectable liver-only colorectal metastases, those with the least disease by any of three measures lived markedly longer - five-year survival 100% with a Fong score of 0 to 2, 78% with metabolic tumour volume under 70 cm3, 67% with an Oslo score of 0 to 2 - and that survival after relapse can run for years on repeated lung metastasectomy. It does not validate any of these thresholds: all three were devised by this group, two were derived in these same patients, the three are so collinear that every Fong 0-2 patient also met both other criteria, no multivariable model or confidence interval is reported, and the favourable groups contain four to thirteen people. Read it as a description of who did well at one centre, not as a selection rule that has been tested.
31674105.funding: Supported by Oslo University Hospital, the Norwegian Cancer Society and the South-Eastern Norway Regional Health Authority. The authors declare no conflicts of interest

limitations: The authors name premature closure of recruitment, mandated by the trial steering committee on the independent data monitoring committee's advice, as the trial's primary limitation, while arguing that the mature analysis shows it did not change the conclusion
Overall survival was a secondary endpoint; the authors state there was no adjustment for multiple comparisons and no correction of the p value for the previous interim analysis

Baseline characteristics were prognostically less favourable in the cetuximab group (synchronous metastases in 88 of 129, 68%, against 73 of 128, 57%; a metastasis larger than 3 cm in 75, 58%, against 63, 49%), which the authors describe as small and non-significant differences

Extended RAS and RAF testing was retrospective on available samples: the hazard ratio in the all RAS/RAF wild-type population was almost identical but not significant, and numbers in the newly identified mutant group were insufficient for any conclusion
Mismatch repair status was not routinely measured during recruitment and cannot be reliably reported

The 2006 protocol's suggestion of a 10 mm resection margin was never amended although consensus changed; ablation was not permitted by protocol yet was used in some patients at clinician discretion, and other protocol violations are listed in the appendix
Right-sided cancers were few, so the larger apparent harm in that group was not significant, and the authors state that if the study were repeated translational endpoints would be prioritised
critique: The endpoint that stopped the trial no longer supports stopping it. Recruitment was halted in November 2012 when the lower limit of the 95% CI for the progression-free survival hazard ratio exceeded 1; at mature analysis that hazard ratio is 1.17 with a CI of 0.87-1.56 (p=0.304). The paper reports both facts and does not note that the futility criterion is no longer met.

The argument that early closure did not influence the outcome is circular: it is made by pointing to the survival result obtained from the same truncated cohort. Early closure limits precision, and the headline survival p value is 0.036 on a secondary endpoint with no multiplicity adjustment and no correction for the interim look.

The revised target was 268 KRAS wild-type patients and 212 progression events; 272 patients were recruited but only 257 were KRAS wild-type and formed the analysis population, and the number of progression events reached is not stated against that target anywhere in the paper.

Prespecified quality-of-life and cost-effectiveness endpoints were abandoned, with the stated reason that the trial was negative. A trial reporting a 26-month survival deficit, 16% grade 3-4 rash and 10% grade 3-4 mucositis has the strongest possible case for reporting what patients experienced, and does not.

Death ascertainment differs between the two endpoints. Overall survival uses NHS Digital registry data with an assumption that anyone not recorded dead is alive and censored two months before the status date, while progression-free survival censors patients lost to follow-up at last assessment irrespective of a death later received from NHS Digital. The two curves are therefore built on different information about the same patients.

The imbalance in baseline prognosis - synchronous disease 68% against 57% and a metastasis over 3 cm 58% against 49% - is dismissed using the subgroup analyses, which are the least reliable part of the paper: fourteen prespecified exploratory interaction subgroups, no multiplicity control, and the key estimates resting on small strata with wide intervals (node-negative HR 2.22, 95% CI 1.11-4.41; no adverse feature HR 2.35, 1.37-4.03). The primary model is unadjusted, with the minimisation-factor-adjusted model relegated to a sensitivity analysis whose result is not given in the text.

The arms differ in exposure to the curative treatment: 21 of 129 cetuximab patients never had an operation against 15 of 128, 11 versus 3 of them because of progression. Part of the survival difference is therefore mediated by not being operated on, and the paper does not separate that pathway from a direct effect of the drug.

Post-progression survival (33.5 versus 23.5 months, HR 1.55, 95% CI 1.07-2.24) is presented as evidence that cetuximab produced a more aggressive disease phenotype, but no second-line or subsequent therapy is reported for either arm, and the supporting claim that progression was associated with early death in the cetuximab group rests, in the authors' own words, on visual inspection of the survival curves.

The multisite-progression and post-progression analyses draw on data collected after the interim analysis, which means the comparison is partly built on information gathered once the arms were known and cetuximab had been stopped.

The mechanistic account does not hold together and the paper says so without changing the conclusion: no miR-31-3p subgroup benefiting from cetuximab could be identified, and high AREG/EREG expression was associated with worse outcome here and better outcome in advanced disease. The claim that the finding is robust with no apparent confounding variables sits one page after the admission that the biology is unexplained.

There was no central radiological review of response or progression in an open-label trial whose primary endpoint was progression, and whose subsequent interpretation turns on the pattern and timing of progression events.

The recommendation applies to a population the trial never studied. Today no patient with any RAS or BRAF mutation would receive cetuximab, and the all RAS/RAF wild-type analysis - the only one matching current selection - was retrospective, incomplete and not statistically significant.

The control-arm 5-year survival is described as comparable to the best of any case series despite the inclusion of borderline resectable patients, a comparison made against unmatched historical series and used to argue the quality of the trial's surgery.

A linked Lancet Oncology comment (PMID 32014120, Gholami and Grothey, 'EGFR antibodies in resectable metastatic colorectal liver metastasis: more harm than benefit?', 2020) was identified in PubMed but its text was not read for this record, so its reasoning is not reflected here.
32014119.n: 272 patients with resectable or suboptimally resectable colorectal liver metastases recruited at 39 UK hospitals between February 2007 and October 2012, of whom 257 with KRAS wild-type (codons 12, 13 and 61) tumours form the primary analysis population (128 chemotherapy alone, 129 chemotherapy plus cetuximab); 221 underwent an operation. Median follow-up 66.7 months (IQR 58.0-77.5). The revised accrual target was 268 KRAS wild-type patients and 212 progression events
32014119.bottom_line: Establishes that adding cetuximab to perioperative chemotherapy for operable KRAS wild-type colorectal liver metastases shortens life - median overall survival 55.4 against 81.0 months, HR 1.45 (95% CI 1.02-2.05) - with no gain in response, resection or R0 rate, and that the harm falls on the patients with the most favourable disease. It does not explain the effect: the primary progression-free survival endpoint that stopped the trial is no longer significant at maturity, the survival result is a secondary endpoint at p=0.036 with no correction for the interim look, and the molecular analyses offered as mechanism contradict the advanced-disease literature. The practical instruction - do not give cetuximab perioperatively for operable disease - is nonetheless the safest reading, and the control arm's 81-month median is the benchmark worth remembering.
32014119.funding: Cancer Research UK (C317/A7275), supported by the NIHR Clinical Research Network: Cancer, and also supported by a medical grant from Merck KGaA, which supplied the cetuximab and funded the original KRAS testing. The funder is stated to have had no role in design, collection, analysis, interpretation or writing. Four authors declare industry relationships, one of them speakers' fees from Merck Serono

limitations: The authors restate the original trial's limitations, in particular the inclusion of multiple histologies, which is common in stereotactic radiation trials but cannot exclude histology-specific differences in biology
The large majority of prostate cancer patients were allocated to the radiotherapy arm; the authors address this only with a post hoc sensitivity analysis, which has reduced power

They state that the most favourable histologies for this treatment are breast, prostate and kidney, and that these dominate the long-term survivors - 100% of them in the control arm and 70% in the radiotherapy arm
They state that local control assessment is difficult because focal fibrosis can present as an enlarging mass, which may explain the low lung control rates measured by RECIST 1.1
Patients with four to five metastases are under-represented, which led to separate trials for one to three and four to ten metastases
The trial was launched before the immunotherapy era, and the authors note immunotherapy may change the impact of radiotherapy on long-term outcomes
They state the 4.5% grade 5 toxicity rate is higher than in other studies despite dose constraints and peer review of all plans, and that further work is needed on optimal dose
They conclude that phase 3 trials are needed to confirm the survival benefit and to develop predictive biomarkers
critique: The number most relevant to this depot is the worst in the paper: long-term local control after radiotherapy was 50% in the liver, the lowest of any site and significantly below adrenal (100%) and bone (72%), p=0.04. Resection and thermal ablation in colorectal liver metastases achieve local control far above that, which is the comparison a liver surgeon needs and which this trial does not make.

The survival result still comes from a phase 2 screening design with alpha 0.20 in 99 patients. The paper itself cites p below 0.005 as the threshold at which a phase 2 randomised result may be treated as definitive, and its overall survival p is 0.006 - just outside the bar it sets.

Excluding prostate cancer, the histology that was unevenly allocated, the five-year survival difference falls to 33.1% against 16.2% with p=0.085. The authors argue this still meets a phase 2 screening threshold; it does not meet a conventional one, and it is the analysis that removes the trial's clearest allocation imbalance.

The mechanism claimed for the oligometastatic paradigm is contradicted by the trial's own post hoc analysis: time to new metastases did not differ between arms (Gray test p=0.57). Treating all visible lesions did not delay the appearance of new ones, which the authors read as occult micrometastatic disease already present - an interpretation that undermines the rationale for comprehensive local treatment.

The survival gain (22 months) is nearly four times the progression-free survival gain (6.2 months), and the explanation offered is salvage repeat radiotherapy in nine patients, including three of the ten five-year survivors. That makes the result contingent on intensive surveillance and repeated treatment, not on the initial intervention.

Long-term lesional control is computed per lesion (65 of 104 against 26 of 57) with no clustering by patient, and the denominators grew from the primary report's 100 and 57 assessable lesions without explanation.

Extending follow-up increased the effect from HR 0.57 (p=0.090) to HR 0.47 (p=0.006) in the same 99 patients. A growing effect with accumulating events in a small trial whose extension was triggered by observing more long-term survivors than expected is exactly the situation in which a point estimate drifts, and the paper does not address the multiplicity created by analysing the same primary endpoint twice.

Control patients continued to receive far more palliative radiotherapy (70% against 24%, p<0.001), so the contrast remains ablative against palliative radiotherapy rather than radiotherapy against none.

Toxicity did not improve with longer observation: treatment-related grade 2 or worse events stayed at 29% against 9%, and the three treatment-related deaths (4.5%) remain, against a survival benefit that is still not conventionally significant once prostate cancer is removed.

Twelve patients reached five years and only one had colorectal cancer, so the long-term benefit this paper is cited for was realised almost entirely in breast, prostate and kidney cancer. For colorectal liver metastases the trial provides a 50% liver control rate and a single long-term survivor.

The control arm's systemic options predate immunotherapy and, for colorectal cancer, predate current biologic selection, so the comparator in the arm against which 28 months is measured is not today's standard of care.
The protocol has no data-sharing plan and the data will not be shared, so neither the sensitivity analysis nor the site-specific control figures can be independently verified.
No English-language linked editorial or comment was found in PubMed; a German-language journal-club commentary exists (PMID 33532894, Dunst, Strahlenther Onkol 2021) and was not read for this record.
32484754.n: The same 99 patients as the primary report, with follow-up extended from 26 to 51 months: 66 randomised to stereotactic ablative radiotherapy plus standard of care and 33 to standard of care alone, at ten centres from 2012 to 2016; primary tumours breast 18, lung 18, colorectal 18, prostate 16, with 19 of 191 lesions hepatic. Fifty-nine deaths (35 and 24), 104 and 57 assessable lesions for long-term control, and 12 patients surviving five years or more, only one of them with colorectal cancer
32484754.bottom_line: With follow-up extended to 51 months the same 99-patient trial shows a larger survival gap - median 50 against 28 months, HR 0.47 (95% CI 0.27-0.81), five-year survival 42.3% against 17.7% - with no new toxicity and no loss of quality of life. It still does not prove benefit: alpha was 0.20, the effect falls to p=0.085 once the unevenly allocated prostate cancers are removed, and the trial's own post hoc analysis shows treating every visible lesion did not delay new metastases (p=0.57), so the gain is attributed to repeat salvage radiotherapy rather than to eradication. For colorectal liver metastases the useful figure is the one buried in the site-specific analysis: local control after stereotactic radiotherapy in the liver was 50%, the worst of any site, and only one of the twelve five-year survivors had colorectal cancer.
32484754.funding: Ontario Institute for Cancer Research and a London Regional Cancer Program Catalyst Grant; the funding bodies had no role in design, collection, analysis, interpretation or writing. Disclosures are held in a linked file not contained in this text; the primary report records grant funding or honoraria from Varian Medical Systems, ViewRay, AstraZeneca, Bayer, Merck, Celgene and MSD for four authors

limitations: Overall survival is not reported: the independent data monitoring committee recommended continued masking until 190 deaths or 12 months after this analysis, and the authors state crossover will be a factor in assessing it
The authors state that interpretation of the RAS-mutant subgroup, which showed no progression-free survival benefit, is limited by small numbers and a high proportion of missing mutation status

They state that no proposed marker of early progression on PD-1 blockade - low tumour mutation burden, JAK mutations, beta-2-microglobulin loss, misdiagnosed MSI-high status, pseudoprogression - is conclusive, so the patients who progress cannot be identified in advance
The influence of hereditary versus sporadic mismatch repair deficiency could not be determined because consent for germline testing was not obtained
They note the proportional-hazards assumption was violated for progression-free survival, and report restricted mean survival time alongside the hazard ratio
The trial was considered successful if pembrolizumab was superior on either primary endpoint, so this report's positive progression-free survival result satisfies the design on its own
critique: The conclusion rests on a single surrogate endpoint. Survival was deliberately masked at 125 of 190 required deaths, and the effective crossover rate to anti-PD-1 or anti-PD-L1 therapy was 59% of the chemotherapy arm - 36% on study plus 35 more patients off study - which means the eventual survival comparison will be between pembrolizumab first and pembrolizumab later, not between pembrolizumab and chemotherapy.

The hazard ratio of 0.60 is reported as the headline despite the paper stating that proportional hazards were violated. The analysis appropriate to crossing curves gives a far smaller effect: restricted mean progression-free survival at 24 months of 13.7 months against 10.8, a difference of 2.9 months.

Nearly a third of pembrolizumab patients (29.4%) had progressive disease as their best response against 12.3% on chemotherapy, so the early period in which the curves cross represents patients actively harmed by withholding chemotherapy - and the paper concedes no validated marker identifies them.

Response rate, the endpoint a surgeon would use to judge conversion potential, favoured pembrolizumab only modestly (43.8% against 33.1%), and the real difference is durability (82.6% against 35.3% of responses ongoing at 24 months) - a distinction that matters for sequencing but not for shrinking a liver before an operation.

The subgroup result that most affects practice is unreliable by the authors' own account: RAS, BRAF and NRAS status could not be evaluated in a quarter to a third of patients, so the apparent absence of benefit in RAS-mutant tumours (HR 1.19, 95% CI 0.68-2.07) rests on an incomplete and underpowered subgroup, and is nonetheless the kind of result that gets used to withhold treatment.

The comparator was investigator's choice of mFOLFOX6 or FOLFIRI with or without bevacizumab or cetuximab, so the control arm is a mixture of regimens chosen after randomisation was known, in an open-label trial.

Eleven randomised patients never started the assigned treatment and the safety populations are 153 and 143 against 153 and 154 randomised, so harms are counted in different denominators from efficacy.

The paper's own framing of the trial's success criterion - superiority on either primary endpoint - means that reporting progression-free survival while masking survival allows the trial to be declared positive before the endpoint that matters is known. The 2020 publication was followed by a separate final survival analysis not contained here.

The trial was designed with sponsor employees, three of whom are authors, and the first draft was written with a sponsor-employed medical writer, in a trial establishing first-line use of that sponsor's drug.

Adverse events of interest were specified by the sponsor regardless of investigator attribution, which shapes the immune-mediated event tally (31% against 13%, grade 3-4 9% against 2%) that is the counterweight to the chemotherapy arm's 66% grade 3 or higher treatment-related toxicity.

For a liver-metastasis pathway the trial is nearly silent: curative-intent surgery was performed in 14 pembrolizumab and 13 chemotherapy patients (9% and 8%), these patients were censored at the date of surgery in the progression-free survival analysis, and no resection, margin, pathological response or post-resection outcome is reported. The paper's relevance is that MSI-high status changes the systemic plan before any liver-directed decision - and that it is the basis on which transplant consensus documents exclude these patients, a use the trial itself does not support.

A linked editorial (PMID 33264550, Grothey, N Engl J Med 2020;383:2283-5) and two letters (PMID 33704946, Battistuzzi and colleagues; PMID 33704947, Sorscher) were identified in PubMed but their texts were not read for this record, so no argument is attributed to them.
33264544.n: 307 previously untreated patients with MSI-high or mismatch repair-deficient stage IV colorectal cancer randomised 1:1 at 192 sites in 23 countries (153 pembrolizumab, 154 investigator's choice chemotherapy); 68% right-sided and 30% left-sided primaries, safety assessed in 153 and 143 treated patients. Second interim analysis at a median follow-up of 32.4 months, with 125 of the 190 deaths required for the final survival analysis and 56 of 154 chemotherapy patients (36%) crossed over on study
33264544.bottom_line: Establishes pembrolizumab as a first-line option in MSI-high or mismatch repair-deficient metastatic colorectal cancer: median progression-free survival 16.5 against 8.2 months, with responses lasting far longer (82.6% against 35.3% ongoing at two years) and a third of the grade 3 or higher treatment-related toxicity. It does not establish survival benefit - that endpoint was still masked at 125 of 190 deaths, and 59% of the chemotherapy arm went on to a checkpoint inhibitor anyway - and it does not establish benefit for everyone: 29.4% progressed as their best response, the curves cross early, proportional hazards failed, and no marker identifies the patients who should have had chemotherapy. For liver metastases it speaks only to sequencing: 9% of patients had curative-intent surgery and they were censored at the operation.

The trial was designed by academic investigators together with sponsor employees, three of whom are co-authors, and the first draft was written with assistance from a medical writer employed by the sponsor.
