limitations: The panel states it found little evidence to recommend specific immunosuppression strategies in this setting, with data mostly extrapolated from the literature on recurrent hepatocellular carcinoma after transplantation
It states there is little evidence to support liver transplantation for resectable disease, and no evidence to support it in patients who present with or develop extrahepatic metastases
It states there is little evidence to recommend routine adjuvant chemotherapy after transplantation and calls for future trials given the potential toxicity
It states the long-term oncological outcomes of the RAPID technique are unclear, with concern about leaving tumour in situ amid circulating hypertrophic growth factors under immunosuppression

It states that living donation circumvents the waiting-list consequences of using deceased-donor grafts but at the expense of risk to the living donor, and that recipients and potential donors must be counselled that re-transplantation will not be offered

It records that organ allocation and waitlist prioritisation are an ethical problem on which agreement about a fair outcome is often unreachable, and defers those decisions to national or centre-level policy
It states that prospective trials are needed to elucidate biological prognostic factors and that this document is a step towards, not an instance of, evidence-based practice
critique: Every statement predates any randomised evidence. The literature search closed on 31 October 2020, three and a half years before TransMet reported, so the only transplant outcome data available to the panel were single-arm series, most of them from one centre.

The numerical gates that decide eligibility are precise and externally unvalidated, and all come from the same small Oslo experience: metabolic tumour volume above 70 cm3 and total lesion glycolysis above 260 g from PET series of a few dozen patients in which the thresholds were themselves derived, and CEA above 80 micrograms/L from SECA-I. A consensus document converts derivation-sample cut-points into eligibility criteria without saying so.

The blanket exclusion of MSI-high and mismatch repair-deficient patients rests on the prospect of needing checkpoint inhibitors after transplantation and the attendant rejection risk, not on any transplant outcome data in such patients - and it excludes precisely the group whose systemic prognosis has since changed most.
The exclusion of BRAF V600E disease is absolute, again without transplant outcome data, in a document written before first-line encorafenib and cetuximab doubled survival in that subtype.

Consensus was defined as 70% agreement, so a statement could become a guideline criterion with nearly a third of the panel against it, and the paper does not report the vote distribution for any individual statement. The record shows final voting by a subset of the panel, and four of 44 statements had to be modified to reach even that threshold.

The literature review was not systematic by any standard: multiple unspecified PubMed searches on three broad terms, English-language papers only despite a stated absence of language limits, further references added by authors where they judged it appropriate, and no inclusion criteria, screening counts or risk-of-bias assessment.

No formal grading of evidence or strength of recommendation is applied to any of the 44 statements, so a reader cannot tell which rest on data and which on opinion - a distinction the panel's own text shows is large.

The preliminary statements were written by the Scientific Committee before the panel voted, so the agenda and the wording were set by a subgroup and the Expert Panel's role was to accept, reject or modify them.

The document sets an outcome target of 5-year survival above 50% without specifying the denominator - transplanted patients or all listed - which is the distinction that moves the Oslo figures by eight percentage points, and without saying what happens to a programme that fails it.

The criteria require at least one line of chemotherapy with response observed for six months and at least a year from diagnosis of non-resectable disease, which guarantees that candidates have already survived and responded for a year or more. A document aimed at identifying favourable biology selects on it and then reports survival as an outcome of the operation.

Transplantation is restricted to non-resectable disease, but no definition of non-resectability is offered beyond multidisciplinary judgement - the same judgement that varies between centres, as CAIRO5's panel data show, and the same judgement that the whole algorithm then depends on.
The panel is 24 clinicians and one bioethicist with no patient or donor representative, no methodologist and no statistician named, and no plan or interval for updating the document.

It is stricter than later guidance: ESMO asks only for disease stabilisation for at least three months no later than third line and sets no MSI, BRAF or PET-volume exclusion, so the same patient can be transplantable under one document and excluded under the other.
No funding statement appears, and no linked editorial or comment on these guidelines was found in PubMed, so no independent published critique informs this record.
34506756.bottom_line: Gives the field its first common vocabulary, selection framework and algorithm for transplantation in non-resectable colorectal liver metastases, and its most useful content is the honesty of its own text: little evidence on immunosuppression, none for extrahepatic disease, none for resectable disease, unclear long-term outcomes for RAPID. It is not an evidence base: every criterion predates any randomised trial, the numerical gates (70 cm3, 260 g, CEA 80) are unvalidated cut-points from the derivation cohorts of one centre, molecular exclusions for MSI-high and BRAF V600E rest on no transplant data at all, and consensus required only 70% agreement with no vote distributions or evidence grades reported. Read it as the terms on which the field agreed to proceed in 2021, not as a test of who should be transplanted.
34506756.funding: No funding statement appears. Three of the 24 panellists declare interests outside the study: honoraria from Astellas Pharma Europe, research grants from Bayer and Roche with consulting fees from AstraZeneca, Novartis and Roche, and symposium honoraria from Merck Serono and Sanofi; all other authors declare no competing interests

limitations: The authors state the trial was not designed or powered for overall survival, and that higher rates of subsequent local therapy including radioembolization in the control arm confound that endpoint
They state that 28 of 215 patients assigned to radioembolization did not receive it, and that the trial ran for eight years in a changing treatment landscape

They state BRAF and NRAS status was not assessed, that only 17% received an EGFR inhibitor first line and 5% second line, and that because the progression-free survival hazard ratio in KRAS wild-type tumours was 0.79 it is uncertain whether radioembolization would add anything to chemotherapy plus EGFR inhibition
They acknowledge unavoidable imbalance in adverse-event reporting between an arm receiving an extra procedure and one not

They note that the meta-analytic threshold at which a progression-free survival hazard ratio implies survival benefit (below 0.77) has been established only in the first-line setting, and no such data exist for second line
The statistical analysis plan was amended after FDA agreement, with an additional censoring rule and a cut-off-date criterion, so the final analysis used 267 events rather than the planned number
critique: The trial is positive on surrogates and flat on survival. Median progression-free survival gained 0.8 months (8.0 against 7.2) and median overall survival was numerically worse with radioembolization (14.0 against 14.4 months, HR 1.07, 95% CI 0.86-1.32). The clinical case therefore rests on about two months of hepatic progression-free survival.

The endpoints were censored in a way that removes the information most relevant to them: patients who received subsequent therapy before their last tumour assessment were censored at that assessment. Since control patients went on to further local therapy including radioembolization more often, the arm with more subsequent treatment is preferentially censored out of the progression analysis.

The analysis plan was changed during the trial with an added censoring rule and a new cut-off criterion agreed with the regulator, and the final analysis rests on fewer events than planned. A device trial whose statistical plan is amended mid-course, with the sponsor collaborating on analysis, invites exactly the scrutiny the paper does not supply.

Testing was one-sided throughout (1-sided p=0.0013 and p<0.0001), and the trial was declared positive if either co-primary endpoint reached significance - a design that nearly guarantees a positive label for a liver-directed treatment whose second endpoint is progression in the liver.

Hepatic progression-free survival is the endpoint a liver-directed therapy must move, and the same pattern seen in SIRFLOX and FOXFIRE - better hepatic control, no survival gain - recurs here. The paper does not report where first progression occurred in each arm, which is the analysis that showed in the resin-microsphere trials that failure simply relocated.

Toxicity is substantially worse and is partly explained away: grade 3 or worse adverse events 68.4% against 49.3%, with three grade 5 events deemed possibly related - radiation-induced liver disease, hepatic failure and portal hypertension at three, three and five months. For a patient who might later need resection, ablation or further liver-directed treatment, that is a loss of hepatic reserve, and no analysis of subsequent liver-directed therapy feasibility is reported.

The control arm was not contemporary standard of care for the half of patients without a KRAS mutation: NRAS and BRAF were never tested, and EGFR inhibitors reached 17% first line and 5% second line. The authors concede the benefit in wild-type disease is uncertain, which means the trial's applicability is confined to KRAS-mutant patients - a subgroup conclusion.

Thirteen percent of the radioembolization arm never received the intervention, which dilutes the intention-to-treat estimate, and the per-protocol survival analysis (15.2 against 14.3 months, HR 0.96) remains null.

The sidedness result contradicts the other randomised radioembolization evidence: here left-sided primaries benefited (HR 0.65) and right-sided did not, while the pooled resin-microsphere analysis found its only favourable survival signal in right-sided tumours. Neither finding survives the other.

The subgroup list reported as prespecified contains six positive strata including one with a hazard ratio of 0.33 for three or fewer lesions, in a trial where 39% of patients had more than ten; no interaction tests or multiplicity adjustment are reported, and the stated absence of post hoc analyses does not address the number of prespecified ones.

Dosimetry was single-compartment at 120 Gy throughout an eight-year trial, predating personalised and segmental dosing, so the intervention tested is already superseded while its toxicity profile is the one reported.
No quality-of-life or patient-reported outcome is reported, in a trial whose benefit is two months of hepatic progression-free survival bought with a 19-point increase in grade 3 or worse toxicity.
A linked editorial (PMID 34541862, Lentz and Messersmith, J Clin Oncol 2021;39:3887-9) was identified in PubMed but its text was not read for this record.
34541864.n: 428 patients with unresectable unilobar or bilobar colorectal liver metastases progressing after oxaliplatin- or irinotecan-based first-line therapy, randomised 1:1 at 95 centres in North America, Europe and Asia between May 2012 and August 2020 from 539 assessed (215 radioembolization plus second-line chemotherapy, 213 chemotherapy alone); 82% had bilobar disease, 39% more than ten lesions, 47% a KRAS mutation, and BRAF and NRAS were never tested. Twenty-eight of 215 allocated to radioembolization (13%) never received it, and the analysis used 267 progression events against the 287 originally planned
34541864.bottom_line: Establishes that adding yttrium-90 glass microsphere radioembolization to second-line chemotherapy in unresectable colorectal liver metastases delays progression - progression-free survival 8.0 against 7.2 months (HR 0.69) and hepatic progression-free survival 9.1 against 7.2 (HR 0.59) - and raises response from 21% to 34%. It shows no survival benefit, with overall survival numerically worse (14.0 against 14.4 months, HR 1.07), at the cost of grade 3 or worse toxicity in 68% against 49% and three deaths from radiation liver disease, hepatic failure and portal hypertension. Both primary endpoints were tested one-sided with either sufficing, patients were censored when they received subsequent therapy, the plan was amended mid-trial, half the cohort was KRAS wild-type but almost none received an EGFR inhibitor, and the device manufacturer collaborated on design and analysis.
34541864.funding: Boston Scientific Corporation sponsored the trial, supplied the device, and collaborated with the steering committee on design and on the collection, analysis and interpretation of data; a company employee is a co-author and is credited with financial and administrative support and with conception and design. Patient-level data are available only on application to the sponsor

limitations: The number of patients was small, so the authors state conclusions should be made with caution
They state there was a risk of selection bias because only patients who received transplants were included
They state the findings should be further investigated in future studies
critique: Thirty percent of recipients recurred, all within 200 days of transplantation - at 92, 121 and 199 days - which the accompanying commentary notes would be alarming in any other transplant oncology indication, and which means sustained response to systemic and local therapy did not identify favourable biology in a third of this highly selected group.

Survival of 100% at 1.5 years with a median follow-up of 1.5 years and a minimum of 0.4 years is a statement about the perioperative period, not about the disease. The commentary printed alongside calls it akin to a technical demonstration of an operation already well established for other indications.

The outcomes of the 79 patients evaluated and not transplanted, and of the 2 who received deceased-donor grafts, are not reported. Without them the selection process that produced these results cannot be assessed, and the paper has no denominator for the strategy it recommends.

Three different centre protocols with three different candidate selection processes are pooled into one cohort of ten, with the centre-specific criteria relegated to a supplementary table; the Methods describe only the common framework, so what any individual patient had to satisfy is not recoverable from the paper.

Prior treatment was heterogeneous and intensive - 40% prior liver resection, 30% hepatic arterial infusion, 30% ablation, a median 22.5 cycles of chemotherapy - so the intervention being reported is the final step of a long individualised sequence rather than a defined treatment.

Total tumour burden at transplantation is not reported. The commentary names this explicitly as unclear, and the paper gives Fong and Oslo scores without lesion number, lesion size or metabolic tumour volume at the time of operation, which are the variables the Oslo group's own work identifies as decisive.

Nine of ten explants contained viable tumour and one carried a positive portal lymph node, so a patient with nodal metastatic disease was transplanted - and that patient developed peritoneal recurrence. Frozen-section nodal assessment is not described as part of the protocol, in contrast to the Oslo series where it excluded 7 of 72 listed patients.

The harms of the operation are substantial in both directions and are reported without being weighed: Clavien-Dindo grade IIIA or IIIB complications in 4 of 10 recipients including hepatic artery thrombosis requiring reoperation and biliary complications, and one donor with a grade IIIB complication requiring evacuation of a haematoma, with median donor blood loss of 525 mL and a range to 1400 mL.

A healthy person underwent a hepatectomy for each of these ten operations. The paper reports donor outcomes but offers no formal risk-benefit framing of exposing a donor to that risk for an indication with 30% recurrence inside seven months, which is the commentary's central objection.

There is no comparator arm. The implied alternative is continued systemic therapy, and the paper does not report what the 79 non-transplanted patients received or how they fared, so no estimate of benefit over the alternative exists within the study.

Internal inconsistencies: the abstract tallies recipient complications as 3 none, 3 grade II and 4 grade III while Table 4 gives 3 none, 3 grade II, 2 grade IIIA and 2 grade IIIB; and the abstract dates the transplants to July 2017 to October 2020 while the Methods give December 2017 to May 2021.

Follow-up is too short for the endpoint that matters and is reported as a Kaplan-Meier estimate anyway: recurrence-free survival of 62% at 1.5 years comes from 10 patients with 3 events and no confidence interval.
No funding statement appears anywhere in the paper.
The invited commentary (PMID 35353145, Shah and Vagefi, 'Let's Walk, Not Run', JAMA Surg 2022;157:530-1) is printed with the article and its arguments are reflected above.
35353121.n: 10 consecutive recipients of living-donor liver transplantation for unresectable liver-confined colorectal metastases at three North American centres, drawn from 91 patients evaluated (12, 13%, achieved sustained disease control and became candidates; 2 with high MELD received deceased-donor grafts). Median Fong score 2.5 (range 1-4), Oslo score 1.5 (0-2), 22.5 chemotherapy cycles (6-37), CEA 7.7 ng/mL, 1.7 years from metastasis diagnosis to transplant; 9 of 10 synchronous, 8 of 10 bilobar, 4 with prior liver resection, 3 with prior hepatic arterial infusion, 3 with prior ablation. Median follow-up 1.5 years (range 0.4-2.9) with 10 living donors
35353121.bottom_line: Shows that living-donor liver transplantation for unresectable liver-confined colorectal metastases can be done safely at experienced North American centres - all ten recipients alive at a median 1.5 years, all ten donors recovered, with four recipient grade III complications and one donor grade IIIB. It establishes nothing about oncological benefit: 30% recurred within 200 days despite sustained pretransplant response, follow-up is a median of 1.5 years, total tumour burden at transplant is not reported, three different centre protocols are pooled into a cohort of ten, and the 79 patients evaluated but not transplanted - the comparison that would show what selection achieved - are not described at all.
35353121.funding: No funding statement appears. Two authors declare grants or personal fees from Medtronic, Integra LifeSciences, Olympus, Fujifilm, Ethicon, Roche, Bayer, AstraZeneca and Novartis outside the submitted work; no other disclosures were reported

limitations: The study was retrospective and the total number of patients is relatively low (n=40), which the authors answer by noting it is the largest material on liver transplantation for colorectal liver metastases worldwide with a very long observation time

Variability in the interval between the PET/CT and transplantation could be a source of bias; the authors argue it was probably not critical because the interval did not differ between the high and low metabolic tumour volume groups
The PET followed a standard clinical protocol without respiratory gating for liver metastases or for detection of lesions at the liver hilum

SECA-1 and SECA-2 eligibility differed - SECA-2 excluded patients with progressive disease and those within a year of diagnosis - so SECA-2 patients may have had more favourable biology, with 5-year survival of 60% against 83%; the authors state the cohorts were pooled and not compared
They note that very small or microscopic residual disease is undetectable by any imaging modality, which is why the recurrence rate after transplantation is high and surveillance matters
critique: The 70 cm3 threshold was derived by ROC analysis in the same 40 patients in which it is then tested, with no bootstrap, cross-validation or external cohort. Its apparent discrimination is fitted to the outcome it is said to predict.

The same ROC procedure produced cut-offs for SUVmax, SUVmean, SUVpeak and tumour-to-background ratio, which are then discarded for failing to separate survival. One fitting exercise is used to validate the parameters that worked and to dismiss those that did not, in the same 40 patients.

The defence of the scan-to-transplant interval does not address the paper's own result. The prognostic effect was significant only among the 20 patients scanned within 90 days (p<0.001) and not among the 20 scanned earlier (p=0.093). Showing that the interval did not differ between metabolic tumour volume groups is not the relevant test, and the recommendation to rescan after three months rests on a split of 20 patients against 20.

Metabolic tumour volume is collinear with every conventional adverse feature and no multivariable analysis is offered: median CEA 95 against 3 ug/L, 11 against 6 metastases, largest lesion 83 against 29 mm, Fong score 4 against 2, progressive disease at transplant 79% against 19%, and two or three lines of chemotherapy 93% against 31%, all p below 0.016. Nothing here distinguishes a PET measurement from 'large-volume disease progressing on multiple lines of chemotherapy', which needs no PET to recognise.

Trial membership confounds the comparison and is not adjusted for. SECA-1 admitted patients progressing on chemotherapy and within a year of diagnosis and gave 60% five-year survival; SECA-2 excluded them and gave 83%. Pooling the two while conceding both the eligibility difference and the 23-point survival difference leaves the metabolic tumour volume effect entangled with which study a patient entered.

The explanation given for better post-recurrence survival in the low-volume group - resectable pulmonary relapse - is contradicted by the paper's own data: the first site of recurrence did not differ significantly (lung in 11 of 26 against 6 of 14, p=0.233). The authors call it the most plausible explanation regardless.

The measure being promoted as a selection criterion does not identify cure. All 14 high-volume and 19 of 26 low-volume patients recurred, and five-year disease-free survival was 21% against 0%, so even the favourable group is mostly recurrent disease managed afterwards.

There is no comparator of any kind - no resection, no chemotherapy, no listed-but-not-transplanted group - so the paper can say that high metabolic tumour volume predicts worse outcome after transplantation but nothing about whether such a patient would do better or worse with any alternative.

Six PET parameters are each tested against overall, disease-free and post-recurrence survival in 40 patients with no adjustment for multiplicity, and the conclusion retains the two that reached significance.

Reproducibility is unaddressed in a paper recommending implementation elsewhere: one scanner, one centre, a fixed 40% SUVmax threshold, no respiratory gating, and no inter-reader, test-retest or cross-scanner agreement data for a liver volume measurement that is known to be sensitive to all of these.

The cohort was pre-filtered by the same test. Every patient had to be PET-negative for extrahepatic disease to be transplanted - in SECA-1 the PET excluded about a third of candidates - so metabolic tumour volume is evaluated only among patients the modality had already selected.

No survival estimate in the paper carries a confidence interval, and Table 1's percentages do not reconcile with its counts (18 N0 patients reported as 55%), so the baseline table cannot be cross-footed.
No linked editorial or comment on this paper was found in PubMed, so no independent published critique informs this record.
36241941.n: All 40 patients transplanted for unresectable colorectal liver metastases at Oslo University Hospital in SECA-1 (n=23) and SECA-2 (n=17) between 2006 and 2018 with an evaluable preoperative 18F-FDG PET/CT; 26 had a total metabolic tumour volume below 70 cm3 and 14 above, and 20 were scanned within 90 days of transplantation
36241941.bottom_line: Shows that across the whole 40-patient Oslo transplant experience, total metabolic tumour volume on preoperative PET separates survivors sharply - 5-year overall survival 76% against 21% and 10-year 50% against 7% below and above 70 cm3 - and that the signal exists only when the scan is recent, which supports rescanning candidates who wait more than three months. It does not establish the threshold or the measure: the 70 cm3 cut was fitted by ROC in these same patients, it has never been tested elsewhere, it tracks CEA, lesion number, lesion size, Fong score and progression on chemotherapy so closely that no independent information is demonstrated, and SECA-1 and SECA-2 were pooled despite differing eligibility and a 23-point survival gap. With no comparator arm, it cannot say what a high-volume patient should be offered instead.
36241941.funding: Open access funding and support from Vestre Viken Hospital Trust, Oslo University Hospital and the Norwegian Cancer Society. The authors declare no conflicts of interest

limitations: The panel states that the scope was designed to address selected areas of uncertainty, so not all possible treatment options have been addressed, particularly for liver-directed therapy
Selection criteria for identifying appropriate surgical candidates and the timing of surgery are explicitly outside the scope of the systematic review

Testing for molecular subtypes was outside scope, and the guideline assumes patients will have access to the molecular testing its own sidedness, RAS, BRAF and mismatch repair recommendations require; HER2-amplified and TRK-fusion disease were also out of scope
The randomised phase 2 SABR-COMET trial did not meet the inclusion criteria because it included only a small proportion of colorectal patients
Many recommendations are graded weak on moderate or lower quality evidence, which under GRADE means most informed people would choose the recommended course and a substantial number would not

The search closed on 20 June 2022, and the guideline disclaimer states the information should not be relied upon as complete or accurate, is not continually updated, and may not reflect the most recent evidence
Cytoreductive surgery is qualified as suitable only for higher-volume or specialised centres and experienced operators
critique: On the one liver question with randomised evidence, the guideline recommends a treatment that failed its trial. EORTC 40983's intention-to-treat progression-free survival hazard ratio was 0.79 (95% CI 0.62-1.02) with no survival benefit; the recommendation for perioperative chemotherapy is graded evidence-based with benefits outweighing harms on the strength of an exploratory analysis restricted to the 83% of patients who were resected (HR 0.73, 0.55-0.97).

The prescribed duration is a trial artefact. Six months of total perioperative chemotherapy is recommended because six months is what EORTC 40983 administered, in a guideline that reports the same trial's primary endpoint as non-significant two paragraphs earlier, and that elsewhere cites evidence that six or more cycles increases surgical morbidity.

The second supporting trial points the other way on the endpoint that matters: JCOG0603 improved disease-free survival (HR 0.67, 95% CI 0.50-0.92) with an overall survival hazard ratio of 1.25 (0.78-2.0). The guideline reports both numbers and reasons from the first.

For SBRT the panel excluded the only randomised trial and recommended on uncontrolled data. SABR-COMET was ruled out for having few colorectal patients, and the recommendation then rests on a pooled analysis of 18 non-randomised single-arm series published 2006 to 2017, in previously treated patients, with no comparator of any kind.

The SBRT evidence contains a signal against itself that is reported and not acted on: the correlation between dose and 2-year overall survival was 0.29. If radiation dose does not track survival, the survival figures quoted (67% at 1 year, 57% at 2 years) are more plausibly describing patient selection than treatment effect.

The SIRT section recommends against routine use and simultaneously describes SIRT as an option to explore for downstaging hepatic metastases to operability - an indication no included study tested. Neither the first-line meta-analysis nor EPOCH had conversion to resection as an endpoint.

Thermal ablation is absent from the guideline entirely. It is not among the interventions listed in the search protocol, so the commonest liver-directed treatment for small colorectal liver metastases is excluded by design, not for want of randomised evidence - CLOCC had been published in 2012 and 2017.

Several inclusion rules narrow the evidence base without justification: where more than one systematic review or trial report addressed a question, only the most recent was retained; non-English publications were excluded; and conference data were excluded unless published within two years. A guideline built on single most-recent reviews inherits each review's choices without examining them.

The public review consisted of a two-week open comment period that required submitting a confidentiality agreement before commenting, and the guideline does not report what comments were received or what changed in response.

No update interval is specified: ASCO states it will determine the need to update on the basis of formal review. A guideline whose own disclaimer says it is not continually updated also sets no date at which it expires.

The search closed before most of the evidence a liver surgeon now works from. COLLISION, TRANSMET, BREAKWATER, CheckMate 8HW and the CAIRO5 report all postdate 20 June 2022, and all four of the first concern exactly the patients this guideline's liver questions address.

The cost section discusses out-of-pocket burden at length but presents no cost-effectiveness analysis of any liver-directed recommendation; the analyses it does cite concern molecular testing and anti-EGFR selection, and report costs per quality-adjusted life year above conventionally accepted thresholds.

One patient representative sat on a panel of around twenty clinicians, and nothing in the document records how patient input affected any recommendation, despite shared decision making being invoked as the fallback for every weak recommendation.

The conflict-of-interest statement is a statement about ASCO's policy rather than about the relationships, which run to more than a hundred lines of declared industry funding at the head of the manuscript, in a guideline that recommends for and against specific drugs and devices.
No linked editorial or comment on this guideline was found in PubMed, so no independent published critique informs this record.
36252154.bottom_line: Gives a clear, GRADE-graded statement of first-line systemic therapy in metastatic colorectal cancer - doublet chemotherapy for most, anti-EGFR only for left-sided RAS wild-type disease, no oxaliplatin HIPEC - and confirms that surgery should be offered to anyone resectable. It answers almost none of the questions a hepatobiliary surgeon asks: resectability, future liver remnant, staged hepatectomy, conversion strategy and the timing of surgery are all declared out of scope, thermal ablation is excluded from the search protocol altogether, SBRT is recommended on 18 uncontrolled series after the only randomised trial was excluded, and the perioperative chemotherapy recommendation rests on the resected subgroup of a trial that missed its primary endpoint. Its search closed in June 2022, before COLLISION, TRANSMET, BREAKWATER and CheckMate 8HW.
36252154.funding: All funding for the administration of the project was provided by ASCO. The panel's disclosures, printed ahead of the manuscript, list consulting or advisory roles, speakers' bureaux, stock, patents and institutional research funding from the manufacturers of most of the drugs and devices considered, including Bristol Myers Squibb, Merck, Roche/Genentech, Amgen, Bayer, Pfizer, AstraZeneca, Taiho, Servier, Guerbet and InSightec; ASCO states that in accordance with its policy the majority of panel members did not disclose any relationship constituting a conflict

limitations: Overall survival was not mature at the time of this report and will be published separately; the authors state twice that definitive conclusions should await it
FOLFOXIRI was not investigated in patients with a left-sided RAS and BRAF wild-type tumour, so the trial does not identify one optimal induction regimen across the whole population

The baseline unresectability criterion - no R0 achievable with resection alone in one stage - means some patients could have been treated locally upfront by adding ablation or by a two-stage resection with or without portal vein embolisation

The authors note that the relevance of progression-free survival as a surrogate for overall survival has been questioned, and that reporting a conversion rate without long-term outcome may be misleading
Panel surgeons varied in their resectability assessments, which the authors report and interpret as an argument for panel review rather than single-surgeon judgment

Adjuvant chemotherapy after local treatment was given to only a small number of patients, which the authors attribute mainly to Dutch guidelines not recommending it, since its value after downsizing is unknown
critique: The resectability endpoint rests on a panel that mostly did not agree. Consensus among panel surgeons was present in 345 of 521 baseline evaluations (66%) and in only 286 of 689 follow-up evaluations (42%); where surgeons split, the panel chair cast the deciding vote. In more than half the follow-up assessments the conversion endpoint was therefore decided by one surgeon's opinion.

Where evaluations fell outside the scheduled panel windows, or after local treatment had been given, or once the panel had called a patient permanently unresectable, the local investigator's assessment was used instead - in a trial where investigators and patients were unmasked to allocation.

The negative comparison was closed early for futility and so cannot support its conclusion. Groups C and D needed 256 events and were stopped in March 2022; the resulting hazard ratio of 1.11 (95% CI 0.84-1.48) is compatible with anything from a 16% benefit to a 48% harm from panitumumab, yet the Interpretation states panitumumab showed no clinical benefit.

The paper states the interim efficacy boundary (p 0.006 or less) but never states the adjusted significance level at the final analysis under the Hwang-Shih-DeCani spending function, so a reader cannot check whether the primary p=0.032 cleared the boundary that actually applied.

The randomised comparisons were redefined mid-trial. Until protocol amendment 7.0 in February 2017 allocation depended on RAS status alone, and 14 patients with right-sided or BRAF-mutant tumours were randomised into groups C and D. They stay in the modified intention-to-treat analysis of the comparison they do not belong to, and the per-protocol analysis excluding them is relegated to the appendix.

The chemotherapy backbone was not randomised in either comparison: FOLFOX versus FOLFIRI was chosen by local investigator and patient preference. Centre preference was a stratification factor, which balances the arms without making the backbone comparable within them.

Response and resectability came apart completely in groups C and D - objective response 53% versus 80% (p<0.0001) and depth of response 33% versus 49% (p<0.0001) with complete local treatment identical at 58% in both arms (p=1.00) - and the paper's explanation (vessels, biliary structures, too many segments) is offered as a possibility to be analysed in future, with no supporting data. Depth of response was a post hoc endpoint, and patients without post-baseline imaging were simply classed as not evaluable and dropped from it.

The entry definition of unresectability excludes exactly the techniques the participating centres use - ablation and staged hepatectomy - and only a minority were judged permanently unresectable. Most patients therefore entered a conversion trial while being locally treatable under a broader contemporary definition, which the authors state and then set aside on the grounds that stratification protects the comparison. It protects internal validity and says nothing about what the reported conversion rates mean outside the trial.

The price of the 1.6-month median progression-free survival gain with the triplet is itemised in tables but never weighed: grade 3 or worse adverse events 59% versus 76% (p=0.0027), dose reductions in 55% of group B, serious adverse events in 52%, seven treatment-related deaths in group B, and postoperative Clavien-Dindo grade 3 or worse complications in 15% versus 27% (p=0.076) after a regimen that doubled two-stage surgery (11% versus 28%).
Three patients (2%) had local treatment performed against panel advice, so the conversion endpoint includes operations the adjudicating body did not endorse.

Adjuvant chemotherapy after local treatment is reported only as given to few patients, without arm-level numbers, in a trial whose arms converted at different rates - so post-conversion management, which bears directly on the progression-free survival endpoint, is both uncontrolled and unreported.

Survival data existed at analysis and were withheld: the paper prints 219 deaths (75%) in groups A and B and 125 (54%) in groups C and D, then defers the endpoint to a separate publication while recommending FOLFOXIRI-bevacizumab as the preferred regimen.

The trial was funded by unrestricted grants from Roche and Amgen, whose drugs are the two targeted agents being compared in groups C and D, and the comparison between them was the one closed for futility.
A linked Lancet Oncology comment (PMID 37329890, Imai and Baba, 2023) was identified in PubMed but its text was not available here, so its objections are not reflected in this record.
37329889.n: 530 patients with previously untreated, liver-only colorectal metastases centrally judged unresectable, randomised at 46 Dutch and one Belgian centre from 584 assessed (148 group A, 146 group B, 118 group C, 118 group D); 521 in the modified intention-to-treat analysis after nine exclusions (147, 144, 114, 116). Median age 62, 327 men (62%); median 12 liver metastases across 6 segments, most synchronous and with the primary tumour still in situ. Median follow-up 51.1 months
37329889.bottom_line: Establishes that for initially unresectable liver-only colorectal metastases with a right-sided or RAS/BRAF-mutant primary, FOLFOXIRI plus bevacizumab lengthens progression-free survival by a median of 1.6 months and raises complete local treatment from 37% to 51% against a doublet, and that for left-sided wild-type disease panitumumab raises response from 53% to 80% without converting a single extra patient (58% in both arms). 37329889.funding: Unrestricted scientific grants from Roche and Amgen, the Netherlands - the manufacturers of bevacizumab and panitumumab, the two targeted agents compared in groups C and D; the funders are stated to have had no role in design, data collection, analysis, interpretation or writing.
