limitations: The classifier was developed only in patients undergoing surgery, so it is untested for ablation or stereotactic radiotherapy

The authors state that the magnitude of the concordance probability estimates reflects the substantial clinical heterogeneity of colorectal liver oligometastases, and that larger cohorts are needed to clarify the role of molecular subtyping

They state that no gold standard reference existed in the validation cohort against which the computed subtypes could be checked, so biological plausibility analyses had to stand in for a reference standard

They present the classification as prognostic only, warranting further study as a possible predictive biomarker, and report no significant interaction between subtype or integrated risk group and cetuximab randomisation
Three patients had to be dropped from the integrated risk group analysis because the clinical risk score could not be computed from available data

They acknowledge from their own earlier work that consensus molecular subtypes leave about a third of liver metastases unclassifiable, which is why the metastasis has to be staged separately from the primary
critique: The study is described as the first clinical validation, but the reference standard the classifier was trained against is the authors' own similarity network fusion clustering of the discovery cohort. The 96% accuracy therefore measures agreement with an unvalidated set of labels, and in the validation cohort there is no reference at all - as the Outcomes section concedes - so no accuracy figure applies to the 147 patients whose subtypes anchor every result.

The low-risk integrated group that supplies the headline 78% 5-year overall survival has a 95% CI of 44 to 93%, which implies a handful of events, yet neither the number of patients nor the number of deaths in that group is printed in the text, the figure or Table 2.

The overall survival comparison across the three subtypes failed its stated test (log-rank p=0.083). Significance is recovered by collapsing stromal with canonical (p=0.045), a pairwise regrouping that is not the prespecified hypothesis - which was that immune would beat canonical and stromal - and is reported without correction for having tried both.

The integrated grouping is not monotone in its own inputs: canonical, the worst subtype, enters the low-risk group whenever the clinical risk score is low, while stromal appears in both the intermediate and high groups. Low and intermediate 5-year progression-free survival are 44% and 40%, indistinguishable, so the three-level scheme separates one group from two rather than three from each other.

The improvement in discrimination is small and its intervals overlap almost entirely: Gonen and Heller's K from 0.55 (0.49-0.61) to 0.62 (0.57-0.67) for progression-free survival and 0.59 (0.52-0.66) to 0.63 (0.56-0.70) for overall survival. No test of the difference between concordance statistics is reported, no comparison against a model containing an arbitrary three-level variable, and no calibration assessment of any kind.

Two of the senior authors hold issued patents on diagnosis and triage of patients with colorectal liver metastases and provisional patents on molecular subtyping to personalise treatment - that is, on the classifier being validated here. The disclosure is made, but the recommendation that the classification be taken forward as a predictive biomarker and a stratification factor in future trials comes from the patent holders.

147 patients are analysed out of the 257 randomised in New EPOC, selected by having had resection and usable archival metastasis tissue. No comparison of the included 147 with the excluded patients is shown, and no accounting of why tissue was unavailable, so the validation cohort's representativeness of the trial is untested.

Discovery and validation used different assay platforms - whole transcriptome RNA sequencing plus miRNA profiling on one side, microarray on the other - and a 31-feature expression classifier was carried across that change with no bridging or platform-concordance analysis in the main text.

The two cohorts are not comparable in clinical risk (clinical risk score 2 or more in 85% of validation against 63% of discovery, more than one metastasis in 78% against 42%), so the integrated groups are not populated the same way in the cohort where the thresholds were set and the cohort where they are tested.

The time-to-event clock differs between cohorts - date of surgery in discovery, date of randomisation in validation - yet the paper reports progression-free and overall survival as highly concordant between them (eFigure 6), a comparison of intervals measured from different origins.

The biological corroboration is circular: single-sample gene set enrichment and immune deconvolution are run on the same expression data from which the subtypes were computed, so they can only reproduce the clustering that defined them, not confirm it against an independent measurement such as stained sections in this cohort.

Roughly half of the validation cohort was randomised to cetuximab, which shortened survival in New EPOC itself. Cetuximab is entered as a covariate, but the absolute survival figures - including the 78% that is the paper's selling point - come from a cohort half of whom received a treatment that is no longer given.

The clinical risk score requires CEA, tumour size and tumour number, but the paper never states at what point relative to perioperative chemotherapy those components were recorded in the trial cohort, even though every patient had chemotherapy before resection, so the score may not be measuring what it measured in Fong's untreated surgical series.
No linked editorial or comment on this paper was found in PubMed, so no independent published critique informs this record.
37471075.n: 147 patients from the phase 3 New EPOC trial who underwent hepatic resection and had archival liver metastasis tissue profiled (median follow-up 53.4 months), validating a 31-feature classifier trained in a discovery cohort of 93 patients resected at the University of Chicago and NorthShore between 1994 and 2012; matched primary tumours were available for 124, and 3 patients were excluded from the integrated risk analysis because the clinical risk score could not be computed
37471075.bottom_line: Shows that a biologically derived three-subtype expression classifier applied to the resected liver metastasis separates progression-free survival after hepatectomy (5-year 43% immune, 26% stromal, 14% canonical) in an independent trial cohort, and adds a small amount of discrimination to the Fong clinical risk score. It does not show the classification changes what should be done: the overall survival comparison missed significance across three subtypes, there was no interaction with the only randomised treatment available, and the assay needs resected metastatic tissue, so it arrives after the decision it might inform. The headline 78% 5-year survival in the low-risk integrated group has a confidence interval of 44 to 93% and its denominator is never stated.
37471075.funding: The S:CORT consortium is funded by a UK Medical Research Council Stratified Medicine Consortium programme grant (MR/M016587/1) co-funded by Cancer Research UK, with additional support from the Ludwig Cancer Research Foundation; the funders are stated to have had no role in design, analysis or publication, and the study was not NIH funded. Merck KGaA provided cetuximab for New EPOC. Two senior authors report issued patents for 'Methods and Kits for Diagnosis and Triage of Patients with Colorectal Liver Metastases' and provisional patents for 'Molecular Subtyping of Colorectal Liver Metastases to Personalize Treatment Approaches'; disclosures also include honoraria or grants from Merck, AstraZeneca, Varian, Regeneron, Boehringer Ingelheim, Merck Serono and Pierre Fabre, and equity in several biotechnology companies

limitations: The section headed Limitations contains no limitation of the study. It states that SECA-I patients had good quality of life to three years, that transplantation is cost-effective against modern oncological treatment, that the major obstacle internationally is graft scarcity, that only 1 of 11 extended-criteria grafts failed, and that the RAPID technique may expand the donor pool
The authors state elsewhere that disease-free survival is not a valid measure of efficacy in this setting, because recurrence is compatible with long survival
They report that the cohort spans several protocols with different entry criteria and that no adjuvant chemotherapy was given to any patient
They state that one RAPID patient who died of complications 1.4 months after transplantation is excluded from all analyses except disease-free and overall survival

They note that a primary tumour in the ascending colon, an Oslo score of 3 to 4, a lesion of 5.5 cm or more, CEA above 80 ug/L, progression on chemotherapy and nine or more metastases all predict poor outcome, and conclude that selection should require an Oslo score of 0 to 1 and a metabolic tumour volume under 70 cm3
critique: The paper has no limitations section despite having one by title, so every methodological objection below is unacknowledged.

The selection rule the paper concludes with would have admitted a small fraction of its own cohort. An Oslo score of 0 describes 10 patients and a Fong score of 0 to 2 describes 19 of 60; the 88.9% ten-year survival rests on 10 patients and the 100% five-year survival on the 5 patients with a Fong score of 1. No confidence interval accompanies any of these subgroup estimates.

Both selection instruments were built by this group from patients inside this cohort: the Oslo score was derived in SECA-I and the 70 cm3 metabolic tumour volume threshold by ROC analysis in the SECA-1 and SECA-2 patients, all of whom are included here. The paper presents their performance as a selection recommendation without stating that it is apparent performance in the derivation sample.

The two criteria recommended together are not independent of each other or of the factors they are built from. Largest lesion, CEA, progression on chemotherapy and time from primary resection are the Oslo score's own components and are also reported as separate significant predictors, and metabolic tumour volume tracks all of them. No multivariable model appears anywhere.

Prognostic factors were tested one at a time by log-rank in 60 patients - Oslo score, Fong score, metabolic tumour volume, lesion size, CEA, progression, lesion number, primary site, KRAS, nodal stage - with no correction for multiplicity and no prespecified primary analysis, so the two or three thresholds that separated best are the output of a search.

Survival is reported from the date of transplantation, which conditions on having received a graft. Seven of the 72 listed patients were found at laparotomy to have hilar nodal metastases, three developed extrahepatic disease while waiting and one deteriorated; from acceptance onto the list the figures fall to a median 50.8 months and 42.6% at five years, and that analysis sits in a supplementary figure.

The cohort is six protocols treated as one: SECA-I, four separate SECA-II arms and RAPID, with different prognostic entry criteria, different grafts including 11 extended-criteria donors and auxiliary segment 2-3 transplants, across 14 years of changing systemic therapy. Trial arm is never entered as a covariate and the arms are not compared.

One patient with technically resectable disease was randomly assigned to transplantation and is included; the word nonrandomized appears in the title while a randomised comparison involving at least one patient is folded into the same survival curves without being reported as a comparison.

There is no control group of any kind - no chemotherapy, resection, portal vein embolisation or listed-but-untransplanted cohort analysed as a comparator - so the claim that transplantation may be the best option even for resectable extensive disease is supported only by cross-study comparison with other series.

Recurrence was near universal: 47 of 60 patients (78.3%) relapsed at a median 9.0 months and 94% within two years, with median disease-free survival 11.8 months and 18.3% at five years. The argument that disease-free survival is not a valid efficacy measure converts this into a methodological claim and leaves the survival benefit resting on repeated resection of pulmonary metastases under immunosuppression, which is never costed, counted by operation, or reported as time spent disease free.

The ascending-colon finding - median survival 17.9 months and 10% at five years - rests on 10 patients and is offered as a selection criterion alongside the scores, with no interaction test and no adjustment for the tumour burden that accompanies right-sided disease.

Graft outcomes, rejection, immunosuppression exposure and non-cancer mortality are not reported, although the Limitations section cites the performance of extended-criteria grafts as an argument for expanding the indication.
Quality of life and cost-effectiveness are asserted from the authors' own earlier publications rather than measured here, in the section where the study's limitations should be.

Internal inconsistency: Table 1 gives the Fong score distribution as 5/16/25/10/5 while the text gives 5, 16, 25, 9 and 5 and states that 19 patients scored 0 to 2, so the denominators of the key subgroup cannot be reconciled between table and text.

A linked invited commentary (PMID 37494008, Ellis and D'Angelica, JAMA Surg 2023;158:e232933, 'Who Should Undergo Transplant for Unresectable Colorectal Liver Metastases - Finding the Needle in the Haystack') was identified in PubMed but its text was not read for this record.
37494056.n: 72 patients accepted onto the waiting list and 61 transplanted for colorectal liver metastases at Oslo University Hospital between November 2006 and November 2020 across SECA-I, SECA-II arms A to D and RAPID; 60 of the 61 had non-resectable liver-only disease, median age 57.8, median 8 lesions (range 1-53) with largest 35 mm (3-130), all previously treated with fluorouracil and most with irinotecan and oxaliplatin, 12 with prior liver resection and 7 with prior ablation, and none given adjuvant chemotherapy. Eleven listed patients were never transplanted, 7 for hilar nodal disease found at laparotomy
37494056.bottom_line: The largest and most mature transplant series in colorectal liver metastases: 61 patients over 14 years, median overall survival 60.3 months and 50.4% at five years, with the best-selected tenth - Oslo score 0 - reaching 88.9% at ten years, and survival after relapse of 37.1 months on repeated metastasectomy. It does not validate the selection rule it recommends: the Oslo score and the 70 cm3 PET threshold were both derived in patients included here, the favourable strata hold 5 to 19 people with no confidence intervals, every factor was tested singly with no multivariable model, and survival is counted from transplantation rather than from listing, which drops the 11 of 72 patients who never got a graft and takes five-year survival from 50.4% to 42.6%. The section headed Limitations contains none.
37494056.funding: Supported in part by Oslo University Hospital, the Norwegian Cancer Society and the South-Eastern Norway Regional Health Authority; the funders are stated to have had no role in design, conduct, analysis or reporting. The first author reports grants from the Norwegian Cancer Society and the regional health authority during the study; no other disclosures were reported

limitations: The trial was neither designed nor powered to detect a difference in overall survival, because of the low prevalence of KRAS G12C in colorectal cancer; the authors state overall survival data are maturing and longer follow-up is needed

The authors state that even the planned final overall survival analysis, at about 80 deaths, will not provide sufficient power to detect the hypothesised survival difference under the trial's sample size
The trial was not powered to compare the 960-mg and 240-mg sotorasib groups with each other, although the paper concludes in favour of the 960-mg dose
Objective response was not formally assessed, as it sat last in the hierarchical testing sequence behind overall survival
The population was composed primarily of White and Asian patients, with one Black patient enrolled

The authors acknowledge the control regimens have been superseded: SUNLIGHT (trifluridine-tipiracil plus bevacizumab) and FRESCO-2 (fruquintinib) have since shown survival benefit over the monotherapies used as standard care here
critique: The 240-mg comparison does not meet the trial's own significance boundary. Table 2 states the boundary for 240-mg sotorasib-panitumumab versus standard care as 0.03125, and the observed p value is 0.036. The Discussion nonetheless reports that sotorasib at 960 mg or 240 mg resulted in significantly longer progression-free survival, and the dose-comparison argument is built on top of a comparison that formally failed.

At this interim the alpha available for overall survival was 0.0001, so the reported survival hazard ratios (0.77, 95% CI 0.40-1.45 and 0.91, 0.48-1.71) are uninterpretable as evidence either way, and by the same hierarchical plan the response rate - 26.4% versus 0%, the number the abstract leads with - could not be formally tested at all.

Missing tumour assessments are concentrated in the control arm: 11 of 54 (20.4%) standard-care patients were never assessed, against 2 of 53 (3.8%) and 1 of 53 (1.9%) in the sotorasib arms. In an open-label trial whose primary endpoint is centrally reviewed progression, differential early dropout shortens apparent control-arm progression-free survival, and no sensitivity analysis for informative censoring is reported.

Median duration of response in the only arm with responses was 4.4 months (95% CI 3.6 to not reached) and was not estimable in the others. The brevity of the benefit is in Table 2 and absent from the conclusions and abstract.

The trial was powered assuming a hazard ratio of 0.4 for progression or death and observed 0.48 with a 95% CI of 0.30 to 0.78 on roughly 90 events in 160 patients at 7.8 months median follow-up, so the point estimate is the smaller end of what was planned for and the medians rest on short follow-up with few patients at risk beyond six months.

Right-sided primaries were unevenly distributed - 45.3% of the 960-mg arm against 29.6% of the standard-care arm - and sidedness was not a stratification factor, in a disease where it is strongly prognostic and predictive of EGFR-antibody benefit. The paper reports sidedness only as a subgroup of the experimental arm.

No crossover from standard care to sotorasib is described and no post-progression therapy is reported for either arm, which makes the survival endpoint the trial says it will eventually test uninterpretable before it is run.

No patient-reported outcome or quality-of-life result appears anywhere, yet the Discussion argues the response rate matters because of the 'greater potential to relieve tumour-related symptoms' in late-line disease. The claim is made without the data that would support it.

Every stage of the trial ran through the manufacturer of the experimental drug: Amgen designed it, its employees analysed the data and performed the pharmacokinetic and safety analyses, its funded writers produced the first draft, and it took part in the decision to publish. Four authors are Amgen employees. The authors' attestation of data accuracy does not substitute for independent analysis.

Of 219 patients screened, 59 were not randomised and the paper gives no breakdown of why, on top of the prospective central molecular selection that reduces the eligible population to the 3 to 4% of colorectal cancers carrying KRAS G12C, so the trial population is remote from a general clinic and the paper quantifies neither step.

For this depot's purposes the paper contains no local-therapy outcome at all: no resection, ablation or conversion is reported, and the liver-metastasis subgroup hazard ratio of 0.35 (95% CI 0.20-0.61) comes from an unpowered subgroup forest with no multiplicity control, in patients with progression-free survival measured in months.

A linked correspondence (PMID 38986067, Fojo, N Engl J Med 2024;391:186-7) with an authors' reply (PMID 38986068) was identified in PubMed but its text was not available here, so its objections are not reflected in this record.
37870968.n: 160 patients with chemorefractory KRAS G12C-mutated metastatic colorectal cancer randomised 1:1:1 at 76 sites in 12 countries (53 to 960-mg sotorasib plus panitumumab, 53 to 240-mg, 54 to investigator's choice of trifluridine-tipiracil or regorafenib), from 219 screened; 55 of 160 (34.4%) had died at the data cut-off and median follow-up was 7.8 months
37870968.bottom_line: Shows that in chemorefractory KRAS G12C-mutant colorectal cancer, sotorasib 960 mg plus panitumumab roughly doubles centrally reviewed progression-free survival over trifluridine-tipiracil or regorafenib monotherapy (5.6 vs 2.0 months) and produces responses where the control arm produces none, with tolerable and familiar toxicity. It does not show patients live longer: the trial was designed without the power to test survival, spent an alpha of 0.0001 on it, and its authors concede the planned final analysis will not be adequately powered either. The 240-mg comparison missed its own prespecified boundary (p=0.036 against 0.03125) yet is reported as significant, responses lasted a median 4.4 months, and the comparator was already outdated by publication.
37870968.funding: Funded by Amgen, which makes sotorasib. Amgen designed the trial, oversaw data collection, analysed the data through its own statisticians, performed the pharmacokinetic and safety analyses, funded the medical writers who produced the first draft, and was involved in the decision to submit; four co-authors are Amgen employees

limitations: The authors state the sample size does not allow conclusions on survival: the study was sized to establish feasibility and was not powered for oncological benefit
They state that long-term data on biliary sclerosis and on the safety of conversion surgery after pump plus systemic chemotherapy must be awaited, despite a good short-term safety profile
They state that data on conversion-to-resection rates, pathological response and survival are not yet mature
They note that systemic starting doses had to be cut to Memorial Sloan Kettering levels after the first nine patients because of early liver toxicity
They note there is no consensus definition of borderline resectable disease, and that the successor PUMP-IT trial will use a central panel as CAIRO5 did
critique: The endpoint is whether the treatment can be given, not whether it helps, and the threshold was set where it could hardly fail: 70% of patients completing two cycles. Ninety percent did. Nothing follows about conversion, pathological response or survival, and the paper says so.

There is no control arm in a setting where the comparator is unusually well quantified. CAIRO5 achieved complete local treatment in 37% to 58% of initially unresectable patients with systemic therapy alone, and this study reports a disease control rate rather than a conversion rate, so the two cannot be set side by side - although the 9 of 29 patients who reached conversion surgery or its first stage within six months is the figure a reader will want to compare and it is not presented as an endpoint.

Toxicity is heavy and escalates with exposure: 14 of 31 patients (45%) had a grade 3 or worse event in the first two cycles, and grade 3 or worse chemotherapy toxicity reached 19 of 29 (66%) by six months. A feasibility study that meets its threshold while two-thirds of patients sustain severe toxicity has demonstrated deliverability, not tolerability.

The protocol changed partway through. Systemic irinotecan and fluorouracil doses were reduced to Memorial Sloan Kettering levels after the first nine patients because of hepatic injury, so the regimen reported is not the regimen the first third of the cohort received, and the toxicity figures pool both.

Resectability - the variable that defines the population and would define any benefit - was judged by the two participating local multidisciplinary teams, not by a central panel, and the authors concede there is no consensus on what borderline resectable means. CAIRO5, in the same country, found panel surgeons failed to reach consensus in 58% of follow-up assessments.

Response at the primary evaluation was assessed at a median of seven weeks from pump start in 29 patients, with 5 (17%) already progressing; the 83% disease control rate includes 48% stable disease, which in a conversion setting is not an outcome a surgeon can act on.

Mismatch repair-deficient tumours were excluded and prior systemic therapy was allowed only without progression, so the cohort is filtered for chemosensitivity before the regional treatment is added - the same selection that makes single-arm conversion series look favourable.

The surgical burden is reported as medians without a complication-by-procedure breakdown: the primary tumour was resected at the same laparotomy in 22 of 30 patients with primary anastomosis in 19, and grade 3 or worse surgical or device complications occurred in 5 (16%), but which complications followed which combination of procedures is not given.

Absence of hepatic artery thrombosis, bleeding or biliary sclerosis is reported at six months, which is earlier than biliary sclerosis characteristically appears, and the authors acknowledge this; the paper's safety claim therefore does not cover the toxicity that has historically limited the technique.

The device manufacturer supplied the pumps and the study had no other funding, and the proctoring team from the institution whose results the study was designed to reproduce are co-authors - so the evaluation of transferability was conducted with the originators and the device company inside it.

Thirty-one patients at two centres cannot establish that the technique travels; the relevant historical warning, a 26-centre German intra-arterial trial stopped early for complications, is cited in the companion PUMP protocol and the difference here is intensive proctoring, which is itself the thing that limits generalisation.
PubMed indexes this study with a Randomized Controlled Trial publication type, which is incorrect - the study is single-arm - so a reader relying on database metadata will overstate its design.
No linked editorial or comment on this paper was found in PubMed, so no independent published critique informs this record.
38608150.n: 31 patients with liver-only borderline resectable (6) or unresectable (25) colorectal liver metastases enrolled at two Dutch tertiary centres between September 2020 and November 2022; median 13 metastases (IQR 6-23), all bilobar, Fong score 3 or more in 27 of 31, 84% synchronous, primary tumour in situ in 77%. The pump was implanted in 30 of 31, and 29 were evaluable for response
38608150.bottom_line: Shows that hepatic arterial floxuridine with concomitant FOLFOX or FOLFIRI can be delivered outside the United States: pumps were implanted in 30 of 31 patients, 90% completed two combined cycles against a 70% threshold, device complications were 16% and no hepatic artery thrombosis or biliary sclerosis occurred within six months. It establishes nothing about benefit - there is no control arm, the primary endpoint is deliverability, and conversion, pathology and survival data are explicitly immature. The costs it does document are real: 45% grade 3 or worse events in the first two cycles rising to 66% by six months, and a protocol-wide dose reduction after the first nine patients for liver toxicity. It is the feasibility step before the PUMP-IT and EA2222 randomised trials, and should be read as that.
38608150.funding: The research received no specific grant from a funding agency; Tricumed Medizintechnik GmbH provided the pumps for the study. The authors state no conflicts of interest related to the work. The two centres were proctored by the Memorial Sloan Kettering team, three of whose members are co-authors

limitations: The authors name as their primary limitation the inherent bias in subjective surgical decisions about resection feasibility, together with the absence of any centralised assessment of response or of resection

Objective response rate was chosen as a surrogate primary endpoint rather than overall survival, which the authors call the gold standard, and they state it is unclear whether depth of response or time to surgical failure would serve better

Stratified balanced sampling of the technically unresectable subgroup was not done, leaving more patients with over 10 metastases in the triplet arm (41.7% versus 33.8%), which the authors say may explain the longer progression-free survival in the doublet arm
Overall survival was not mature at the primary analysis, so further analysis after survival matures is needed to know whether the deeper response means anything

The comparison of patients who achieved local treatment against those who did not is acknowledged to be subject to survivor bias, since the converted patients had already survived progression-free long enough to reach surgery
The low rate of grade 3 or worse diarrhoea is attributed to an all-Asian cohort in which no triplet-arm patient carried UGT1A1*6 or *28 polymorphisms, alongside a reduced irinotecan dose
The right-sided subgroup contained only 19 patients and the authors call for further prospective trials in that group
critique: The trial was designed assuming response rates of 80% with the triplet against 60% with the doublet, and the observed doublet rate was 79.7%. The control assumption was wrong by 20 absolute points, so the 146-patient sample had no realistic power for the comparison it was built on - and the primary endpoint still failed (p=0.42) against a threshold the authors set at a two-sided alpha of 0.10.

Two different significance thresholds are used in the same paper: p below 0.1 for the primary endpoint and p below 0.05 for secondary endpoints. The only positive finding, depth of response, is a 4.6-point median difference (59.6% versus 55.0%, p=0.039) among several unadjusted secondary comparisons judged at the stricter threshold.

The reported effect estimates run against the reported proportions. Response was 84.7% with the triplet and 79.7% with the doublet, yet the odds ratio is given as 0.70 (95% CI 0.30-1.67); early tumour shrinkage was 80.6% against 77.0% with an odds ratio of 0.82. The reference category is never stated, so neither estimate can be reconciled with its own percentages.

The same inversion affects the survival result: median progression-free survival was 11.8 months with the triplet and 13.4 months with the doublet, reported alongside a hazard ratio of 0.74 (95% CI 0.50-1.11). As printed, the hazard ratio points the opposite way to the medians it accompanies.

Progression-free survival is defined non-standardly: the methods state that successful resection of liver metastases is considered a continuation of progression-free survival. Converting a patient therefore protects that patient's progression-free survival by definition, so the endpoint absorbs the conversion endpoint rather than being independent of it.

Response was assessed every 8 weeks by local investigators and resectability by the local multidisciplinary team, in an unmasked trial, so the team that judged whether the tumour had shrunk is the team that judged whether it could be removed. The authors flag the absence of central review; they do not note that it bears most heavily on their only positive endpoint.

Unresectability could be met by a lesion count alone (five or more metastases), independently of any anatomical criterion. The paper never reports how many patients entered on count rather than on remnant volume or vascular infiltration, so whether conversion was the real question for most of the cohort cannot be checked.

The efficacy and safety denominators differ without explanation: 72 patients are analysed for response in the triplet arm but 68 for toxicity, meaning four randomised patients never received the assigned regimen and are counted in the numerator population of the primary endpoint.

Fourteen patients (9.6%) were lost to follow-up, unevenly (9 doublet, 5 triplet), in a trial of 146 whose survival endpoints are time to event; no sensitivity analysis for informative censoring is reported.

The conclusion recommends cetuximab plus FOLFOX as the first-line regimen for this population, but the trial was designed to detect triplet superiority and failed; nothing in it was designed to show the doublet non-inferior, and survival was immature at the time the recommendation was made.

The locally-treated versus not-treated comparison adjusts for ten clinical variables (age, sex, tumour location, ECOG, primary site, prior adjuvant therapy, time to metastases, number and size of metastases, resectability) in 146 patients, far too few events per covariate, and is additionally confounded by immortal time, which the authors acknowledge without quantifying.

No quality-of-life or patient-reported outcome is reported, although the triplet produced significantly more grade 3 or worse neutropenia (44.1% versus 27.0%) and the paper's recommendation rests partly on toxicity.

Generalisability is restricted in ways the paper applies only to toxicity: the cohort is entirely Chinese, under 70, ECOG 0-1, 87% left-sided and 95% synchronous, with no UGT1A1 polymorphism carriers in the triplet arm and a reduced irinotecan dose of 150 mg/m2. The efficacy conclusion is stated without the same qualification.
No linked editorial or comment on this trial was found in PubMed, so no independent published critique informs this record.
38728364.n: 146 RAS/BRAF wild-type patients with initially unresectable liver-only colorectal metastases enrolled at seven Chinese centres from April 2018 to December 2022 (72 cetuximab plus FOLFOXIRI, 74 cetuximab plus FOLFOX); 142 received at least one course and form the safety population (68 and 74); 87% left-sided, 95% synchronous, aged 18 to 70 with ECOG 0-1; 14 patients (9.6%) were lost to follow-up and median follow-up was 26.2 months
38728364.bottom_line: Shows that adding irinotecan to cetuximab plus FOLFOX in RAS/BRAF wild-type initially unresectable liver-only metastases does not raise response (84.7% versus 79.7%, p=0.42), and that the deeper tumour shrinkage it does produce converts no additional patient to resection (54.2% versus 52.7%) while roughly doubling grade 3 neutropenia. It does not establish that the doublet is the better regimen: the trial was powered only for a 20-point response difference that its own control arm made impossible, its primary comparison simply failed, survival was immature, and response and resectability were both judged locally by the unmasked treating teams. Read with CAIRO5, it is the second trial in this depot in which more shrinkage buys no more surgery.
38728364.funding: National Natural Science Foundation of China (82073302) and Guangdong Basic and Applied Basic Research Foundation (2023B1515020015); the funders are stated to have had no role in design, data collection, analysis, decision to publish or preparation of the manuscript. The authors declare no competing interests. The source of the cetuximab used is not stated

limitations: The authors note heterogeneity in chemotherapy regimens and in immunosuppressive therapy, which followed the policies of local oncologists and hepatologists
Post-transplant chemotherapy was not possible in all patients, mainly because of complications or suboptimal recovery, so its contribution cannot be assessed

They state that patient selection can still be improved, by molecular biology and by detecting microscopic residual disease with circulating tumour DNA, and note that their recurrence rate resembles SECA-II
The restricted mean survival time analysis was performed because the proportional hazards assumption was not met and was not prespecified in the protocol
The required number of deaths was re-estimated during the trial, from 29 to 50, because some patients allocated to transplantation did not receive it

They state the trial's reproducibility depended on strict adherence to eligibility criteria and on guaranteed prioritisation for organ allocation, and argue only that this could conceivably be generalised to other transplant centres
critique: The per-protocol analysis that produces the 73.2% five-year survival is biased in both directions at once. From the transplant arm it removes patients who never reached transplantation, who progressed on the pre-transplant scan, or who waited three months or more after their last chemotherapy - that is, the early failures. From the chemotherapy arm it removes the nine patients who went on to resection or transplantation - that is, the best outcomes. The hazard ratio moves from 0.37 to 0.16 as a result, and the intention-to-treat figure of 56.6% against 12.6% is the only randomised estimate in the paper.

Proportional hazards did not hold, so the hazard ratios that headline the abstract describe an effect that varies over time. The analysis appropriate to that, restricted mean survival time, was not prespecified and gives a far more modest framing: a gain of 12.6 months (95% CI 4.9-20.4) over five years.

The event requirement was revised mid-trial from 29 to 50 deaths after it became clear that allocated patients were not all being transplanted. Changing the information requirement in response to observed protocol deviation preserves nominal power but means the final analysis was not the one designed.

Recurrence and progression were declared equivalent for analysis - recurrence after removal of the entire liver and progression of disease left in place are treated as the same event - and progression-free survival was then analysed only in the per-protocol population, so the endpoint that most favours the intervention is computed in the population that most favours it.

The trial is open label and no independent central review of progression in the chemotherapy arm is described. The central panel's role was to confirm permanent unresectability at diagnosis and after chemotherapy, not to adjudicate the endpoints.

Three different populations are used for three classes of result: intention-to-treat for overall survival, per protocol for progression-free survival, quality of life and postoperative complications, and an as-treated population for safety. The definitions of major protocol deviation sit in an appendix.

Quality of life is described as descriptive only and its data are in an appendix, so the trade-off a patient is being offered - a graft, lifelong immunosuppression, 34% severe morbidity, 8% retransplantation, renal complications in 22%, diabetes in 17%, rejection in 8% - is never set against the survival gain in any quantitative form.

The result is contingent on an organ allocation arrangement rather than on the operation: national organ-sharing organisations agreed to prioritise these patients so that 79% were grafted within two months of their last chemotherapy cycle. Patients with normal liver function have low MELD scores and cannot compete without exception points, and the paper contains no analysis of what the diverted grafts cost other candidates or of how dropout would rise with longer waiting.

Selection was severe and defined the population twice over: the panel rejected 63 of 157 patients, including 13 for equivocal unresectability, so the trial enrolled only patients who were both definitely unresectable and definitely chemotherapy-responsive, aged 65 or under, ECOG 0-1, BRAF wild-type, within three chemotherapy lines, with CEA under 80 or a 50% fall, and all but one with a low Oslo score. Ninety-four patients over five and a half years across twenty centres is under one patient per centre per year.

Protocol deviation was large in both arms and undermines the trial's premise: 11 of 47 allocated to transplantation did not receive it (9 for progression) and 9 of 47 allocated to chemotherapy underwent resection or transplantation. A fifth of patients judged permanently unresectable by a central panel were nonetheless resected or transplanted outside their allocation.

The chemotherapy arm had no protocol regimen, no mandated sequencing and no prescribed later lines, so the comparator is whatever each centre chose, in a trial whose survival difference is attributed to the operation.

The claim of a real potential for cure rests on 42% of transplanted patients being disease free at last follow-up, which counts patients rendered disease free by later lung surgery or ablation; recurrence occurred in 72% of per-protocol recipients and five-year progression-free survival was 19.9%.

Minor internal inconsistencies: per-protocol five-year survival is 73.3% in the Summary and 73.2% in the Results, and first-line targeted therapy in 76 of 94 patients is given as 80% in the Summary and 81% in the Results.

A linked Lancet Comment (PMID 39306454, Heinemann and Stintzing, 'Liver transplantation in metastatic colorectal cancer: a new standard of care?', 2024;404:1078-9) was identified in PubMed but its text was not available here, so its arguments are not reflected in this record.
39306468.n: 94 patients aged 18 to 65 with ECOG 0-1, BRAF wild-type colorectal cancer and permanently unresectable liver-only metastases responding for at least three months on no more than three chemotherapy lines, randomised 1:1 at 20 European centres between February 2016 and July 2021 out of 157 assessed, 63 of whom the central panel excluded; median age 54, median 20 liver metastases at diagnosis, median 21 chemotherapy cycles, and all but one recipient with a low Oslo score at randomisation. 38 of 47 allocated patients were transplanted at a median 50.5 days; the per-protocol populations are 36 and 38; median follow-up 59.3 months
39306468.bottom_line: The only randomised trial of liver transplantation in colorectal liver metastases, and it shows a large survival gain in a tightly defined population: five-year overall survival 56.6% against 12.6% by intention to treat, HR 0.37 (95% CI 0.21-0.65), with 42% of recipients disease free at last follow-up. The 73.2% figure that is usually quoted is per protocol and is inflated from both sides - early failures removed from the transplant arm, the nine resected or transplanted patients removed from the control arm - and proportional hazards did not hold, so the honest effect size is the intention-to-treat curve or the unprespecified 12.6-month gain in restricted mean survival. Reproducing it needs a central panel that rejects 40% of referrals, a national agreement to graft low-MELD patients within two months, and acceptance that three-quarters will recur and be operated on again.

limitations: Early cessation of accrual on the predefined stopping criteria makes it more difficult to draw definitive conclusions on non-inferiority for overall survival, specifically in the under-represented intermediate (n=91) and high (n=21) disease burden subgroups
Whether a subset of patients might have benefited more from surgical resection than from thermal ablation remains unclear

Including patients with both few and many metastases, and allowing resection of non-ablatable lesions and ablation of non-resectable lesions, might have influenced outcomes in some subgroups, potentially obscured by the broad inclusion criteria

The study was not powered to compare ablation approaches (percutaneous 57%, laparoscopic 7%, open 37%) or ablation alone against ablation plus resection (27 patients, 18%), either of which could have influenced overall outcomes
The April 2021 amendment excluding solitary deep-seated metastases requiring major hepatectomy likely reduced the number of eligible candidates and potentially affected outcomes in the control group
Procedures were done in dedicated high-volume centres by experienced operators, so the results cannot be automatically generalised to centres with less experience
Induction chemotherapy, although evenly distributed between groups (20% vs 24%), might have affected oncological outcomes, particularly in comparison with other geographical regions
critique: The trial claims a high likelihood of non-inferiority on a projected conditional power of 90.5% rather than on the data: the observed overall survival HR is 1.05 with a 95% CI of 0.69-1.58, and the upper bound exceeds the prespecified non-inferiority limit of 1.30, so by the trial's own criterion non-inferiority was not demonstrated. The paper nowhere states this.

The conditional power figure is explicitly calculated assuming six more years of recruitment at the observed accrual rate; a projection about a trial that was then stopped is presented in the abstract and Interpretation as the trial's finding.

The two arms were heavily cross-contaminated. Only 90 of 148 control patients (61%) had resection alone and 118 of 148 (80%) ablation alone: 27 ablation-arm patients (18%) also had a lesion resected and 52 resection-arm patients (35%) also had a lesion ablated. What was compared is two mixed local-treatment strategies, not ablation against resection.

Thirty-six percent of ablations were open and only 57% percutaneous, with general anaesthesia in 76% of the ablation arm, so the headline safety and length-of-stay advantages cannot be attributed to the ablation modality itself; the per-approach sensitivity analysis sits in the appendix and the trial admits it was not powered for it.

The superior per-tumour local control (HR 0.09, 95% CI 0.01-0.74) is generated by differential retreatment, not differential tumour control. Raw local progression was almost identical (ablation 18 of 148 patients and 25 of 349 target tumours; resection 21 of 148 and 24 of 304), but 16 of 18 progressing ablation patients were retreated versus 7 of 22 in the resection arm, with 15 resection patients carrying 17 untreated progressed tumours. The endpoint is defined as recurrence not retreated, so it measures how willing clinicians were to re-treat.

Per-tumour analyses treat 349 and 304 tumours as independent observations without any clustering by patient, which overstates precision; the per-tumour local control estimate rests on very few events and has a CI spanning an order of magnitude (0.01-0.74).

Baseline imbalances are tabulated but adjustment was only for centre and disease burden. The ablation arm was less fit (ASA 3 in 46 of 148, 31%, vs 27 of 148, 18%; Charlson intermediate 26, 18%, vs 4, 3%) while the resection arm was more node-positive (N0 in 33, 22%, vs 55, 37%). No multivariable model reconciles the two directions.

Molecular data are missing for most patients (RAS missing in 101 and 97, BRAF in 102 and 97, MSI in 50 and 4), yet the figure 3 forest plot reports RAS, BRAF and MSI subgroup hazard ratios as though the whole cohort contributed.

Figure 3 presents 35 univariate subgroup hazard ratios with no correction for multiplicity, and at least two are internally impossible as printed (male sex 0.14, 95% CI 0.70-1.87; left-sided primary 1.31, 95% CI 1.66-2.60), so the subgroup panel used to claim consistency cannot be checked as published.

The margin comparison sets pathology R1 (<1 mm) against imaging-based A1 (<5 mm) - different thresholds measured by different methods - and uses denominators of 274 resected and 322 ablated tumours rather than the 304 and 349 target tumours randomised, with the missing tumours unexplained.

Of 448 patients assessed, 40 were rejected by the panel, 12 later failed eligibility, 54 declined and 42 were excluded intraoperatively before randomisation; none of these 148 are described, so the trial population is a doubly vetted dual-eligible subset whose relation to the patients a surgeon actually sees is not quantified.

The trial was unmasked and the local tumour progression endpoint rests on local radiology reports, with central review used only to resolve discrepancies or ambiguities, in a trial whose funder makes the ablation devices.

A linked Lancet Oncology Comment on this trial (PMID 39848271, Stoffler and colleagues, 2025;26:149-50) was identified in PubMed but its text was not available here, so any objection it raises is not reflected in this record.
39848272.n: 300 patients randomly assigned (148 thermal ablation, 148 resection after four post-randomisation exclusions for non-colorectal pathology), drawn from 448 assessed by the central review panel and 342 enrolled; 48% of the planned sample size of 618
39848272.bottom_line: Shows that in centrally vetted patients with one to ten colorectal liver metastases of 3 cm or less, thermal ablation carries far less morbidity than resection (adverse events 19% vs 46%, no treatment-related deaths vs three, median stay 1 vs 4 days) with no detectable survival difference at 28.9 months of follow-up. It does not establish non-inferiority of overall survival: accrual stopped at 48% of the planned 618 patients on a projected conditional power of 90.5%, and the observed HR of 1.05 has a 95% CI (0.69-1.58) whose upper bound crosses the 1.30 margin. Because roughly a third of each arm also received the other modality for non-target lesions, what the trial compared is two mixed local-treatment strategies rather than ablation against resection.

limitations: The trial was open label, so biases in reporting of treatment assessments are conceivable; the authors argue the high concordance between blinded central review and investigator assessment of progression-free survival (88% in the combination group and 89% with nivolumab) suggests the design did not affect efficacy assessment
Because of the shorter minimum follow-up at this interim analysis, secondary endpoints including duration of response remain immature
Patient numbers in some prespecified subgroups were low, limiting interpretation
Subgroup analyses of progression-free survival and response by line of treatment would have been of interest but treatment lines remain masked under the hierarchical testing plan
Overall survival data remain masked and will be valuable to contextualise the results
critique: The comparison that would license the headline recommendation was negative. The Outcomes section states that progression-free survival for nivolumab plus ipilimumab versus nivolumab in the first-line setting did not meet the prespecified statistical criteria at this interim analysis and remains masked. The Interpretation, abstract and Discussion nonetheless propose the combination as a potential new standard of care, supported only by the separate comparison against chemotherapy.

Overall survival is withheld under the testing plan, but the paper prints all-cause deaths of 103 of 352 (29%) with the combination against 149 of 351 (42%) with nivolumab in the safety section. The reader is handed a 13-percentage-point difference in deaths as a descriptive line while the analysis of that endpoint is masked.

The alpha against which p=0.0003 is judged was recycled. The 0.05 overall error was split 0.044 to the chemotherapy comparison and 0.006 to this one; once the chemotherapy comparison succeeded, 0.024 was passed across for a total of 0.03, and the group-sequential split between this interim and the final analysis is only in the appendix. The nominal p value in the abstract is not the test that was performed.

The primary efficacy population is 582 of 707 randomised immunotherapy patients (82%), because enrolment used local MSI or mismatch repair testing and 125 (18%) failed central confirmation for microsatellite stability, mismatch repair proficiency or unstated other reasons. A trial that depends on a biomarker enrolled a fifth of its patients without it.

The two populations give very different comparator results and this is not explained. Median progression-free survival in the nivolumab arm is 39.3 months in the centrally confirmed population but 18.4 months in all randomised patients, an 18-month swing, while the combination arm barely moves (not reached vs 54.1 months). The all-randomised analysis is described as consistent; what it actually shows is that the patients central testing excluded did far worse on nivolumab alone.

Sex was unevenly distributed - female 192 of 354 (54%) in the combination arm against 163 of 353 (46%) with nivolumab - and the baseline table is described as similar. The hazard ratio was estimated from a stratified Cox model with randomised group as the single covariate, so no baseline characteristic is adjusted for.

The defence against open-label bias is 88% and 89% concordance between central and investigator reads of the same scans. Concordance between two unmasked assessors does not address the mechanisms that matter in an unblinded trial: when imaging was ordered, when a borderline scan was called progression, and when a patient on single-agent therapy was taken off study.

The toxicity cost of the second drug is substantial and is not formally compared: grade 3-4 treatment-related events 78 of 352 (22%) against 50 of 351 (14%), discontinuation of any drug for treatment-related toxicity 48 (14%) against 21 (6%), and two of the three treatment-related deaths (myocarditis and pneumonitis) in the combination arm. No p value, risk difference or number-needed-to-harm appears for any of these.

The quality-of-life argument is exploratory and non-comparative: scores were assessed only in centrally confirmed treated patients with available questionnaire data, against a within-group 10-point threshold, with no completion rates in the main text. The conclusion that the efficacy gain was 'not at the expense of diminished health-related quality of life' rests on the absence of a within-arm change, not on a between-arm test.

Of 1147 patients assessed, 308 were ineligible and 239 of those 'no longer met study criteria' with no further breakdown, so the step between a patient with MSI-high disease in clinic and a patient in this trial is unquantified.

PD-L1 testing is described in the methods and its results appear nowhere in the main text, alongside the acknowledged under-populated subgroups, so the paper offers no basis for identifying who needs two drugs rather than one.

Duration of response was not reached in either arm and is conceded immature, so the response difference (71% vs 58%) and the progression-free survival difference are both statements about curves that have not yet separated into a durable-benefit claim.

For this depot's purposes the trial reports no local therapy at all: patients had unresectable or metastatic disease, resection and ablation were not endpoints, and nothing here addresses whether an MSI-high liver metastasis responding to checkpoint blockade should then be resected.

39874977.n: 839 patients with locally determined MSI-high or mismatch repair-deficient unresectable or metastatic colorectal cancer randomised at 128 hospitals in 23 countries (354 nivolumab plus ipilimumab, 353 nivolumab, 132 chemotherapy) from 1147 assessed for eligibility; the primary efficacy population is the 582 with centrally confirmed status (296 and 286), and 57% of each immunotherapy group was previously untreated. Median follow-up 47.0 months
39874977.bottom_line: Shows that in MSI-high or mismatch repair-deficient metastatic colorectal cancer, adding ipilimumab to nivolumab lengthens centrally reviewed progression-free survival across all treatment lines (HR 0.62, 95% CI 0.48-0.81) and raises response from 58% to 71%, at the cost of roughly doubled grade 3-4 toxicity and discontinuation. It does not show this holds first line, where the same comparison failed its prespecified boundary at this interim and remains masked, nor that patients live longer, since overall survival is withheld even as the paper prints 29% against 42% deaths. Nothing in it addresses liver-directed treatment, so its bearing on colorectal liver metastases is confined to what to give before any local therapy is considered.

limitations: No limitations section; the paper states design features without conceding any limits. The authors note only that overall survival is an interim analysis at 242 of the 297 events expected for the final analysis, that the encorafenib-cetuximab doublet arm was closed on the basis of an external phase 2 study, that the objective response, time to response and duration of response analyses at this cut-off are descriptive, and that MSI-high or mismatch repair-deficient patients were excluded unless unable to receive checkpoint inhibitors
They state that hypothesis testing was one-sided while two-sided p values and confidence intervals are reported in the manuscript by convention
They acknowledge that the first-line encorafenib-cetuximab doublet gave shorter survival than the chemotherapy triplet and offer it only for patients unable to tolerate chemotherapy
critique: Follow-up is grossly asymmetric between the arms being compared: median follow-up for progression-free survival was 16.8 months with encorafenib-cetuximab plus mFOLFOX6 and 9.8 months with standard care. The control arm's curve is estimated over little more than half the observation time, and no sensitivity analysis addresses the resulting difference in censoring.

The response figures that led to accelerated approval and that the paper repeats (65.7% versus 37.4%) are explicitly descriptive at this cut-off; the formally tested comparison was made at an earlier data cut in a response analysis set of 220 patients. Two different analyses, populations and cut-offs are presented under one endpoint.

The Discussion contradicts its own results on toxicity. It states that grade 3 or higher adverse events occurred in more than half the patients when Table S7 gives 81.5%, and that no substantial increase in chemotherapy dose reduction or discontinuation was needed when the same table gives 59.9% against 54.1% and 20.7% against 17.5%. The claim that the events were largely reversible is made with no supporting data.

Almost everything a reader needs to check is in the supplement: the safety summary, the response table, subsequent therapies, the stratification scheme and the subgroup forests are all Tables S1 to S9, leaving the main text to report conclusions rather than data.

The comparator is investigator's choice between mFOLFOX6, FOLFOXIRI and CAPOX with or without bevacizumab, and the main text reports only the bevacizumab proportion. How many control patients received the most active available regimen, a triplet, is not stated, so whether this is a comparison against best standard care cannot be verified.

Nearly three-quarters of control patients who received any further systemic therapy (100 of 139, 71.9%) went on to a BRAF inhibitor-based regimen. The trial therefore compares giving encorafenib first against giving it later, not against withholding it, and the paper reads the result as showing the importance of first-line encorafenib without analysing what happened to the crossed-over patients.

The encorafenib-cetuximab doublet arm was closed not on its own interim data but on the results of a different phase 2 study (ANCHOR). Its outcomes are then reported alongside the randomised arms and used to recommend the doublet for chemotherapy-intolerant patients, which is a non-randomised comparison between a closed arm and a continuing one.

No patient-reported outcome or quality-of-life result appears anywhere, in a regimen that produced treatment-emergent adverse events in 100% of patients, grade 3-4 events in 81.5%, dose reduction in 65.5% and permanent discontinuation in 26.7%. The trade-off the regimen demands is therefore not measurable from this report.

BRAF V600E status could be established by local testing on tissue or blood or by the central laboratory, with no concordance data between methods reported, in a trial whose entire population is defined by that result.
Eligibility was open from age 16 where locally permitted, and no separate accounting of adolescent patients, their dosing or their outcomes appears.

For this depot's purposes the trial contains no liver-directed endpoint at all: resection, conversion and ablation are neither protocol interventions nor outcomes, despite liver metastases in roughly two-thirds of patients, and the liver-metastasis subgroup appears only as one line of a forest plot. Whether a BRAF V600E liver metastasis responding to this regimen should then be resected is untouched.

The manufacturers of both targeted drugs are inside the trial - Pfizer as sponsor for encorafenib and Merck KGaA supporting it for cetuximab - and the sponsor funded the medical writing. The paper does not state who collected, held or analysed the data.
No linked editorial or comment on this trial was found in PubMed, so no independent published critique informs this record.
40444708.n: 637 patients with previously untreated BRAF V600E-mutant metastatic colorectal cancer randomised in the phase 3 portion across 28 countries between November 2021 and December 2023: 158 to encorafenib-cetuximab, 236 to encorafenib-cetuximab plus mFOLFOX6 and 243 to investigator's choice chemotherapy, of whom 197 (81.1%) also received bevacizumab. Liver metastases were present in 62.3% and 65.8% of the two main arms. At the January 2025 cut-off 242 deaths had occurred, 81.5% of the 297 expected at final analysis
40444708.bottom_line: Establishes that first-line encorafenib and cetuximab added to mFOLFOX6 roughly doubles median survival in BRAF V600E-mutant metastatic colorectal cancer, from 15.1 to 30.3 months (HR 0.49, 95% CI 0.375-0.632), with progression-free survival of 12.8 against 7.1 months and response in two-thirds of patients - bringing this subtype's prognosis close to BRAF wild-type disease. It does not establish what it costs or how it should be sequenced: survival is an interim result, control-arm follow-up is nearly seven months shorter, 72% of control patients later received a BRAF inhibitor anyway, and a regimen causing grade 3-4 toxicity in 81.5% of patients is reported without a single patient-reported outcome. Nothing in it speaks to resection, so for a liver surgeon it changes the systemic plan and the expected prognosis, not the operative decision.
