Medical writing support was provided by Nucleus Global and funded by Pfizer

limitations: No limitations are stated anywhere in the paper. The only concession is the recommendation itself that adjuvant therapy after resection may improve disease-free survival but lacks overall survival evidence and should be used with caution (Grade III, Class 2B)
The authors state that the 2017 consensus could no longer meet clinical needs and that this edition summarises the latest domestic and international progress and gathers expert opinion
They state that the full-length consensus, the evidence categories and the recommendation grade definitions are all in an online supplement rather than in the published article
critique: No consensus methodology is described at all: no panel composition beyond the author list, no Delphi or voting process, no agreement threshold, no literature search, no dates, no inclusion criteria and no record of disagreement. A document of 31 graded recommendations gives the reader no way to know how any of them was arrived at.

The evidence base cannot be audited from the published paper. The full text, the grade definitions and the supplementary tables are all deferred to an online supplement, so every Grade and Class in the four published pages is an unverifiable label.

Grading uses the Chinese Society of Clinical Oncology recommendation grade and evidence class rather than GRADE, so the grades cannot be set beside the ESMO, ASCO or NCCN statements a tumour board reads alongside them; a Class 2B here is not a GRADE low-quality recommendation.

The most prescriptive surgical steers carry the weakest grades. Preferring simultaneous resection for synchronous disease and requiring intraoperative ultrasound in every surgical patient are both Grade III, Class 2B - that is, expert opinion - and the randomised and registry evidence on the timing of colorectal and liver resection, including the higher mortality of combined major hepatectomy, is not reconciled anywhere.

Liver transplantation for unresectable colorectal liver metastases is absent entirely, in a 2025 document published after TransMet, so the question of what to do with a patient whose disease is permanently unresectable but confined to the liver has no answer here.

The technical thresholds a hepatobiliary surgeon needs are unspecified: adequate residual liver volume is never defined, and two-stage hepatectomy, portal vein embolisation and ALPPS receive no criteria, no volume target and no recommendation.

Advising caution about adjuvant therapy after resection (Grade III, Class 2B) while recommending neoadjuvant chemotherapy for four or more metastases or a clinical risk score above 2 (Grade II, Class 1B) leaves the perioperative question unresolved: regimen, total duration, and the choice between perioperative and postoperative delivery are not addressed, and EORTC 40983 - the only adequately powered trial in the question - is not reconciled with either recommendation.

Molecular testing is recommended across five tiers down to POLE/POLD1, tumour mutational burden and PD-L1 at Grade III, Class 2B, with no statement of what action follows a positive result at the weaker tiers, so the testing recommendations outrun the treatment recommendations.

The headline local-therapy recommendations are given without the data that would let a reader weigh them: chemoembolisation and hepatic infusion chemotherapy are recommended after systemic failure at Grade I, Class 2A, and the combination of interventional and systemic therapy is said to beat either alone, with no effect size, no trial cited in the published text and no mention that the randomised radioembolization trials were negative for survival.

Stereotactic radiotherapy is recommended for selected patients at Grade II, Class 2A with no dose, no lesion size limit and no acknowledgement that randomised evidence in colorectal liver metastases does not exist.

The surgical benchmark offered - 48.2% five-year survival after resection of primary and metastases - is the authors' own institutional figure from a single reference, used to frame a national consensus.
No patient representative, methodologist or statistician is identified among the authors or the 23 acknowledged reviewers, there is no plan or date for updating, and no external review is described.
The title says 2024 edition while the article was published online on 10 July 2025, so the evidence cut-off is unstated and at least a year behind the publication date.
No linked editorial or comment on this consensus was found in PubMed, so no independent published critique informs this record.
40640089.bottom_line: Sets out, in four pages, what a Chinese multidisciplinary consensus panel recommends across the whole colorectal liver metastasis pathway, organised usefully around whether no evidence of disease is achievable, potentially achievable or not - with liver MRI before any local treatment, universal molecular testing, and locoregional therapy after systemic failure. It is not an auditable guideline: no consensus method, search strategy or agreement threshold is described, the evidence base and the grade definitions are held in an online supplement, and the grading system does not map onto the Western guidelines a tumour board reads alongside it. For a liver surgeon the gaps matter most: no definition of an adequate remnant, no criteria for staged hepatectomy or ALPPS, and no mention of transplantation at all.
40640089.funding: No funding statement appears. Conflicts of interest are declared as 'None' for all authors. The consensus was issued by five branches of the China International Exchange and Promotive Association for Medical and Health Care and led from the Chinese Academy of Medical Sciences Cancer Hospital, with 23 further professors acknowledged as content reviewers

limitations: The guideline states that recommendations rest on current scientific evidence and the authors' collective expert opinion, and that the relevant literature was selected by the expert authors - there was no systematic review
It states that statements without grading were considered justified standard clinical practice by the authors
ESCAT scores were defined by the authors themselves, assisted where needed by the ESMO Precision Oncology Task Force

ESMO-MCBS scores are stated to be correct only at the time of publication, with readers directed to online scorecards for current values, and regulatory approval status is reported as at the time of writing
The evidence and reasoning behind the epidemiology, pathology, staging, locoregional treatment and follow-up sections are held in online supplementary material rather than in the article
critique: The reasoning behind the recommendations most relevant to a liver surgeon cannot be checked from the paper. Oligometastatic disease, locoregional treatment of metastatic sites and liver transplantation are each handled in two or three sentences with the substance deferred to Supplementary Material Section 4, so the published text gives the conclusions without the evidence.

The transplantation criteria are looser than the surgical community's on exactly the two points that are contested. ESMO accepts sustained disease control of more than three months up to third line; the IHPBA consensus requires six months of response and at least a year from diagnosis of unresectable disease. ESMO sets no MSI or mismatch repair exclusion and no PET tumour-volume ceiling, both of which IHPBA makes absolute.

The [II, A] transplantation recommendation rests essentially on one randomised trial whose result depended on a negotiated national agreement to graft low-MELD patients within two months of chemotherapy. The guideline notes that organ policy prioritisation must be met and says nothing about what to do in systems that grant no exception points, which is the operative barrier everywhere outside the trial's countries.

Recommending thermal ablation over liver resection for metastases under 3 cm [II, B] is stated without qualification for lesion position, proximity to vessels or biliary structures, achievable margin, or the ability to repeat treatment - the variables that COLLISION's own data show determine whether ablation works, and in a trial whose arms were a third contaminated with the other modality.

Hepatic arterial infusion is grouped with chemoembolisation and radioembolisation as [III, C] intensification or salvage in liver-dominant disease. That lumps a technique with randomised adjuvant data after complete resection together with two that failed to show survival benefit in randomised trials, and leaves no route to adjuvant hepatic arterial infusion at all.

The guideline tells the reader that prognostic scores must not be used to withhold curative-intent strategies, then lists the same factors - number of organs, number of lesions, prognostic scores, time to metastases, BRAF and mismatch repair status, CEA, nodal status - as the [IV, B] basis for deciding who gets upfront local treatment. The instruction and the algorithm pull in opposite directions and the resolution is left to the multidisciplinary team.

Resectability assessment is mandated at baseline, every two to three months and again in later lines [IV, A], but no definition of resectability or of an adequate future liver remnant is given, and the CAIRO5 experience - panel surgeons failing to reach consensus in 58% of follow-up assessments - shows that an unqualified instruction to reassess does not produce a reproducible answer.

Several recommended regimens are approved by the FDA but not the EMA at the time of writing, so a European reader following the guideline is directed to treatments unavailable to them, and the guideline reports the status rather than reconciling it.

Grades cannot be read across to other guidelines. ESMO's level-of-evidence and grade-of-recommendation system is defined only in a supplementary table, and a reader comparing this document with ASCO's GRADE-based statement or the IHPBA consensus has no mapping between them.

No patient representative, methodologist or statistician is identified among the authors, no external review beyond the ESMO Guidelines Committee is described, and no fixed update interval is given - updating is deferred to the website's Express Update and Living Guideline mechanism.
The disclosure burden is extensive and the guideline's own method is expert selection of literature by those same authors, which is the combination that guideline methodology exists to constrain.
No linked editorial or comment on this guideline was found in PubMed, so no independent published critique informs this record.
41990853.bottom_line: The current European statement of what to do across the whole metastatic colorectal cancer pathway, and the first major guideline to recommend liver transplantation as a curative-intent option for highly selected permanently unresectable liver-only disease [II, A], alongside thermal ablation over resection for lesions under 3 cm [II, B], repeated resectability assessment every two to three months, and a fully molecular first-line algorithm. It is an expert-opinion document, not a systematic one: the authors selected the literature themselves, the evidence behind the locoregional and transplantation sections sits in supplementary material, and the transplant filter is materially looser than the IHPBA consensus on response duration, MSI status and PET tumour volume. It also offers no definition of resectability or of an adequate remnant, and no route to adjuvant hepatic arterial infusion.
41990853.funding: No external funding was received; production costs were covered by ESMO from central funds, and ESMO funded the medical writing and editing support provided by its own staff and by Kstorfin Medical Communications. The disclosure section runs to several pages of advisory board, speaker, expert testimony and institutional research funding relationships with the manufacturers of nearly every drug recommended, including Amgen, Merck, Merck Serono, MSD, Roche/Genentech, Bristol Myers Squibb, Pierre Fabre, Servier, Bayer, Takeda, Pfizer and Revolution Medicines

limitations: The authors list a limited sample size (n=25), a single-centre design and the potential selection bias inherent in non-randomised cohorts, and name extended follow-up as the study's strength
They state that relapse-free survival is not a valid metric for evaluating the efficacy of transplantation in this disease

They report that 22% of SECA-I and 16% of SECA-II patients died of recurrent disease more than five years after transplantation, and conclude that 10-year rather than 5-year survival is the more appropriate measure

They state that one patient was transplanted despite progressive disease, after an outside CT scan whose result was unknown to the centre, and that one patient died of hepatic artery thrombosis about four weeks after transplantation

They concede that if borderline resectable patients were also considered, a negative impact on the transplant waiting list is to be expected, and that broader criteria would oblige most programmes to rely on living donation or extended-criteria grafts
They note that full inclusion and exclusion criteria and the immunosuppression protocol are not restated here but referenced to the SECA-I publication
critique: The cure estimate, which is the paper's novel claim, is a post hoc patient-by-patient judgement with no prespecified definition, and the paper gives three different answers: a maximum of 15 of 25 in the abstract, up to 13 of 25 in the discussion, and about 50% in the conclusion. A reader cannot tell which patients were counted or on what rule.

Forty-eight percent of patients relapsed, all within 24.3 months, with median relapse-free survival of 24.3 months. The response - that relapse-free survival is not a valid metric here - converts the study's central negative finding into a methodological assertion, in the same paper that claims half the cohort was cured.

The cure claim and the relapse data sit uneasily together: of the twelve who relapsed, nine had surgery as first treatment and two are counted as having no evidence of disease 36.1 and 93.4 months after pulmonary metastasectomy. Patients rendered disease free by a second operation are being counted towards the curative potential of the first.

Survival is reported from transplantation with no intention-to-treat analysis from listing, so patients who were accepted and never transplanted - the group that in the companion 72-patient report took five-year survival from 50.4% to 42.6% - are invisible here.

Selection was so tight that the cohort contains one patient each with an ascending-colon primary, a pN2 primary and progressive disease at transplant, two with metabolic tumour volume above 70 cm3 and two KRAS mutants. The 78% five-year survival therefore describes a population assembled to exclude every known adverse factor, and the paper's own simulation puts that population at 2 to 3 patients per year per 5.5 million people.

The prognostic rules the paper hands forward - exclude ascending-colon primary, pN2 primary, or KRAS and TP53 co-mutation unless observed beyond 24 months, and require an Oslo score of 2 or less - are derived from this group's own earlier reports on overlapping patients and are now applied to a cohort of 25 containing one patient in each of those categories. Nothing here tests them.

No confidence interval accompanies the five- or ten-year survival percentages, and the median overall survival interval is very wide (128.2 months, 95% CI 74.8-181.6), which is the honest measure of what 25 patients support.

There is no control arm in this report. Benefit is argued by comparison with TransMet's chemotherapy arm, with the group's own historical cohorts, and with published hepatocellular carcinoma transplant survival - all cross-study comparisons between differently selected populations.

The baseline tables exclude the patient who died of postoperative complications, so the denominator shifts between 25 for survival and 24 for every characteristic, and a 4% operative mortality in patients whose own livers worked is reported without being set against the benefit.

Graft outcomes beyond the fatal hepatic artery thrombosis are not reported: no rejection rate, no immunosuppression exposure, no late graft function, no second malignancies, in a cohort followed for a median of eight years on immunosuppression.

No quality-of-life or patient-reported outcome is measured; quality of life and cost-effectiveness are cited from the group's earlier publications, and the health-economic argument is reduced to a threshold (acceptable if mean survival exceeds three years) taken from one reference.

The allocation argument rests on assertions about a single national programme: one centre performing about 100 transplants a year, so adding a few patients will not materially affect the waitlist, extended to the claim that the indication is probably manageable in a wider range of programmes internationally.

The willingness-to-donate figure invoked to support living donation - that most next of kin would donate the left lateral sector for an expected life extension of 12 months or less - is cited from a separate survey and is used to justify exposing healthy donors in an indication where half the patients relapse.
No linked editorial or comment was found in PubMed, which is unsurprising for a very recent publication, so no independent published critique informs this record.
42572136.n: 25 consecutive patients transplanted for non-resectable liver-only colorectal metastases at Oslo University Hospital between April 2012 and November 2023 in SECA-II (24 synchronous in arm C, one metachronous in arm B), none given adjuvant chemotherapy; median 5 lesions (range 1-47), tumour burden score 7.7, Oslo score 1 (0-2), Fong score 2, all with CEA below 33 ug/L and largest lesion under 5.5 cm, only 2 of 24 with metabolic tumour volume above 70 cm3. Median time from diagnosis to transplant 23.3 months; follow-up closed 1 January 2025 with median follow-up of survivors 97.2 months, 14 patients past 5 years and 6 past 10
42572136.bottom_line: The most mature single-arm transplant data available: 25 stringently selected patients with median overall survival of 128.2 months, 78% at five years and 52% at ten, with half the cohort relapse-free beyond four years and one operative death. It does not establish a cure rate: the cure count is a retrospective case-by-case judgement reported as 15, 13 and about 50% in three places in the same paper, 48% relapsed within two years, and patients re-rendered disease free by lung metastasectomy are counted towards the transplant's curative potential. The selection that produced the result - CEA under 33, every lesion under 5.5 cm, almost nobody with an adverse prognostic factor - identifies, by the authors' own simulation, two or three patients a year in five and a half million.
